Dr. Kern is inclined to look upon 427 <term>Saka</term><note>The Saka era, an ancient Indian calendar system beginning in 78 AD; thus 427 Saka is 505 AD.</note> as marking the year of the birth of Varāha Mihira who, as appears from a passage quoted by Bhāu Dājī, died in Saka 509 <note>587 AD</note>.

All these views clearly have no further foundation than the passage of the Pañchasiddhāntikā about the calculation of the <term>ahargaṇa</term><note>The number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note>. The view that 427 Saka is the year of Varāha Mihira’s birth we may set aside without hesitation. Dr. Kern was led to that hypothesis partly by the consideration that the Pañchasiddhāntikā, which in one place refers to Āryabhaṭa’s views, could hardly have been composed in 505 A.D. when Āryabhaṭa—born in 476 A.D.—was only 29 years old. We now know—from Dr. Kern’s edition of the <term>Āryabhaṭīya</term><note>The seminal astronomical work of Āryabhaṭa.</note>—that Āryabhaṭa composed his work in 499 A.D. already, so that he might very well have been quoted in a book written <insert>written</insert> <note>Correcting the original typo "writtten."</note> in 505 A.D. The other argument brought forward by Dr. Kern, namely that Varāha Mihira died in 587, certainly goes some way to prove that the Pañchasiddhāntikā was not written in 505, but not that Varāha Mihira was born in the latter year. The text of the Pañchasiddhāntikā enables us at present to judge of the position of Varāha Mihira with regard to the date 427 Saka. From the chapters on the <term>Sūrya Siddhānta</term><note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most influential Indian astronomical texts.</note> it appears that Varāha Mihira considers that year to be the epoch of his <term>karaṇagrantha</term><note>A practical astronomical manual used for quick calculations.</note> from which all astronomical calculations have to start; for all the <term>kshepa</term><note>Additive constants or corrections used in astronomical formulas.</note> quantities involved in the different rules, given in those chapters for finding the mean places of sun, moon, and planets, can be accounted for satisfactorily on that basis. I have no doubt that also the kshepa quantities stated in the Romaka and <term>Pauliśa</term><note>The Pauliśa Siddhānta, another of the five systems, often associated with Hellenistic influence.</note> Chapters admit of being explained on the same supposition, but unfortunately we have so far not succeeded in finding the clue to their right understanding. Now it would certainly be most satisfactory, if we could assume that the Pañchasiddhāntikā was composed in the very year which it selects for its astronomical epoch, or at any rate within a few years of that year; for as nearness of the epoch tends to facilitate all astronomical calculations and, at the same time, to minimize the inaccuracies resulting from the fact that karaṇa rules are often only approximatively correct, it is the interest and the practice of karaṇa writers to choose for their epoch a year, as little remote as may be from the time of the composition of their treatises. The positive statement, however, made by Āmarāja (as quoted by Bhāu Dājī) about the date of Varāha Mihira’s death does not favour such an assumption; and we moreover find that the deduction of 427 forms part of a rule which in the end is said to be ‘in’ or ‘according to’ the Romaka Siddhānta. # INTRODUCTION.

The last circumstance indeed, taken by itself, would not suffice fully to convince me, that the date 427 Śaka <note>The Śaka era begins in 78 A.D.; thus 427 Śaka corresponds to 505 A.D.</note> is not one of Varâha Mihira’s own choosing; for the phrase ‘according to the Romaka Siddhânta’ might only mean that the general principles on which the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The count of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note> is calculated (*viz.* the equations between solar years and lunar months, and again between civil days and lunar days) are taken from the *Romaka Siddhânta*, while at the same time the fixation of the initial epoch—a point comparatively unessential and moreover specially requiring to be settled anew in the case of each new <term>Karaṇa</term> <note>A concise astronomical treatise or handbook used for practical calculations.</note>—might be due to Varâha Mihira. But as, after all, 427 Śaka cannot, for the reason stated above, be the date of the composition of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ*, we may admit that the whole rule about the <term>ahargaṇa</term>, inclusive of the <term>kshepa</term> <note>An additive constant or "interpolation" used to adjust calculations to a specific starting point.</note> quantity 427, was borrowed by Varâha Mihira from the *Romaka Siddhânta*, as was assumed by Bhâu Dâjî already. It is true that we are unable to assign a sufficient reason for Varâha Mihira’s choosing to take over the epoch of one of his *Siddhântas* <note>Scientific astronomical treatises.</note> rather than to fix his own, which would have been a comparatively easy matter. There may have been special circumstances rendering the year 427 Śaka a more convenient starting point than a later year; but I am not for the present able to point out any such.

For the time of the composition of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* itself there would thus remain the period between 505 and 587 A. D., so that we shall probably be not far wrong in fixing it about the middle of the sixth century.

A further question, however, arises in connexion with the date 427 Śaka. Admitting that it was taken over by Varâha Mihira from the (or a) *Romaka Siddhânta*, have we to understand thereby the original Romaka,\* and consequently to fix the date of that work as late as 505 A. D? This question is one of interest in itself, and moreover has a bearing on the more general question as to the period to which we have to assign the beginnings of the modern, scientific, phase of Hindû astronomy.

For reasons, which I shall set forth after having finished the survey of the contents of the five *Siddhântas*, I consider it altogether improbable that any of those treatises should have originated so late as 505 A. D., *i. e.*, not earlier than, let us say, forty or fifty years before the composition of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ*. Meanwhile I wish to direct attention to a special circumstance which seems to favour the conclusion, that the original *Romaka Siddhânta* at any rate was composed earlier than the date mentioned.

From the third stanza of the first chapter it appears that already before the composition of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* the *Romaka Siddhânta* had

been commented upon (<term>vyākhyāta<note>original: "vyâkhyâta"; a Sanskrit term meaning explained, interpreted, or commented upon</note></term>) in some way or other by Lāṭadeva. Now it is not of course impossible that Lāṭadeva’s commentary (<term>vyākhyāna<note>original: "vyâkhyâna"; an explanatory work or exposition</note></term>) was merely an ordinary explanatory commentary, composed at some time or other in the period intervening between A.D. 505 (supposing this to have been the date of the original *Romaka*) and the year (let us say about 550) in which the *Five Astronomical Treatises* (<term>Pañchasiddhāntikā<note>The major work by Varāha Mihira which summarizes five earlier astronomical systems</note></term>) was written. Another alternative, however, appears to me the more probable one, for the following reason. I do not consider it likely that Varāha Mihira should have mentioned Lāṭadeva at all in connection with the *Romaka*, had he been nothing more than an ordinary commentator of that work. The fact that he does so mention him seems rather to indicate that Lāṭadeva occupied a somewhat more independent position with regard to the *Romaka*, possibly that of a writer who recasts an earlier work, or adapts it to a later epoch. That Lāṭadeva was more than a mere scholar (<term>scholiast<note>A commentator on ancient texts</note></term>), appears, moreover, from the fact that Brahmagupta refers to him as an astronomical writer, and, what is particularly important, that Varāha Mihira himself, in XV. 18, thinks it worth while to quote the opinion of Lāṭa (of whose identity with the Lāṭadeva of the first chapter I see no reason to doubt) concerning the time of the day from which the count of days (<term>ahargaṇa<note>original: "ahargaṇa"; literally 'heap of days,' the number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a given date</note></term>) has to be calculated. And the details given in this last quotation lead us a step further. It is there said that according to Lāṭa’s view the beginning of the astronomical day has to be reckoned from the moment when the sun has half set at the City of the Greeks (<term>Yavanapura<note>original: "Yavanapura"; likely referring to Alexandria or a similar western Greek-influenced city used as a prime meridian</note></term>). Now this very same view, which here is mentioned as peculiar to Lāṭa and as such contrasted with the diverging views of other astronomical writers on the same subject, is found incorporated in the rule (I. 8) which professes to teach how the count of days has to be calculated according to the *Romaka Siddhānta*. That rule we therefore are entitled to look upon not as directly borrowed by Varāha Mihira from the old original *Romaka Siddhānta*, but rather as constructed by Lāṭa on the elements of that work in such a form as to answer the requirements of his time, and transferred, by Varāha Mihira, from Lāṭa’s work to the *Pañchasiddhāntikā*. Hence the date 427 of the Era of the Scythians (<term>Śaka<note>original: "Śaka"; an era beginning in 78 A.D., making the date 505 A.D.</note></term>) also has to be taken, not as the date of the original *Romaka Siddhānta*, but rather as the date of Lāṭa or, more definitely, as the date which Lāṭa, in his comment on—or adaptation of—the *Romaka* chose for his epoch. How much older the original *Romaka Siddhānta* may have been, is a point which we will touch on below.

Concerning the special character of Lāṭa’s work we may conjecture that it stood to the *Romaka Siddhānta* in somewhat the same relation as practical manuals (<term>Karaṇas<note>original: "Karaṇas"; concise astronomical handbooks used for calculations</note></term>) generally stand to comprehensive treatises (<term>Siddhāntas<note>original: "Siddhântas"; established systems or fundamental astronomical treatises</note></term>). In conclusion I point out that some connection between Lāṭa and the *Romaka Siddhānta* seems to follow also from the statement made by Brahmagupta in the passage quoted above.

<page-num>XXXII</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

at length *namely* that Śrîsheṇa took the elements of the mean motions of the planets from Lâṭa. For unless Lâṭa himself had taken these elements from the Romaka <note>The "Romaka" refers to a system influenced by Roman or Alexandrian Greek astronomy</note>, there would appear no reason whatever why the work of Śrîsheṇa, who according to Brahmagupta had borrowed all other elements from other sources, should have been called a ‘Romaka’ <term>Siddhânta</term> <note>Siddhânta: A comprehensive astronomical treatise or "established tenet"</note>. We can, on the other hand, understand that a Hindu astronomical work should adopt the name of that Siddhânta with which it agreed in the rules for calculating the mean motions of the planets; for the latter constitute the most characteristic item by which a Siddhânta distinguishes itself from other works of the same class.

<margin>Pauliśa Siddhânta.</margin>
The Pauliśa Siddhânta <note>Named after "Pauliśa," often identified by scholars as Paul of Alexandria</note> next calls for a short review.

The fundamental information about this Siddhânta *namely* that concerning the formation of the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>ahargaṇa: The "heap of days," or the total number of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a specific date</note> is contained in stanzas 11-13 of the first chapter which unfortunately appear in the *Manuscripts* in so corrupt a form that we are unable satisfactorily to explain the details. The leading principles of the calculation may however be discerned, all the more readily as they seem not to present any altogether new feature. The number 976 (<gloss>seasons—seven—nine—divided</gloss> <note>original: "ritu—sapta—nava—bhaktâḥ"</note>) which in stanza 11 is exhibited as a divisor, no doubt indicates the number of solar days after the lapse of which a lunar month has to be intercalated, and the 63 of the same stanza (<gloss>three—seasons</gloss> <note>original: "tri—ritu"</note>) seems to refer to the number of lunar days going to one <term>avama</term> or omitted lunar day. The two next stanzas then most probably state the corrections which the employment of the stated round numbers renders it necessary subsequently to apply; the amount and mode of those corrections we are however unable to extract from the incorrect text.—The Pauliśa Siddhânta, thus, in order to find the total of civil days, which have elapsed from a certain epoch up to a given date, takes the usual steps through <term>adhimâsas</term> <note>adhimâsas: Intercalary or "extra" months added to align the lunar and solar years</note> and <term>avamarâtras</term> (<term>tithipralayas</term>) <note>avamarâtras/tithipralayas: "Omitted days" in the lunar calendar to account for the fact that a lunar day (tithi) is shorter than a solar day</note>, does not, however, base its calculation on any cyclic period comprehending integral numbers of years, lunar months and omitted lunar days; but reaches its aim in a more direct manner by establishing small aggregates of days which approximately contain one intercalary month or one omitted lunar day, and subsequently applying an appropriate correction.

Our imperfect understanding of the details of the text prevents us from deriving from the two stanzas discussed the exact length of the year and the month according to the Pauliśa Siddhânta. The length of the year, however, follows from another passage *namely* III. 1. which teaches how to find the sun’s mean place, and bases on the assumption of a year of 365 days, 6 hours, and 12 minutes.

The rule for finding the place of the moon, given in the former part

of the second chapter,* is of a nature widely differing from the corresponding rules exhibited by the best known **Siddhântas** <note>Siddhântas are traditional Indian astronomical treatises</note>. It therefore puzzled us for a very long time—all the more as the text the two Manuscripts exhibit is just in that place far from correct—, until light fell on it from a somewhat unexpected quarter. If we indeed had noticed from the outset that the divisor 3031 mentioned in stanza 2 is the same as the one which the **Romaka Siddhânta** (viii. 5.) employs for finding the place of the moon's **kendra** <note>kendra: the anomaly or angular distance from a planet's furthest point (apogee)</note>, we might have penetrated more quickly to the sense of the rule given in the **Paulíśa Siddhânta**; but that circumstance escaped our attention at the time, and the first clue to the solution of the difficulty was actually supplied by the observation that the contents of the earlier part of chapter II. of the **Pañchasiddhântikâ** show clear analogies to the methods employed, according to Warren and Bailly, by the astronomers of certain parts of southern India for the purpose of finding the mean and true places of sun and moon. According to Warren (**Kâla Saṅkalita** pp. 118 ff.) the astronomers of all those regions of the Deccan where the Tamil language is spoken make use, for calculating the longitudes of sun and moon, of a peculiar process called by him the solar or **Vakiam** <note>Vakiam: from the Sanskrit 'Vakya', meaning 'sentence' or 'mnemonic phrase' used to remember astronomical tables</note> process, whose characteristic feature is that it enables us to find the true places without having previously ascertained the mean ones. This is accomplished (if we limit ourselves in what follows to the processes concerning the moon which alone are analogous to those employed in the **Paulíśa Siddhânta**) by directly calculating how many times within a given <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>ahargaṇa: the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date</note> the moon has returned to her apogee or perigee, rejecting the days within which complete revolutions have been performed, and taking the true motion for the remaining days. To that end there are established periods, comprising integral numbers of days, within which the moon performs a certain number of anomalistic revolutions, and by these periods the given *ahargaṇa* is divided in succession; the quotients may then be rejected each time, and only the last remainder taken into account for finding the moon's place. These periods are four in number, called† **Vedam**, **Rasa Gherica**, **Calanilam**, and **Devaram**. The **Devaram** consists of 248 days which comprise 9 complete anomalistic revolutions of the moon; the **Calanilam** comprises 3031 days = 110 revolutions; the **Rasa Gherica** comprises 12372 days = 441 revolutions; the **Vedam** again is a certain multiple of the **Rasa Gherica** and comprises 1,600,984 days. The given *ahargaṇa* is at first divided by 12,372; again the remainder by 3,031; and again the remainder by 248.

<page-num>XXXIV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

The remainder of this last division—called by Warren <note>John Warren, author of the 'Kala Sankalita' (1825), a key work on Indian time-keeping</note> *Chandra Vakiam Dhurmavahanam* <note>Sanskrit: 'Moon-sentences' or lunar mnemonic tables</note>—is then used as the argument of a table which gives the moon’s true place and true motion for each day of a period of 248 days (equal to 9 anomalistic revolutions <note>The time it takes the moon to go from its closest point to Earth and back again</note>).——If, on the other hand, the moon’s mean place is required, use is made of certain constant quantities indicating the amount of the moon’s mean motion during each of the periods stated above, to which there is finally added the moon’s mean motion during the days indicated by the last remainder. For one *devaram* <term>for instance</term>, the moon’s mean motion, according to the Telugu Astronomers, amounts to 27° 44' 6" (entire revolutions being rejected); during one <term>Calanilam</term> <note>A specific astronomical cycle used in South Indian calculations</note> to 11 signs 7° 31' 1", and so on.

Now the rules given in the beginning of the second chapter of the *<term>Pañchasiddhāntikā</term>* <note>A 6th-century astronomical treatise by Varāhamihira</note> are analogous to those of the Telugu Astronomers. The periods employed there for calculating the moon’s place are two in number; one called *<term>ghana</term>* and comprising 3031 days, which is identical with the *<term>Calanilam</term>* of the Telugus; and another called *<term>gati</term>*, which consists of 248 ninths of a day, and thus represents one anomalistic month. No reference appears to be made to longer periods such as the *<term>Vedam</term>* and the *<term>Rasa Gherica</term>* of the Telugus; periods of the latter kind are indeed not required for the purposes of a *<term>Karaṇa</term>* <note>A concise astronomical handbook used for practical calculations</note> whose rules are meant to be applied only to comparatively small *<term>ahargaṇas</term>* <note>The number of elapsed days since a specific epoch</note>. If then we retrench from a given number of days all the entire *<term>ghanas</term>* contained in it, and again retrench from the remainder all the entire *<term>gatis</term>* which it comprehends, the last remainder alone is required for calculating the moon’s true place; for it indicates what fraction of the current anomalistic revolution the moon has performed, and a simple rule, or table-will then suffice to show the amount of equation of the centre <note>The correction needed to account for the moon's elliptical, rather than circular, orbit</note> which has to be added to—or subtracted from—the moon’s mean longitude in order to render it true. Another set of rules is, however, required for enabling us to assign the mean longitude of the moon. This want the *<term>Pañchasiddhāntikā</term>* supplies by stating the total amount of mean motion accomplished during each *<term>ghana</term>*, and each *<term>gati</term>*; so that we have, in each given case, to multiply those amounts by the number of elapsed *<term>ghanas</term>* and *<term>gatis</term>* and add up the results. It then remains to find the mean motion for the fraction of the non-completed *<term>gati</term>*, and to determine the corresponding amount of equation of the centre. Rules for these procedures—or for a part of them—are most probably contained in stanzas 5 and 6, which we however are unable to explain.

It further can hardly be doubted that stanzas 4—9 of the third chapter return to the moon, and give some further rules for ascertaining her true place and motion; this the general wording of the passage, and terms such as *<term>ghana</term>* and *<term>gati</term>* which occur in it, seem clearly to indicate. But we have not

# INTRODUCTION.

succeeded in unriddling those stanzas; and are therefore also not in a position to explain why they, if bearing on the teaching of the same <term>Siddhânta</term> <note>A Sanskrit term for a comprehensive astronomical treatise or "established conclusion."</note> as the former half of chapter II., should yet be separated from the latter by an intervening set of rules concerning altogether different matters.

The rule for finding the true place of the sun (III. 2, 3) resembles the corresponding rule of the <term>Romaka Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Roman" or "Greek" astronomical system adapted into Indian science.</note>, in so far as it does not teach a general process for finding the <term>equation of the centre</term> <note>The correction applied to a planet's mean position to find its true position, accounting for the elliptical nature of its orbit.</note> for any given <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its furthest point from Earth (apogee).</note>, but merely states the amount of the equation for each thirty degrees of anomaly. The degrees of the anomaly are however not reckoned from the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>, but from the first point of Aries, so that the equation of the centre can be added to—or subtracted from—the sun’s mean longitude without any preliminary deduction of the mean longitude from the longitude of the apogee.\* The latter quantity is estimated at 80 degrees. Stanza III. 17. contains a corresponding rough statement of the sun’s mean daily motion during each month of the solar year; here too we miss a general rule enabling us to calculate the true motion for any given time.

The estimation of the length of the revolution of the moon’s node <note>The points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic (the sun's path).</note> given in III. 26. differs but little from that made in the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most influential works in Indian astronomy.</note> and the great majority of Hindû astronomical works.—The greatest latitude of the moon is put equal to 270' (III. 31). But here also—as above in the case of the Romaka Siddhânta—we meet with another rule which appears to presuppose a greatest latitude of 240' only, viz., the rule given in VI. 5. for calculating the duration of total obscuration during a <term>lunar eclipse</term>. A similar rule on the other hand which likewise seems to belong to the <term>Paulisa Siddhânta</term> <note>An astronomical system often associated with the Greek astronomer Paulus Alexandrinus.</note> (VI. 6) again seems to be based on the assumption of the moon’s greatest latitude amounting to 270'.

The processes prescribed in the Paulisa Siddhânta for the calculation of lunar and solar eclipses are of a very rough nature and much less accurate than the corresponding operations according to the Romaka and Sûrya Siddhântas. The author of the Paulisa apparently aimed at nothing further than the establishment of convenient numerical formulas, gave no exposition of the general theory of the subject, and, for the sake of ease of calculation, introduced merely approximative values. No rule is prescribed for ascertaining the true (apparent) dimensions of sun, moon, and shadow at the time of an eclipse From VI. 4. it seems to follow that the mean value of the moon’s diameter is supposed to amount to 34', and that of the shadow to 76'. -># INTRODUCTION.<-

What different values seem, however, to result from Chapter VII, stanza 6, which also appears to imply a statement of the sum of the diameters of the sun and moon. It is difficult to speak on these points with assurance, as the details of the rules cannot in all cases be explained with full confidence, and several entire stanzas have remained altogether obscure to us.

The stanza VII. 1. gives the ordinary rule for calculating the parallax in longitude <note>The apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions</note>. We are unable to point out any rule for determining the parallax in latitude.

Among other items of doctrine which appear to be based on the <term>Pauliśa Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Treatise of Paul," one of the five early systems of Indian astronomy, often linked to Greek influence</note> there may be noted the interesting statement of the difference in longitude of <term>Yavanapura</term> <note>Literally "City of the Greeks"</note> on the one, and <term>Ujjayinî</term> and <term>Benares</term> on the other hand, which agrees fairly well with the assumption of <term>Yavanapura</term> being Alexandria.* Next the rule (III. 14) for calculating the difference in longitude of two places whose distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note> is known; an approximative rule which would give tolerably correct results for places not very remote from each other. — The same chapter (21) also contains the famous, often quoted, statement regarding the former position of the solstice, in which the word ‘right’ (<term>yukta</term> <note>original: "yukta," meaning joined, fit, or correct</note>), as we now see, can only be explained from the context in which stanza 20 stands with the preceding one.

We may also mention in connection with the <term>Pauliśa Siddhânta</term> the table of sines given in the fourth chapter, although it is doubtful from which Siddhânta it was borrowed by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>The 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath who compiled these texts</note>. It may have been common to the three scientific Siddhântas; the values assigned in it to the different sines are employed by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> throughout the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> <note>The "Five Astronomical Treatises"</note>, wherever such are required. The most interesting feature of the table is that it bases on a subdivision of the Radius into 120 parts and of each of those 120 parts into 60; instead of subdividing the Radius, in the ordinary Indian fashion, into 3438'. It thus closely follows the Greek fashion of expressing the values of sines, only preferring to divide the Radius into 120 parts instead of sixty. In the majority of cases the agreement of the stated values of the sines with those given by <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The famous Greco-Egyptian mathematician and astronomer</note> is as close as possible, taking into account that the latter writer subdivides his hundred and twentieth parts of the diameter into minutes and seconds, while the table in the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> subdivides into sixtieth parts only. There are however a small number of cases in which the agreement is not complete. The Sanskrit text had in a few places to be emended to a considerable extent, and it thus is not impossible that a more correct text would exhibit an even closer agreement with <term>Ptolemy</term>.

On the other hand the circumstance that the amount of each sine is not stated directly, but has to be arrived at by the summation of the amounts of all the preceding sines <note>This refers to a cumulative method of calculation where errors would typically compound over time.</note> favours the presumption of the emendations made being the right ones on the whole; for if they were not, the table as it now stands might be expected to show greater, and more regularly progressing, deviations from the true values of the sines than it actually does.

It may be noted that, in case of the table of sines basing on a Greek prototype, the plan of subdividing the Radius—and not the diameter—into 120 parts would have enabled the borrower to take over, without any change, the amounts assigned in the Greek table to the chords of the angles, and to insert them in his own table as the values of the sines of half those angles.

We finally have to compare the information about the Pauliśa Siddhânta given in the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* <note>A 6th-century astronomical treatise by Varâha Mihira summarizing five earlier systems.</note> with what we know from other sources about the same work, or at any rate a work of the same name. The sources alluded to are principally Bhaṭṭotpala's commentary on Varâha Mihira's *Bṛihatsaṃhitâ*, and Pṛithûdaka Svâmin's commentary on Brahmagupta's *Sphuṭa Brahmasiddhânta*, and from them Colebrooke already extracted the most noteworthy points. It appears that the Pauliśa Siddhânta, known to the two Scholiasts <note>Scholars or commentators on classical texts.</note> referred to, was a work following the same general methods as the *Sûrya Siddhânta*, Âryabhaṭa and all the later astronomers; at any rate it agreed with the great majority of Hindû astronomical works in establishing a <term>mahâyuga</term> <note>A "great age" or cosmic cycle consisting of 4,320,000 years.</note> which contains an integral number of <term>sâvana</term> <note>Civil days, measured from sunrise to sunrise.</note> days etc. and of revolutions of the planets. The data proving this are to be found in Colebrooke's essays vol. II. p. 365; from them it also follows that the length of the year, according to the Pauliśa Siddhânta, amounts to 365 days, 6 hours, 12 minutes, 36 seconds. Now, in spite of the corruption of the text of those passages in which Varâha Mihira treats of the Pauliśa Siddhânta, it is clear that the work of that name whose contents are summarized in the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* followed a plan altogether different from that of the Pauliśa Siddhânta referred to by Bhaṭṭotpala. I need not restate here in detail what has been remarked above about the methods employed by the Pauliśa of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ*; it will be remembered that in calculating the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The "heap of days"; the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note>, and the mean as well as true places of the planets, it employs peculiar methods of its own, which sharply distinguish it from the Pauliśa of Bhaṭṭotpala and works constructed on analogous lines. The length of its year amounts to 365 days, 6 hours, 12 minutes, while, on the other hand, the length of the year of the Pauliśa known to Bhaṭṭotpala is the same as that of the year of the *Sûrya Siddhânta* known to Varâha Mihira. And if any of the rules, given in the last chapter of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* for calculating the places of the planets, base—as not improbably

they do—on the Paulis'a Siddhânta <note>One of the five systems of astronomy; often associated by scholars with Greek influence, possibly named after "Paulus of Alexandria"</note>, they supply an additional feature marking off the two Paulis'a Siddhântas from each other.

We are thus led to the conclusion that the Paulis'a Siddhânta also has in the course of time undergone recasts, and that that form of it which was known to Bhaṭṭotpala <note>A 10th-century commentator on Indian astronomical works</note> widely differed from its original form, so widely indeed that there is some reason for wondering that the later work could go by the same name as the earlier one.

<margin>Vasishtḥa Siddhânta.</margin>
About the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta <note>The "Treatise of Vasishtḥa," another of the five systems</note> the Pañchasiddhântikâ <note>The "Five Treatises," the compendium by Varâha Mihira</note>, as exhibited in the two Manuscripts at our disposal, gives only very scanty information. Varâha Mihira, indeed, places the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta, together with the Paitâmaha Siddhânta <note>The oldest and most primitive of the five systems</note>, in the lowest rank of the works whose tenets he reproduces; yet it appears strange that its teaching should not be treated at somewhat greater length. If anything, it is the small space allotted to the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta in the text of the Pañchasiddhântikâ as here edited, which might induce us to suppose that certain parts of the work are missing in our Manuscripts. It is indeed—as I already have remarked above when discussing the allotment of the different chapters of the Pañchasiddhântikâ to the different Siddhântas—a somewhat difficult task to ascertain, how much of the matter contained in the Pañchasiddhântikâ in its present form has to be traced back to the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta. With confidence we may recognise its teaching only in the rules given in the second part of the second chapter which are, at the end, designated by Varâha Mihira himself as being founded on the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta, and which moreover are of a quite peculiar character, marking them off very decidedly from the doctrines of the other Siddhântas. The rule, given in stanza 8 for calculating the length of the day at any time of the year, is similar to that of the Paitâmaha Siddhânta in so far as assuming an equal daily increase; but it differs from it regarding the length of the shortest and longest days. The rules, given in stanzas 9—13 for finding the length of the shadow, the mean longitude of the sun and the <term>lagna</term> <note>The ascendant; the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</note> are also of a very primitive nature; but yet superior to what a work of the type of the Paitâmaha Siddhânta could supply.

We may infer from them that the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta no longer operated with <term>nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in early Vedic astronomy</note>, but subdivided the sphere into signs, degrees and minutes; and we also notice that it knew about the so-called <term>lagna</term> i. e. the ecliptic point which is on the eastern horizon at any given time. But, apart from this, the methods are so rude, and so completely omit to distinguish between mean and true astronomical quantities, that the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta can hardly be included within Scientific Hindû Astronomy.

<summary>The author argues that the Paulis'a Siddhânta was significantly altered over time and critiques the Vasishtḥa Siddhânta for its primitive methods, noting its transition from lunar mansions to degrees while still lacking scientific precision.</summary>

<page-num>XXXIX</page-num>
->INTRODUCTION.<-

That the rules concerning the motions of the moon contained in the former part of the second chapter are of an entirely different character, has been remarked above already (p. XI). In spite of this it is, as said in the same place, not altogether impossible that they should base on the teaching of the <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta (The "Treatise of Vasishṭha," one of the five early Hindu astronomical systems)</term>, which may have borrowed various rules and methods from different sources. The point must be left unsettled for the present.—The <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term> is not referred to in any other part of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ (The "Five Treatises," the main work by Varâha Mihira)</term>, with the exception of a colophon <note>A concluding statement in a manuscript providing facts about its production</note> in the last chapter, about which something will be said later on.

There yet remains the question as to the relation of the <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term>, known to <term>Varâha Mihira (A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath)</term>, to that <term>Siddhânta</term> of the same name about which we know from later commentators, chiefly those repeatedly referred to in the course of this introduction. From them <term>Colebrooke (Henry Thomas Colebrooke, a pioneering European Orientalist)</term> already has imparted some information about a <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term> which he ascribes to <term>Vishṇu Chandra</term>, on the authority of the last line of the passage quoted above (p. XXVI) from <term>Brahmagupta (A famous 7th-century mathematician and astronomer)</term>. The right interpretation of that line clearly depends on the way in which the preceding lines concerning <term>Śrîsheṇa’s</term> treatise are explained. Following the version of them given by me above we have to translate *“and by Vishṇu Chandra, taking the same (astronomical elements) the Vâsishṭha (Siddhânta) (was disfigured)”* *i. e.* <term>Vishṇu Chandra</term>, by borrowing various items of doctrine from different sources, gave to the original <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term> the same variegated, incongruous appearance which <term>Śrîsheṇa</term>, acting in an analogous manner, had imparted to the original <term>Romaka Siddhânta (The "Roman/Greek Treatise," showing Western influence)</term>. To the existence of a <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term>, older than the recast by <term>Vishṇu Chandra</term>, there moreover testifies the seventh line of the passage from <term>Brahmagupta</term>, which apparently says that <term>Śrîsheṇa</term> borrowed the (numbers of the) elapsed years and (planetary) revolutions of the <term>yuga (An immense cycle of time in Hindu cosmology)</term> from a <term>Vâsishṭha (Siddhânta)</term>; and the second half of that line further seems to intimate that that <term>Vâsishṭha</term> was composed by, or at any rate somehow connected with, <term>Vijayanandin</term>. An astronomical writer of that name is mentioned by <term>Brahmagupta</term> in another place also, and—which is of some importance as more definitely indicating his time—also by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> himself who, in the last chapter of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> (XVIII. 62), refers to <term>Vijayanandin</term> as having given rules for the calculation of the places of the planets.

Neither <term>Vijayanandin’s</term> nor <term>Vishṇu Chandra’s</term> treatises appear to have come down to our time. The (*Laghu*) <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta (The "Short" or "Lesser" Vasishṭha treatise)</term> which we possess\* does not evince any relationship either to that <term>Vasishṭha Siddhânta</term> which was known to <term>Varâha Mihira</term>, or to the work of <term>Vishṇu Chandra</term>, with some details of which we are rendered acquainted by <term>Brahmagupta</term> and later commentators.

<page-num>XL</page-num>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

Having thus taken a survey of the chief doctrines of the five <term>Siddhântas</term> <note>Siddhântas: Established astronomical treatises or "solutions" of Indian science.</note> as exhibited in chapters I—XVII of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> <note>Pañchasiddhântikâ: "The Five Astronomical Treatises," a 6th-century compendium by Varâha Mihira.</note>, and before examining in detail the contents of the last chapter, a few remarks may be added about what <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>Varâha Mihira: A prominent 6th-century Indian astronomer and mathematician.</note> states in XV. 33—38 about the longitudes and latitudes of certain stars. What authority he follows therein, we are unable to say.

The statement referred to gives the longitudes and latitudes of a small number of junction-stars of <term>nakshatras</term> <note>nakshatras: Lunar mansions or sectors of the sky through which the moon passes.</note>. How the longitude and latitude are measured, the text does not define; we can only presume that the <term>Siddhânta</term> which <term>Varâha Mihira</term> here extracts followed the usual Indian method viz. of referring the stars outside the ecliptic to the latter circle, not by latitude-circles, but by declination-circles, so that the quantities stated are what Whitney, in his translation of the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term>, calls polar longitudes (<term>dhruva</term> <note>dhruva: The fixed polar longitude of a star.</note>) and polar latitudes (<term>vikshepa</term> <note>vikshepa: The celestial latitude or "deflection" of a star.</note>). The degrees of (polar) longitude are, as in the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term>, taken from the beginning of the <term>nakshatra</term> (=twenty-seventh part of the ecliptic) to which the junction star belongs. The latitudes are, in a peculiar manner, expressed not in degrees, but <term>hastas</term> <note>hastas: Literally "hands" or "cubits," used here as a unit of angular measurement.</note>, which we are enabled to turn into degrees by remembering that one <term>hasta</term> comprises thirty-four <term>angulis</term> <note>angulis: Literally "fingers," a smaller subdivision of the hasta.</note>, and that the diameter of the moon—here assumed equal to 34 minutes—is divided into fifteen <term>angulis</term>. We give the results, in a tabular form, adding at the same time, in order to facilitate comparison, the corresponding statements made in the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> (Whitney p. 321.)

# INTRODUCTION.

Why <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> should have confined himself to stating the longitudes and latitudes of seven <term>junction stars</term> <note>Stars used as reference points to mark the boundaries of lunar mansions</note> only, remains unaccounted for. Possibly the Manuscripts are defective just at that place. The details given concerning those seven stars (supposing our interpretation of the text to be correct) diverge so widely from the corresponding statements of the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note> that, considering the incompleteness of the material, a critical comparison of the two appears hardly feasible at present.—About the rule concerning the <term>heliacal rising</term> <note>The first time a star becomes visible in the dawn before sunrise</note> of <term>Canopus</term> (XIV. 39—41) a few remarks will be made further on.

I now proceed to the examination of the last chapter of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> <note>The "Five Astronomical Treatises," the major work by Varâha Mihira</note>, which is one of the most interesting but at the same time most perplexing of the whole work. The text itself apparently does not state to what <term>Siddhânta</term> <note>Astronomical treatise</note> the rules about the planets, constituting the matter of the chapter, have to be traced. To some indications given in the colophons <note>End-notes in a manuscript providing publication details</note> I will refer later on.

A survey of the contents of the chapter shows that it consists of two different sets of rules, of which the former extends from **stanzas** 1—60, while the latter, preceded by some personal remarks on the part of **Varâha Mihira**, comprises **stanzas** 66 up to the end. I begin by analysing, as far as feasible, the former set of rules.*

The plan generally followed in this part of the work is to state at first for each planet a rule enabling us to calculate how many (**heliacal**) risings of it have taken place within a given <term>ahargana</term> <note>The number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</note>, or—in other words—how many <term>synodical revolutions</term> <note>The time it takes for a planet to return to the same position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth</note> it has performed. To that end we are directed to divide the <term>ahargana</term> by the duration of the different <term>synodical revolutions</term>. In **Venus**’ case the rule prescribes (**stanzas** 1 and 2) to divide the <term>ahargana</term> by 584, and to add to the remaining days the eleventh part of the quotient of the division; i. e. in other words, the length of **Venus**’ <term>synodical revolution</term> is estimated at 584 — 1/11 days. In the same way it follows from **stanzas** 6 and 7 that one <term>synodical revolution</term> of **Jupiter** is estimated at 399 — 1/9 days; from **stanzas** 14 and 15 that one revolution of **Saturn** amounts to 378 1/11 days; from **stanzas** 21 and 22, that one revolution of **Mars** is estimated at 780 days minus 161 <term>vinâdikâs</term> <note>A small unit of time; 60 vinâdikâs make one nâdikâ</note> (=, about, 2/45 th of a day); and from **stanzas** 36 and 37, that one <term>synodical revolution</term> of **Mercury** is supposed to amount to 115 days plus 52 <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> plus 45 <term>vinâdikâs</term> (for the rules given there imply that 8 <term>synodical revolutions</term> occupy 927 days plus 2 <term>nâdikâs</term>).

* It will be observed that the English translation of that chapter confines itself to a literal rendering of the **Stanzas**. The following, systematic, discussion of the contents of the chapter is meant to supply the place of explanatory notes to the translation.

<page-num>XLII</page-num>
# INTRODUCTION.

In the second place the rules teach us how to calculate the amount of sidereal motion <note>The movement of a planet relative to the "fixed" stars.</note> performed by the planets within the given number of synodical revolutions <note>The time it takes for a planet to reappear in the same position relative to the Sun, as viewed from Earth.</note>.—Stanza 1 says that during one period of rising, *i. e.* during one synodical revolution, Venus passes through 7 signs, 5 degrees, and 30 minutes, and this is indeed the approximate motion of Venus within 584 - 1/11 days, if we suppose its mean motion to be the same as that of the sun, and reject the entire revolution performed.

In Jupiter’s case we are directed (stanza 7) to multiply the number of synodical revolutions contained within a given <term>ahargana</term> <note>Sanskrit: "heap of days"; the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch used in Indian astronomy.</note> by 36, and to divide by 391; which shows that 391 synodical revolutions are supposed to be about equal to 36 sidereal revolutions. This is indeed nearly the case; for if, basing on the duration of a synodical revolution of 399 days (not 399 - 1/9 days) and on the assumption of 364,220 sidereal revolutions of Jupiter being performed within a <term>mahâyuga</term> <note>Sanskrit: "great age"; a vast cosmic cycle of 4,320,000 years used in Hindu chronology.</note> of 1,577,917,800 days, we calculate the sidereal revolutions performed during the lapse of 391 synodical revolutions, we find 36 revolutions plus about four degrees. And for these four degrees also an allowance is made, *viz.* in stanza 10, where we are told to multiply the number of risings by five, to divide by eight, and to take the result as minutes; for (240 minutes × risings) / 391 is nearly equal to (5 × risings) / 8.

The rules for calculating the sidereal motions of the other planets are of a similar nature. Assuming the sidereal revolutions of Saturn within one <term>mahâyuga</term> to amount to 146,568, the quantity of sidereal motion within a period comprising 256 synodical revolutions of 378 days each is equal to nine revolutions minus four degrees + eight minutes. We are hence directed (st. 15) to multiply the risings of Saturn by 9, and to divide by 256; and (st. 17) to multiply the risings by 3, to divide by 32, and to look on the result as minutes to be deducted; for 4 degrees + 8 minutes = 248 minutes, and 248/256 = 31/32.

For Mars we have the assumption (st. 22) that fifteen synodical revolutions comprise eighteen sidereal revolutions; hence we multiply the number of the risings by eighteen and divide by fifteen. The quotient which indicates the entire revolutions is rejected; the remainder, multiplied by 12 and divided by 15, gives the mean place of Mars in signs and so on. In Mercury’s case, finally, 389 synodical revolutions are supposed to be equal to 123 sidereal revolutions; hence st. 37 directs us to multiply the given number of synodical revolutions by 123, and to divide by 389.

So far the rules contained in the last chapter can be satisfactorily explained. We now however are met by a series of rules whose rationale <note>The underlying logic or mathematical basis.</note> we are unable to assign. Hitherto we have been told how to calculate firstly

# XLIII
## INTRODUCTION.

Now, from these remainders—which represent in both cases a certain number of days—the mean motion and the mean position of the planet at a given time can be calculated without difficulty; but what is required, and what the rules of the text apparently mean to supply, are directions enabling us to determine, roughly at least, the true place of the planet at the end of the given <term>ahargaṇa</term>. We are, however, unable to point out the general principles on which the rules are constructed.

I begin with Saturn in whose case the rules appear to be simpler than in that of the other planets (setting aside Venus about which later on). Stanza 15 directs us to multiply the number of the synodical revolutions by 9, and to divide by 256, the quotient of the division indicating, as explained above, the number of completed sidereal revolutions. The remainder, the text goes on to say, is the ‘*pada*.’ <note>Literally 'step' or 'quadrant'; here referring to the fractional remainder of a cycle</note> The remainder—which alone is required for the calculation of the true place of a planet—is thus denoted by the same term which, as we have seen above, was employed in the Pauliśa (or Vasishṭha) Siddhānta <note>Ancient Indian astronomical treatises</note> to denote the remainder of days from which the true place of the moon is ascertained. The text then goes on to distinguish three different amounts of the *pada*, *viz.* 30, 127 and 99; and it will be observed that the sum of the three fractions 30/256, 127/256, 99/256 amounts to 256/256 *i. e.* one entire revolution. There are further mentioned certain additive, or subtractive, quantities, which have to be applied in case of the *padas* reaching the mentioned amounts, and it certainly appears probable that those quantities are, in some way or other, connected with the equation of the centre <note>The correction required to account for the elliptical nature of an orbit</note>, which has to be added or subtracted in order to render the planet’s place true. But we are quite unable to demonstrate, by a satisfactory explanation of the three amounts, the truth of this hypothesis. The text finally (in 18, and 19) states certain amounts of motion which Saturn performs within the three *khaṇḍas* <note>Parts or segments of a whole</note>, *i. e.*, apparently, the three fractions of a revolution (30/256, 127/256, 99/256) which were mentioned above. But here again we meet with a difficulty; for while the text states for the two first *khaṇḍas* the following amounts: 1$^s$ 15° 51' and 5$^s$ 28° 35', a calculation of the mean motion proceeding on the data of the text gives 1$^s$ 12° 11' for 30/256$^{th}$ of a revolution, and 5$^s$ 27° 34' for 127/256$^{th}$ of a revolution. It is indeed by no means unlikely that the discrepancy may be owing to the circumstance of the text wishing to state the amount of true—not mean—motion; but

The emendation of the text—<note>original: "mūnayo liptāś chatur-guṇāḥ sapta"</note> "seven minutes multiplied by four" <note>This refers to a specific numerical coding system used in Sanskrit astronomical verses.</note>, stanza 19—which is based on the erroneous quantity stated in the commentary must on that account be rejected. The text finally gives (stanzas 19 and 20) a statement of the different phases of Saturn’s motion in the course of one <term>synodic revolution</term> <note>The time it takes for a planet to reappear in the same position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth.</note>, dividing that period into seven minor periods, and mentioning the amount of motion during each.

We have similar rules in Jupiter’s case. There too (stanza 7) we are told to take the remainder of the division whose quotient indicates the completed <term>sidereal revolutions</term> <note>The time it takes for a planet to complete one full orbit around the Sun relative to the fixed stars.</note>, and to term it <term>pada</term>. Again three different <term>padas</term> are distinguished (stanza 9), whose sum amounts to one complete revolution (180/391 + 195/391 + 16/391 = 391/391), and for each of these <term>padas</term> there is stated a certain additive or subtractive quantity of obscure meaning. And again there are stated three different amounts of motion which do not very widely differ from the amounts of mean motion that Jupiter performs within each of the three fractions of a revolution stated above; the amounts given in the text being 5 signs, 9 degrees, 30 minutes; 6 signs; 13 degrees, while the calculated amounts are 5 signs, 15 degrees, 43 minutes; 5 signs, 29 degrees, 33 minutes; 14 degrees, 44 minutes. Here too we can only conjecture that what is aimed at is a statement of the true motion within the given intervals. But, in addition to these rules which so far are strictly parallel to those concerning Saturn, we have, in stanza 8, some additional directions concerning mean and true quantities whose sense has remained quite obscure to us, so that even the attempted literal rendering of the words of the text—which has been given in the translation—must be looked upon as altogether tentative and provisional.—Stanzas 12 and 13 exhibit a statement of Jupiter's apparent motion during each of nine minor periods into which the entire synodical period of the planet is subdivided.

With regard to Mars again another plan is followed, of which the details however have likewise remained obscure to us. In Mars’ case the text, after having given the rules, explained above, for finding the elapsed synodical and sidereal revolutions, proceeds (in stanza 24) to make a statement regarding the difference of the planet’s mean and true places, it being obscure, however, in what way the true place is supposed to be found, and then declares that the course (<term>châra</term>) of Mars will be stated according to the different motions (<term>gati</term>). To judge from stanza 35, these motions appear to be eight; and as the text mentions the terms <term>vakra</term> <note>Retrograde motion; when a planet appears to move backward.</note>, <term>anuvakra</term> <note>Continued or secondary retrograde motion.</note>, <term>anugati</term> <note>Following or direct motion.</note>, <term>ativakra</term> <note>Swift retrograde motion.</note>

<page-num>XLV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

and *śīghra* <note>Sanskrit: "fast" or "rapid" motion</note>, we may assume that we have to do with something like the eight kinds of motion enumerated in *Sūrya Siddhānta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, likely dating to the 4th or 5th century CE</note> II. 12, among which we meet with *vakra* <note>retrograde motion</note>, *anuvakra* <note>somewhat retrograde or "re-retrograde"</note> and *śīghra*. But most of the details we must leave unexplained, owing partly to the corruption of the text, and partly to the obscurity of the subject. Stanzas 25 (conclusion) and 26 state the periods intervening between the time of the heliacal setting <note>the moment a planet disappears into the sun's glare</note> of Mars and its conjunction (when it becomes *niramśa* <note>literally "without degrees," meaning the planet has no longitudinal distance from the sun</note>), and between the conjunction and its heliacal rising <note>the moment a planet first becomes visible in the dawn before sunrise</note>. The meaning of stanzas 27 and 28 is obscure. Stanzas 29—32 treat of the motion of Mars in three of its *gatis* <note>Sanskrit: "gaits" or modes of motion</note> (compare the 'threefold' in 32), of which the '*vakra*' i. e. no doubt the retrograde motion is the first; the nature of the two other motions we are unable to explain, the text exhibiting only the vague term, '*anugati*' <note>following motion</note> (in 29). In stanza 33 we meet indeed with the terms *vakra*, *ativakra* <note>excessively retrograde</note> and *anuvakra*, and we hence suppose that those three motions are referred to in 29—32 also; but, considering the various senses in which the terms *ativakra* and *anuvakra* are used by different authorities, we do not attempt to assign the meaning they bear in our text.

For Mercury the text, after having given the general rules for synodical <note>motion relative to the sun as seen from Earth</note> and sidereal <note>motion relative to the fixed stars</note> motion, at once states the amount of supposed true motion for eight periods of days whose total aggregate amounts to 380 days, the amount of true motion being 360 degrees. From this latter circumstance it appears that what is aimed at is a statement of the different phases of true motion during one mean revolution of the planet (which, of course, is viewed as equal to one mean revolution of the sun). Why, however, the corresponding period of days is said to amount to 380 days (rather than to 365), we are not able to explain, although so much may be suggested that the discrepancy is most probably due to a mixing up of sidereal with synodical motion. The text then goes on to give a general rule (obscure to us) about the adjustment of mean and true motion (stanza 41), and thereupon gives a detailed account (42—53) of the difference of Mercury's motions according to the sign of the ecliptic <note>the path of the sun across the sky</note> in which the planet stands at the time. We are unable to account for those rules by calculation.

There now only remains to be noticed, in the first set of planetary rules, what is said about the true motions of Venus in stanzas 3—5. The treatment of this latter planet differs from that of all other planets inasmuch as it appears not to take into account the influence of the equation of the apsis <note>a correction for the elliptical shape of the orbit</note>, but limits itself to a rough representation of the true motions in so far as depending on the equation of the conjunction <note>a correction for the observer's position on Earth</note>. The difference is quite intelligible, if we remember that the eccentricity of Venus' orbit is very much smaller than that of any other planet. The text specifies the true mo-

Out of these, 584 constitute one synodical revolution <note>The time it takes for a planet to reappear in the same position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth.</note> of Venus, while the last 26 days must be viewed as the period within which Venus, after having performed one synodical revolution and having again entered into conjunction with the Sun, advances so much as again to become visible in the west.

Obscure and unsatisfactory as are many details of this first set of planetary rules, we yet recognise with sufficient clearness that the elements on which they are based do not greatly differ from those generally employed in <term>Hindû</term> <note>Indian</note> astronomy. The periods of sidereal <note>Relative to the stars</note> and synodical revolution diverge very little from the ordinary ones, and the calculation of the true places appears to presuppose the recognition of the two separate planetary inequalities <note>The variations in a planet’s speed and position caused by its elliptical orbit and the Earth's motion.</note> (excepting the case of Venus as noticed above). But we begin to feel on strangely new and unsafe ground when now turning to the second set of rules for the calculation of the planetary motions, which are contained in stanzas 66—81 of the last chapter.

The position and appearance of these rules are anomalous from several points of view. On the rules explained above which come to a conclusion in stanza 60, there follow a few stanzas which look very much as if they were meant as concluding stanzas of the whole work, the author mentioning in them his name, and drawing a parallel between his own performance and the less successful efforts of other astronomers. But these, *at first sight* <note>original: "primâ facie"</note> final, stanzas are followed in their turn by a further stanza (65) which seems to be meant by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A famous 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath.</note> as an introduction to another set of concise planetary rules (<term>astronomical rules for the planets</term> <note>original: "grahakârikâ tantram"</note>); for although the rules extending from stanza 66 to the end of the book are comprised in 16 stanzas (or in seventeen, if we add to them stanza 65), it yet seems most probable that the ‘eighteen <term>âryâs</term>’ <note>A specific meter or verse form in Sanskrit poetry.</note> mentioned in stanza 65 refer to this concluding portion, with which possibly one of the stanzas preceding 65 may have to be counted, or which originally may have contained one stanza more than our manuscripts exhibit.

The matter contained in this concluding portion is of a comparatively simple nature. The rules at first teach how to calculate for each planet the number of synodical revolutions which have taken place within a given <term>count of days</term> <note>original: "ahargaṇa"; the number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch.</note>, and then state the chief phases of motion within each synodical revolution, or half revolution as in Venus’ case. No rules are given for calculating the true motions.

To meet in Indian astronomy with a set of numerical quantities widely differing from those generally accepted is indeed so startling, that one at first feels strongly inclined to doubt of the soundness of the text, especially if one remembers the generally unsatisfactory state of the two available Manuscripts of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* <note>term: Pañchasiddhântikâ. We therefore can, for the present, hardly help accepting the rules as they stand, in spite of their startling uniqueness.

It remains to consider from which *Siddhântas* Varâha Mihira <note>A prominent 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath.</note> may have borrowed the matter of the entire last chapter. The text itself appears to contain no indication on that point; there are however two colophons <note>Notes at the end of a manuscript section providing titles or authorship.</note> which furnish some—possibly accurate—information. After stanza 5 the Manuscripts read, *“Venus in the Vâsishṭha-siddhânta,”* <note>original: "Vâsishṭha-siddhânte śukraḥ"</note> and at the end of the chapter, *“The star-planets in the Paulīsa-siddhânta.”* <note>original: "Paulīsasiddhânte târâgrahâ ḥ"</note> If we accept the former statement as true, it would follow that the *Vâsishṭha-siddhânta* possessed an accurate knowledge of the length of the planetary revolutions; for although the statement directly refers to Venus only, it is—for reasons not requiring to be set forth at length—altogether improbable that the *Vâsishṭha Siddhânta*, or in fact any *Siddhânta*, should have been well informed about the theory of one planet only. The last set of rules especially is perplexing, and, were it not for the direct assertion made in the colophon, nobody I suppose would be inclined to trace the determinations of periods given in it to a <term>Siddhānta</term> which seems to have been specially dependent on Greek teaching.

During that period nothing of importance seems to have been elaborated but the doctrine of the quinquennial <note>five-year</note> lunisolar <term>yuga</term> <note>A cycle of time used to reconcile the movements of the sun and moon</note>. The authors of all the works mentioned share the same essential characteristics, in so far as displaying a very imperfect knowledge of the mean motions of the sun and moon (and, some of them, of the planets also), and connected therewith, of the length of the years and months; being altogether unacquainted with true motion as distinguished from mean motion; teaching an equal daily increase or decrease of the length of the day; dividing the sphere into twenty-seven or twenty-eight <term>nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions or sectors of the sky through which the moon passes</note>; entertaining utterly fantastic notions about the constitution of the earth and the universe; and evincing a very marked tendency to work out in minute detail large sets of numerical rules founded on altogether insufficient premisses. They all moreover, with the exception of the Jaina books, agree in fixing the winter-solstice at the beginning of the <term>nakshatra</term> Dhanishṭhâ. That from this latter circumstance no conclusion can be drawn as to the time when the different works mentioning it were composed, is at present admitted pretty generally. For it is neither possible to derive from the given data, with any degree of accuracy, the time when the original observation was made; nor, even if that could be done, would the result prove anything regarding the period when the works in question were composed, since it is quite clear that the place of the solstices having once been ascertained was adhered to and stated in works composed many centuries after it had ceased to be true. That in Varâha Mihira's account of the teaching of the Paitâmaha <term>Siddhânta</term> <note>One of the five early astronomical systems or "solutions"</note> the calculation of the quinquennial <term>yuga</term> is made to start from 2 Śâka <note>The year 80 AD in the Shaka era calendar</note>, has been mentioned above.

There are two chief points in which those early works have influenced later scientific astronomy. The latter derived from them firstly the idea of a <term>yuga</term>—that is, a cyclical period, at the end of which the heavenly bodies return to the same relative positions which they occupied at the outset. And in the second place, the writings of the earlier period already show, fully developed, the peculiar Indian lunar calendar which treats the <term>tithi</term>—that is, the thirtieth part of a synodical month—as the true chronometrical unit, so that in all calculations of the length of elapsed periods, and of the position of heavenly bodies, the sum of natural days can be ascertained only through a previous knowledge of the number of elapsed lunar days.

That the summer solstice formerly was at the middle of *Âshleshâ* <note>A lunar mansion or constellation in the Indian zodiac.</note>, but in his time at the beginning of *Punarvasu* <note>Another lunar mansion; the shift indicates the precession of the equinoxes.</note>, appear to be viewed by him as two distinct facts, each to be taken by itself. That the similarities observed between the Greek and *Hindû* systems are due to a transfer of the elements of the former to India, will at present be hardly called into doubt; and it certainly appears highly probable that the *Paulisá* and *Romaka Siddhántas* <note>The "Paulisa" is often linked to the Greek name Paulus, and "Romaka" refers to the Roman/Byzantine world.</note> were the earliest Sanskrit works in which the new knowledge imported from the West was embodied. That these two works were in some special way dependent on Greek astronomy, has since a long time been inferred from their names; and that conclusion is now confirmed by what we learn from *Varáha Mihira* <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath.</note> about their contents. It certainly is no fortuitous coincidence that one of those two *Siddhántas* whose names point to the west, used the tropical solar year, and calculated its *ahargaṇa* <term>ahargaṇa: the count of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term> for the meridian of *Yavanapura* <note>Literally "City of the Greeks," likely referring to Alexandria or a similar Hellenistic center.</note>, and that the other expressly stated the difference in longitude of *Yavanapura* and *Ujjayinî* <note>A city in central India used as the prime meridian for Indian astronomers.</note>. And that they were the first representatives of Greek astronomy in India, is at any rate highly probable, as we have no information about older astronomical works of hellenizing <note>Influenced by Greek culture or science.</note> tendencies. While, thus, the general question as to the sources of scientific *Hindû* astronomy admits of one answer only, doubts begin to suggest themselves as soon as we proceed to ask, from what particular Greek works the early *Siddhânta* writers may have borrowed, and to what time the first transmittence of astronomical knowledge has to be assigned. Professor Whitney to whom we are indebted for the most thorough discussion of these matters (translation of the *Sûrya Siddhânta* pp. 470 ff.) has expressed the opinion that the absence, from the *Hindû* system, of any of the improvements introduced into Greek astronomy by Ptolemy <note>The famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer of the 2nd century AD.</note> seems to favour the conclusion that the original transmission of astronomical knowledge into India took place before Ptolemy; which at the same time would account for the many differences in detail between the *Hindû* system and the teaching of the *Syntaxis* <note>Also known as the Almagest, Ptolemy's definitive work.</note>.—Now with this view we certainly may agree so far as to consider it altogether improbable that the *Hindû* system should have based directly on Ptolemy’s work. (for instance)</note>, to mention only one out of a vast number of cases, the different dimensions assigned to the epicycles <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex orbits of planets.</note> of the planets by the Indians and Ptolemy respectively? But nevertheless it would be risky to conclude therefrom that the beginnings of scientific Indian astronomy go back to a time earlier than that of Ptolemy. The whole question indeed is rendered incapable of decisive treatment by the fact that our knowledge of Greek astronomy prior to Ptolemy is so very imperfect; a few points however which bear upon it may be briefly referred to.

As well known, the theories of the sun and moon were settled in all important points by Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) considered the founder of trigonometry.</note> already and merely borrowed from him by Ptolemy. It would therefore not be impossible that any scientific Indian work, confining itself to an exposition of the motions of those two heavenly bodies and of rules for the approximate calculation of their eclipses, should have originated in the period intervening between Hipparchus and Ptolemy. Hipparchus again had already given determinations of the mean periods of revolution of the planets, which Ptolemy found means to correct in some very unimportant details only. On the other hand, it had indeed not escaped Hipparchus that the true motions of the planets can be satisfactorily explained, only if we recognize two distinct inequalities; but he had not undertaken to separate those inequalities in each case, and so to establish a workable theory of the planets. The latter achievement Ptolemy distinctly claims for himself, and we therefore must conclude that any Indian works—such as *for instance* the *Sûrya Siddhânta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit text of Indian astronomy.</note>—in which the anomaly of the apsis <note>The variation in a planet's speed due to its elliptical orbit.</note> and the anomaly of the conjunction <note>The variation in a planet's position relative to its distance from the sun.</note> are clearly distinguished are later than Ptolemy from whom alone, directly or indirectly, they could have derived their theory. In spite of what we have learned from the *Pañcha Siddhântikâ* <note>A compendium of five astronomical systems compiled by Varāhamihira.</note>, we are unfortunately not yet sufficiently informed about the entire contents of the earlier *Siddhântas* <note>Sanskrit astronomical treatises.</note> to apply the preceding remarks to a determination of their age. The *Pañcha-siddhântikâ* says nothing about any planetary rules being given in the *Romaka Siddhânta* <note>The "Roman" or "Greek" astronomical treatise.</note>, and that treatise, in its original form, might therefore possibly have been one confining itself to a system of lunisolar <note>Relating to the combined motions of the sun and moon.</note> astronomy, such as could have been established on the teaching of Hipparchus alone. That among the works which represent the first remodeling of Indian astronomy on Greek lines there should have been some which treated of the sun and moon only, will not be considered unlikely, if we remember, firstly, that the theory of

those two heavenly bodies <note>The sun and the moon</note> suffices for the construction of a calendar, and, secondly, that also the purely astronomical works of an earlier period—such as the <term>Jyotisha Vedânga</term> <note>An ancient Indian manual on astronomy for Vedic rituals</note>, the <term>Paitâmaha Siddhânta</term> <note>A foundational astronomical treatise</note> known to <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note>, and the <term>Sûrya Prajñapti</term> <note>A Jain astronomical text</note>—do not treat of the motions of the planets. But none of these considerations *compel* us to date the <term>Romaka Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Roman Treatise," an Indian astronomical work influenced by Western methods</note> earlier than <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The famous 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note>, while on the other hand the very name of the treatise seems to point to a time when the fame of <term>Rome</term> had become so great that even in the distant east her name naturally attached itself to new views and doctrines entering <term>India</term> from any western country *i. e.* to a time hardly earlier than the century of <term>Ptolemy</term>.

The <term>Vâsishtha</term> and <term>Pauliśa Siddhântas</term> <note>Two of the five early Indian astronomical systems</note> treated of the planets also, as we learn from the last chapter of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term> <note>A compendium of the five astronomical systems by Varâha Mihira</note>. The earlier set of rules given there apparently distinguishes the two planetary inequalities; but as we understand the text only very partially, I cannot undertake to discuss the connexion of those rules with <term>Greek</term> science. Of the rules given in the last part of that chapter it might perhaps be conjectured that they represent a stage of the theory of the planets more primitive than that of <term>Ptolemy</term>; for what is stated there about the true motions of the planets, apparently takes into account only the more conspicuous anomaly which depends on the planet's position with reference to the sun, while the anomaly dependent on the planet's distance from the apsis <note>The point in an orbit closest or farthest from the center</note> is neglected. That the mean motions attributed to the planets in that chapter differ in an altogether unaccountable way from the true ones (and hence also from those determined with such extraordinary accuracy by <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>A 2nd-century BCE Greek astronomer who discovered the precession of the equinoxes</note>, and adopted from him by <term>Ptolemy</term>), I have remarked above already. But these facts do not, after all, supply valid reasons for supposing any knowledge of astronomical matters to have reached <term>India</term> from <term>Alexandria</term> before the time of <term>Ptolemy</term>. That certain details in the <term>Indian</term> system appear more primitive than <term>Ptolemy's</term> teaching, may simply be due to the fact that the <term>Indian</term> astronomers, with their strictly practical tendency, did not aim at any great accuracy, and neglected what in their view, would not affect the result of their calculation to an appreciable degree. And there is yet another, and in my view, very important consideration which may account for the divergencies from <term>Ptolemy</term> on the part of <term>Indian</term> works, of a date later than his; a consideration which <term>Biot</term> <note>Jean-Baptiste Biot, a French physicist and historian of science</note> already has repeatedly suggested. It is by no means impossible that the astronomical knowledge which the <term>Hindûs</term> have worked up in their <term>Siddhântas</term> was not derived from any of the great scientific works of the <term>Alexandrian</term> astronomers, but rather from an altogether different class of books *viz.* the manuals used by <term>Greek</term> astrologers (as <term>Biot</term> suggests) and, as we may not improbably add, almanac makers. The astronomical views of men belonging to those classes
