may reasonably be presumed to have been rather imperfect, and to have diverged in more than one point from the theories of the great scientific astronomers; they might have borrowed from the latter whatever appeared indispensable, neglected what seemed likely to cause greater trouble in calculation than would be justified by the results, and, at the same time, preserved elements of older, long antiquated, doctrines. The rules given in their manuals might not improbably have resembled in their form the rules met with in the early Indian <term>Siddhântas</term> <note>Siddhânta: A Sanskrit term for a formal treatise or established system of astronomy.</note>, especially the <term>Pauliśa Siddhânta</term> <note>An early Indian astronomical work, often thought to be influenced by the Greek astronomer Paul of Alexandria.</note>, which apparently did not even hint at the theory of the subject, but only aimed at enabling the practical astronomer or astrologer to perform with the greatest possible ease and rapidity the calculations absolutely necessitated by his profession. The assumption of the earliest scientific (or quasi-scientific) Indian astronomers being acquainted, not with the writings of men like Hipparchus or Ptolemy or Theon, but only with works of the class mentioned above, would I believe help to render the whole process of transmission more intelligible. Whatever distinguished the teaching of the practical calculators of Alexandria from that of the scientific men, would in that case have perpetuated itself in the Indian treatises, and would thus from the outset have differentiated the latter from works of the class of the <term>Syntaxis</term> <note>Referring to Ptolemy's "Almagest," originally titled the "Mathematikē Syntaxis" or Mathematical Compilation.</note>. The fact of there having been transmitted, not a complete astronomical system, but only practical rules joined perhaps with vague indications of general principles would moreover, I think, account satisfactorily for the many differences in point of theory which distinguish the completed Indian system from its Greek prototype. That a work of the class of the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>One of the most important and enduring Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy.</note> should spring directly from a work such as the Syntaxis, would be almost incomprehensible, even if we made the very largest allowances for the tendency, on the part of the Indian adaptator, to harmonize the new foreign doctrine with indigenous tradition and modes of computation, and to simplify his original to as large an extent as possible. But if we, on the other hand, suppose that only a very imperfect knowledge of Greek astronomy was transmitted to India, and that Indian <term>Jyautishas</term> <note>Jyautishas: Practitioners of Jyotisha, the traditional Indian science of astronomy and astrology.</note> endeavoured to erect on that basis a complete system of their own, we can understand how there came into existence works of the type of the Sûrya Siddhânta, which, although evincing a fundamental dependence on Greek astronomy, yet show unmistakeable traces of originality in numerous details, remaining indeed in by far the greater number of cases inferior to their original, yet hitting here and there on new devices and methods of undeniable merit and ingenuity. The perfect Indian system would in that case have to be characterized, not either as a mere loan from the Greeks, nor as a mere adaptation in the ordinary sense of the word, but rather as a combination, and further development proceeding on partly original lines,

We next must enquire whether the older *Siddhântas* <term>Siddhânta: A comprehensive Sanskrit astronomical treatise</term> themselves furnish any indications of the time when they were composed, and so indirectly of the time when Greek astronomy was introduced into India. The evidence on that point which is supplied by the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* <note>The "Five Treatises," a compendium authored by Varâha Mihira.</note> itself as understood by me is as follows. Varâha Mihira I suppose to have written his treatise about the middle of the sixth century (see above p. 30), and to have taken for his epoch the year 505 A.D. which I understand to indicate the time of the astronomical writer Lâṭa, who himself is said by Varâha Mihira to have commented on the *Romaka Siddhânta* <note>The "Roman Treatise," which shows significant Western/Alexandrian influence.</note>. The latter treatise therefore must have been composed at some time anteceding—and possibly considerably earlier than—505 A.D. That the *Romaka Siddhânta*—and in fact the other four *Siddhântas* also—are a good deal earlier than Varâha Mihira, is confirmed by the general attitude of that writer with regard to the works on which his treatise is based. Varâha Mihira clearly distinguishes, on the one hand, individual and manifestly modern writers, to particular views of whom he refers in a few places, without however crediting them with complete independent systems which it would be necessary to abstract; and, on the other hand, treatises of generally recognised authority, not to be neglected by any writer who aims at giving a complete survey of the astronomical doctrines current at that time in India. Of the class of writers referred to, Varâha Mihira mentions Lâṭa, Âryabhaṭa, the teacher of the Greeks <note>original: "guru of the Yavanas." Yavana was the term used in ancient India for Greeks and other Westerners.</note>, Siṃha, Vijayanandin and Pradyumna. Of Lâṭa we have reason to suppose that he flourished about 505; of Âryabhaṭa we know that he composed his treatise, termed *Laghv-âryabhaṭîyam* <note>The "Small" or "Brief" work of Âryabhaṭa.</note>, in 499. Whether the other writers mentioned by Varâha Mihira were earlier or later than Âryabhaṭa, there is so far nothing to show. But it is certainly an intrinsically probable view that the authoritative treatises, to the exposition of whose doctrines Varâha Mihira devotes his work, and which to him appear to exhaust Indian astronomical learning, were earlier than the individual writers to detached views of whom he alludes incidentally, and whom he manifestly does not in any way consider superior to himself.

This conclusion is in conflict with a view expressed with more or less definiteness by several writers on Hindu astronomy, according to which Âryabhaṭa is the oldest of scientific Hindu astronomers; for three at any rate out of the five *Siddhântas* which we suppose to be earlier than Âryabhaṭa have to be classed as scientific works. Had he held that position, he would of course have been entitled to have his doctrines fully abstracted by a writer like Varâha Mihira, who constituted it his special task to summarize all the more important theories current at his time. But, as remarked above, to Varâha Mihira Âryabhaṭa clearly is only one of those numerous writers, who occupied a position not unlike his own, as being engaged in remodelling, and possibly here and there improving on, the teaching of the received Siddhântas <note>term: Siddhânta (established astronomical systems or treatises)</note>. I cannot, in this place, enter into a full discussion of Âryabhaṭa’s doctrines; but even a somewhat superficial examination shows that they stand in a particularly close relation to the *Sûrya Siddhânta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most influential early Indian astronomical texts</note>, whose teaching they indeed modify and attempt to correct in many details, but yet unmistakably follow on the whole. This becomes evident, if we compare the *Âryabhaṭîyam* <note>Âryabhaṭa's primary work</note> on the one hand with the *Pauliśa* and *Romaka Siddhântas* <note>Two of the five early astronomical systems; the Romaka likely refers to Roman/Greek influence</note> as summarized by Varâha Mihira, and on the other hand with the *Sûrya Siddhânta* as reported by the same author, or, for the matter of that, with the *Sûrya Siddhânta* in its modern form, although we have had occasion to remark that in some points the old treatise agreed with Âryabhaṭa’s teaching more closely than its modern recast. Varâha Mihira therefore, in only occasionally directing attention to special views held by Âryabhaṭa, did all that could be expected from him.

The presumed priority of works of the nature of the *Sûrya Siddhânta* to treatises of the stamp of the *Âryabhaṭîyam* is moreover strongly confirmed by a consideration of the general form of the two. The former, even in its modern shape, is a diffuse, loosely written, ill arranged treatise; the latter, on the other hand, is a compact, highly finished and systematical compendium which, like other works of similar kind, is much more appropriately viewed as marking the end of a certain phase of literary development than its beginning. In a certain sense indeed Âryabhaṭa may perhaps be said to occupy both positions at once. Belonging to a later period than that in which the new astronomical theories had for the first time been embodied in works such as the *Pauliśa*, *Romaka* and *Saura Siddhântas*, he yet may at the same time have been, among astronomers and mathematicians, the earliest of that group of polished writers, who aimed at summarizing and systematizing in treatises, distinguished by conciseness and elegance of form and style (and apparently most of them composed in the *Âryâ* metre <note>A specific poetic meter used in Sanskrit verse</note>), the contents of the less ambitious literary products of the preceding period. This at any rate is possible, and, as far as our present knowledge goes, not improbable, although we cannot positively assert that no writers of a similar type had come forward before Âryabhaṭa’s time. Lâṭa, whom I consider to have been an author of the same class, appears to have been a somewhat younger contemporary of Âryabhaṭa. That the other writers quoted by Varâha Mihira and Brahmagupta, all of whom we may assume to have had aims similar to those of Âryabhaṭa, should have been younger than the latter astronomer, is barely possible.

Originality of doctrine can thus hardly be claimed for Âryabhaṭa, even if we understand originality in the limited sense of teaching what had not before been taught in India. The only, and indeed weighty, exception is the doctrine of the revolution of the earth on its axis, if indeed that also had not somehow been transmitted from Greece. Âryabhaṭa’s work is the only Indian one, known to us, in which that doctrine is set forth, and Brahmagupta ascribes it to him; but yet it is not quite certain whether it originated with Âryabhaṭa, or was an opinion held by others also and merely adopted by him. In chapter 13 <note>original: "XIII"</note> of the *Five Astronomical Treatises* <note>original: "Pañchasiddhântikâ"</note> Varâha Mihira when attempting to refute it does not intimate that it belonged specially to Âryabhaṭa.

The great fame which Âryabhaṭa no doubt enjoyed we are thus not able to account for quite satisfactorily. It may have been due partly to the finished conciseness of his performance, a feature always highly esteemed by Hindus; partly perhaps also to his peculiar system of notation. His astronomical work is moreover the oldest among those known to us in which there appears a chapter on mathematical science in midst of the astronomical rules, and the astronomical matter itself is exhibited in two separate sections, a <term>sphere section</term> <gloss>gola pâda</gloss> and a <term>mathematics section</term> <gloss>gaṇita pâda</gloss>. Not improbably he really was the first to effect this amalgamation of the results of native mathematical science with the astronomical science of foreign extraction, and to render the exposition of the astronomical theory clearer and more systematical by a well founded subdivision of topics; and that also might account for part of his reputation.

There is one further point which requires to be touched upon in a discussion of the possible age of the <term>Astronomical Treatises</term> <gloss>Siddhântas</gloss> on which Varâha Mihira’s work bases, *namely* <note>original: "viz."</note> the position of the initial point of the sphere from which all longitudes are reckoned. Now, for fixing the precise whereabouts of the first point of Aśvinî <note>The first lunar mansion or sign of the Hindu zodiac</note> we have to avail ourselves of the statements as to the longitudes of certain stars which are made in various old astronomical treatises, the earliest of them being the Sûrya Siddhânta <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most foundational texts of Indian astronomy</note>, according to which the so-called yogatârâ <note>term: junction star; the principal star of a lunar mansion used for astronomical calculations</note> of the asterism Revatî has no, or almost no, longitude *i. e.*, coincides, or nearly coincides, with the first point of Aśvinî. And as that junction star which has been identified with ζ piscium <note>Zeta Piscium, a star in the constellation Pisces</note> had the same longitude as the vernal equinox <note>The moment the sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of spring</note> in 572 A. D., the latter year is supposed to mark approximately the beginning of the scientific period of Hindû astronomy. If, instead of following the majority of writers, we prefer to adhere strictly to the statement made in the Sûrya Siddhânta, according to which the longitude of the junction star of Revatî is not zero but 359° 50', we are led to 560 A. D. instead of 572.

This determination of the beginning of the scientific period of Hindû astronomy has of course always rightly been looked upon as roughly approximative only, since we have no good reasons for believing that the Hindûs of that period were able to perform so difficult an operation as the determination of the place of the equinox with great accuracy. That the beginnings of scientific astronomy have to be dated back another seventy years at any rate, already follows from the admitted time of Âryabhaṭa <note>The first of the great mathematician-astronomers from the classical age of Indian mathematics</note> alone. That the Siddhântas on which Varâha Mihira drew, among them the old Sûrya Siddhânta, were also older than 572, follows from Varâha Mihira’s own time. Professor Whitney <note>William Dwight Whitney, a 19th-century American linguist and editor of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, who has discussed most thoroughly the bearings of the statements which the Sûrya Siddhânta makes about the longitudes of the junction stars, points out that if, instead of relying solely on the longitude assigned to ζ Piscium, we compare the longitudes assigned to the junction stars of all the 27 nakshatras <note>term: lunar mansions; the 27 divisions of the sky through which the moon passes</note> with their actual longitudes in 560 A. D., a certain uniformity of error observable in the statements of the Sûrya Siddhânta leads us to suspect that the measurements of position on which the list was established were made from an equinox situated about 1° to the east of that of A. D. 560 and hence at a time preceding the latter date by about seventy years.

At any rate the Sûrya Siddhânta supplies us with data enabling us to decide what point of the fixed sphere is supposed to mark the first point of Aśvinî. But these data fail us, if we turn to other astronomical works. As we have seen above, the Pañchasiddhântikâ <note>The "Five Treatises," a compendium of Greek, Egyptian, Roman, and Indian astronomy authored by Varâha Mihira</note> itself, where stating the longitudes of certain junction stars, says nothing about the junction star of Revatî, and from what it says about other junction stars we are unable to draw any well settled inferences. that Varâha Mihira <note>A celebrated 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note>, whom we suppose to have written the *Five Astronomical Treatises* <note>original: "Pañchasiddhântikâ"</note> about the middle of the sixth century, should have agreed with the *Sun Treatise* <note>original: "Sûrya Siddhânta"</note> in giving no, or almost no longitude, to the star Zeta Piscium <note>The star marking the end of the Revatî constellation</note>.

But what, we must proceed to ask, did Âryabhaṭa <note>A foundational mathematician-astronomer of the classical age of Indian mathematics</note>, and his predecessors, such as the authors of the *Roman* <note>original: "Romaka"</note> and *Paulisa Treatises* <note>original: "Pauliśa Siddhântas"</note>, understand by the first point of Aśvinî <note>The first lunar mansion or constellation in the Indian zodiac</note>? The *Short Treatise of Âryabhaṭa* <note>original: "Laghvâryabhaṭîyam"</note> says nothing about the longitudes of junction stars <note><term>junction stars</term>: specific stars used to mark the boundaries or positions of the lunar mansions (nakshatras)</note>, and we are therefore unable to determine what point of the sphere coincided, in Âryabhaṭa's view, with the first point of Aśvinî. The same remark applies to writers whom we may suppose to have anteceded Âryabhaṭa. That the authors of the *Roman* and *Paulisa* already treated the first point of Aśvinî as the initial point of the sphere, appears to follow from the *Five Astronomical Treatises*; but nothing shows that they supposed the small star Zeta Piscium to be situated just at that point. To me it appears most probable that the earliest scientific Treatises <note>original: "Siddhântas"</note> used the term 'the first point of Aśvinî' in the same sense as the Greeks used the term 'the first point of Aries' *viz.* to denote, not a fixed place in the sphere, but simply the place of the vernal equinox <note>The moment the sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of spring</note>. From the term, the 'beginning of Aśvinî' <note>original: "aśviny-âdi"</note> so much indeed follows that, when it was first coined, the vernal equinox was, according to the observations of the Hindû astronomers, somewhere to the west of the asterism Aśvinî and to the east of the asterism Revatî; but about the exact point meant to be indicated by that term we know nothing. If indeed the limits of the lunar mansions <note>original: "nakshatras"</note> had been accurately defined already before the period of the Treatises, the term 'beginning of Aśvinî' would have from the beginning indicated a definite place in the fixed sphere; but there is nothing to show that that was the case, and, as pointed out by Professor Whitney, it certainly is intrinsically improbable that the small star Zeta Piscium should ever have marked any important point in the sphere before the time when it actually happened to coincide with the vernal equinox. Thus to the author of the *Roman* for instance the term 'the first point of Aśvinî' may have meant a spot one or two or three or four or five degrees east of Zeta Piscium, any spot indeed lying to the east of the junction star of Revatî and to the west of the junction star of Aśvinî. Later on, let us say about the middle of the sixth century, it was observed that the place of the equinox coincided, or nearly coincided, with the junction star of Revatî, and as at that time the fixed sidereal system <note>A system of tracking stars based on their fixed positions rather than the shifting equinoxes</note> had exclusively established itself in India, that star has ever since been held to mark the beginning of the sphere. But the earliest testimony we have for this its position is the statement which the *Sun Treatise*, as known at present, makes about the longitudes of the junction stars, and that statement in no way proves that the same view was set forth in other books of a presumably earlier date.

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

The preceding remarks merely aim at showing that there is no evidence for the earliest <term>Siddhântas</term><note>Siddhântas are traditional Indian astronomical treatises or "established conclusions."</note> having identified the place of the vernal equinox with that of the star Zeta Piscium, and that we hence are not compelled to look for the beginnings of scientific Indian astronomy in a period not earlier than the fifth century. I do not on that account wish to assign the old Siddhântas to a very much earlier time. All I am interested in is to show the possibility of there having intervened between the early Siddhântas and Varâha Mihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath.</note> a period of sufficient length to account for the authoritative position which the former manifestly occupy in the view of the author expounding their doctrines. Every requirement may I think be looked upon as satisfied if we suppose the <term>Romaka</term><note>The "Roman" or Greek-influenced treatise.</note> and <term>Paulîśa Siddhântas</term><note>A treatise often associated with the name Paulus Alexandrinus.</note>* to have been composed not later than about 400 A.D.

---

The present edition of the <term>Pañchasiddhântikâ</term><note>Literally "The Five Astronomical Treatises," a compendium by Varâha Mihira.</note> is founded on two Manuscripts, belonging to the Bombay Government. The text of the better one of those two Manuscripts is reproduced in the left hand columns of our edition, while the foot notes give all the more important different readings from the other Manuscript. A comparison of the traditional text with the emended one, as given in the right hand columns of the edition, will show that the former had, in many cases, to be treated with great liberty. Not unfrequently the emended text is merely meant as an equivalent in sense of what we suppose Varâha Mihira to have aimed at expressing, while we attach no importance to the words actually employed in the emendation. The many quotations from the Pañchasiddhântikâ, which are to be met with in Bhaṭṭotpala’s commentary on Varâha Mihira’s <term>Bṛihatsaṃhitâ</term><note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work on astrology and divination.</note>, and which as a rule exhibit the text in a more correct form than the Manuscripts of the Pañchasiddhântikâ, have been of great help to us. In a complete <term>apparatus criticus</term><note>original: "apparatus criticus"; the critical notes and list of variants used by an editor to document the history of a text.</note> of the Pañchasiddhântikâ Bhaṭṭotpala’s readings would of course have to be exhibited in full; but as Bhaṭṭotpala’s text itself has come down to us in a very questionable condition only, we have, for the present, refrained from doing more than tacitly availing ourselves of Bhaṭṭotpala’s readings wherever they seemed to deserve preference. A few stanzas quoted by Bhaṭṭotpala and manifestly belonging to the Pañchasiddhântikâ, although not to be met with in our Manuscripts, we have inserted in the emended text.

---

* I take this opportunity of correcting, according to my present views, the translation of Chapter I, verse 10. As the translation stands, the last words of that stanza would make an interesting statement as to the relative ages of the Romaka and Paulîśa Siddhântas. But I at present have little doubt that the words <note>original: "na atichire"</note> "not at a great distance" do not mean, "which is not much older" but rather "with no great distance" (or "difference"), the meaning of the text being that the results of a calculation of the <term>ahargaṇa</term><note>The "heap of days," or the number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note> according to the principles of the Paulîśa do not differ very much from those of a calculation proceeding on the data of the Romaka Siddhânta.

<summary>The author argues for a 4th-century origin for the Romaka and Paulîśa Siddhântas and describes the methodology used to reconstruct the Pañchasiddhântikâ from flawed manuscripts and later commentaries.</summary>
<keywords>Indian astronomy, Varâha Mihira, Siddhântas, manuscript tradition, Bhaṭṭotpala, Romaka Siddhânta, Paulîśa Siddhânta, ahargaṇa, textual criticism</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory remarks by George Thibaut regarding the editorial methodology used for the Pañchasiddhântikâ.</meta>

<page-num>LXI</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

What, in the attempt to reconstitute the text of an astronomical or mathematical work, has chiefly to be kept in view, is of course to arrive at rules which are capable of being proved mathematically. This consideration, has, in more than one place, led us to introduce changes even where such appeared hardly to be required by the external form of the traditional text. I may quote, as an example, the rule for calculating the heliacal rising <note>The first visible appearance of a star in the dawn before sunrise.</note> of Agastya <note>The Sanskrit name for the star Canopus.</note>. The considerable deviation from the text of the Manuscripts which our emended text exhibits in that place appears to be absolutely called for by the general principles on which such calculations have to be performed according to all scientific Hindu treatises, and is moreover justified, as my collaborator shows in the Sanskrit Commentary, by the circumstance that the result of the emended rule of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* <note>A 6th-century astronomical treatise by Varâha Mihira; the title means "Five Treatises."</note> agrees with a statement made by Varâha Mihira in the *Brihatsamhitâ* <note>The "Great Compilation," an encyclopedic work by the same author covering astrology and divination.</note>. In a few cases, notably in the last chapter, where we were unable to emend the readings of the Manuscripts in any satisfactory way, Pandit Sudhâkara <note>Sudhâkara Dvivedî, a renowned mathematician and astronomer who assisted Thibaut.</note> has substituted for the traditional text, rules founded on the general principles of Hindu astronomy; a proceeding which will hardly be objected to, as the cases in question are pointed out in the Commentary, and as side by side with the substituted text the traditional text is exhibited in full.

->G. Th.<- <note>George Thibaut (1848–1914), the primary editor and translator.</note>

<summary>George Thibaut explains the editorial decision to prioritize mathematical accuracy over literal manuscript readings, specifically regarding the star Canopus and the contributions of Pandit Sudhâkara Dvivedî.</summary>

Multiply the midday shadow by ten and divide thirty-six <note>original: "rasa-hutāśa" (six and three, read right-to-left as 36)</note> by the result. In the afternoon, subtract this from a half-circle <note>180 degrees</note>; when added to the Sun's position, this becomes the *Lagna* <term>Lagna: The ascending point of the ecliptic on the eastern horizon</term>. || 36 ||

The minutes of the arc between the Sun and the *Lagna* should be subtracted from a half-circle, whether before or after noon. One should then create a divisor from the sum of zero, the sky <note>zero</note>, and eight <note>forming the number 800</note> divided by eight. || 37 ||

The result, minus twelve and increased by the midday shadow, is to be known as the shadow according to the Concise Vasiṣṭha Siddhānta. || 38 ||

### Section on the Calculation of Asterisms and Planets

Multiply by twelve hundred <note>sky-sun</note> and subtract the fire-fire-eater <note>original: "agni-hutāśana", representing 33</note> <gloss>43831</gloss>. Having divided by the "form-fire-wealth-fire-eater-actions" <note>the number 43831</note>, the mean position of the Lord of the Day <note>the Sun</note> and the anomaly <term>Anomaly: The angle used to calculate a planet's irregular motion</term> plus twenty degrees is found. || 39 ||

Eleven, eight, and six; seventy minus one; seventy plus zero; nine times six; and the square of the other <note>the next number</note>. These are the additive minutes <note>arc-minutes</note> corresponding to the signs of the anomaly. || 40 ||

Ten, eight, eight, and seventy; seventy-one; nine times six; and the square of five <note>25</note>. These are the increments by which the mean Sun becomes the true <note>corrected</note> Sun. || 41 ||

From the half-motion multiplied by seven, plus one-seventh, the daily motion is found. From the end of the half-motion, subtract the minutes from nine, seven, and eight <note>879</note>. || 42 ||

---

The result minus twelve, combined with the midday shadow; that is the shadow to be known in the Concise Vasiṣṭha Siddhānta. || 13 ||

# Pañcasiddhāntikā
<page-num>98</page-num>

### [Left Column]

By the method of the sequence of the <term>Chara-nāḍīs</term><note>The "ascensional difference," or the difference in time between the rising of a celestial body on the equator versus a specific latitude</note>, the diameter of the day-circle and other values are known. At the time of setting, the same procedure applies; for the remaining planets, the logic should be carefully considered. || 51 ||

From the sum of the squares of the shadow and the <term>Gnomon</term><note>The vertical pillar of a sundial, usually 12 units high</note>, take the square root. Divide the <term>Radius</term><note>original: "Trijyā"</note> multiplied by the Gnomon by this root. This result, multiplied by the <term>Sine of the Equinoctial Latitude</term><note>original: "Viṣuvajjīvā"</note> and divided by the <term>Sine of the Co-latitude</term><note>original: "Lamba-jyā"</note>, gives the <term>Amplitude of the Sun</term><note>original: "Sūryāgrā"; the angular distance of the rising sun from the East point</note>. || 52 ||

The Sine of the Sun's declination multiplied by the Radius and divided by the Sine of the Co-latitude is to be subtracted from or added to the Sun's amplitude at the beginning of Aries or Libra. This result, multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow and divided by the Radius, || 53 ||

gives the result in digits, which is the <term>Koti</term><note>The vertical side of a right-angled triangle</note>. The square root of the difference between the square of that shadow and the square of the Koti is the <term>Bāhu</term><note>The horizontal side or "arm" of the triangle</note>. In determining the directions, this should be applied correctly to the Koti according to the equality of the measure. || 54 ||

The distance between the shadow and the East-West line is multiplied by the Radius and divided by its own hypotenuse. If the directions are the same, take the difference; if different, add the Sun's amplitude. || 55 ||

The result is multiplied by the Sine of the Co-latitude and divided by the Sine of the declination; from this, the Sun's position is found. By this same method derived for the Sun, the positions of the other planets should also be calculated. || 56 ||

## Thus ends the Fourth Chapter, the Chapter on Calculations.

From the difference of the declinations, added to or subtracted from the square of the Gnomon... taking the square root of the difference of the declinations, and multiplying by the latitude... || 1 ||

The result, from the difference between the Moon and the Sun, should be added when the latitude is favorable to the declination...

<column-break/>

### [Right Column]

By the method of the sequence of the <term>Chara-nāḍīs</term>, the diameter of the day-circle and the preliminary steps are to be understood. At the time of setting, the same procedure applies; for the remaining planets, the logic should be carefully considered. || 51 ||

From the sum of the squares of the shadow and the Gnomon, take the square root. Divide the Radius multiplied by the Gnomon by this root. This result, multiplied by the Sine of the Equinoctial Latitude and divided by the Sine of the Co-latitude, gives the Amplitude of the Sun. || 52 ||

The Sine of the Sun's declination multiplied by the Radius and divided by the Sine of the Co-latitude is to be subtracted from or added to the Sun's amplitude at the beginning of Aries or Libra. This result, multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow and divided by the Radius, || 53 ||

gives the result in digits, which is the Koti. The square root of the difference between the square of that shadow and the square of the Koti is the Bāhu. In determining the directions, this should be applied correctly to the Koti according to the equality of the measure. || 54 ||

The distance between the shadow and the East-West line is multiplied by the Radius and divided by its own hypotenuse. If the directions are the same, take the difference; if different, add the Sun's amplitude. || 55 ||

The result is multiplied by the Sine of the Co-latitude and divided by the Sine of the declination; from this, the Sun's position is found. By this same method derived for the Sun, the positions of the other planets should also be calculated. || 56 ||

## Thus ends the Fourth Chapter, the Chapter on Calculations.

From the difference of the declinations, added to or multiplied by the difference of the Gnomon... taking the square root of the difference of the declinations, and multiplying by the latitude... || 1 ||

The result, from the difference between the Moon and the Sun, should be added when the latitude is favorable to the declination...

-> The sun indeed wanders directly above the gods <note>The "gods" refers to those living at the North Pole (Meru)</note> and directly above the city of Avanti <note>Modern-day Ujjain, a primary meridian in ancient Indian astronomy</note>. || 10 || <-

-> In this way, the shadow vanishes <note>at the zenith</note>; from that point onward, the shadow falls to the north for those in northern regions. For those in southern regions, the midday shadow falls to the south. || 11 || <-

-> When the sun stays in Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, the day belongs to the gods; when it enters Cancer and the following signs, it is their night. To those who have stated this regarding the inhabitants of Meru, I offer my salutations. || 12 || <-

-> In those very northern signs like Aries and the rest, even when the sun has turned back <note>after the solstice</note>, how is it that it remains visible to some and not to others staying there? || 13 || <-

-> In the visible half of the circle <note>the celestial hemisphere</note>, the accumulation of signs and degrees is the distance from the zenith. These ninety degrees should be imagined as segments starting from the point of rising. || 14 || <-

-> Each single degree consists of nine hundred yojanas <note>term: yojana; an ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> minus a ninth part. For those on the same north-south line, this is directly perceptible in the sky from the center. || 15 || <-

-> Thus, by ninety degrees, eight hundred yojanas are observed <note>This refers to the earth's curvature or specific latitudinal distances</note>. At a place of that measure, the observer's sunrise occurs at the time of another's midday. || 16 || <-

-> Ujjayinī is situated directly north of Laṅkā <note>The theoretical intersection of the equator and the prime meridian</note> on the same longitude. Their midday occurs simultaneously, though the length of the day differs except on the equinox. || 17 || <-

<note>Technical Vocabulary:
- **Pancasiddhantika**: The "Five Treatises," a major astronomical work by Varahamihira.
- **Mahija/Kuja**: Names for the planet Mars (literally "Born of the Earth").
- **Nadi/Vinadi**: Units of time used in ancient Indian astronomy.
- **Retrograde (Vakra)**: The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky.
- **True/Mean Motion (Sphuta/Madhyama)**: The difference between the calculated average position of a planet and its actual observed position.
</note>

->|| Auspiciousness ||<-

# Now begins the commentary on the *Pañcasiddhāntikā* <note>The Five Astronomical Treatises</note>, titled *Pañcasiddhāntikā-Prakāśikā* <note>The Illuminator of the Five Treatises</note>, composed by Sudhākara.

---

->Salutations to Lord Rāmacandra.<-

---

> To Lord Rāma, the lotus of the Solar Dynasty, together with Sītā,
> I offer constant remembrance while I explain the *Karaṇa* <note>A practical astronomical manual</note> born of Varāhamihira.
> Because the original manuscripts were unavailable, many words have become corrupted;
> May the wise and noble scholars correct the many errors written here using their own intellect.

1. Now, for the obstacle-free completion of the work, the author performs an auspicious invocation: "To the Sun, Vasiṣṭha, and others..."
Here, it is only fitting to offer salutations to those Teachers by whom the science of light <note>Jyotiḥśāstra or Astronomy/Astrology</note> was expanded and from whom the knowledge of this science was obtained. Having saluted them, he declares his intention in the following verse.

2. "From the opinions of the former Teachers..."
The *Bīja* <note>A correction factor applied to astronomical calculations to ensure they match observed reality</note> is a specific refinement intended to unify observation and calculation. I am prepared to speak that very secret and hidden essence, derived from the opinions of former Teachers, in its entirety and correctness—this is the connection of the text. To refute the idea that this *Bīja* is merely my own invention, the phrase "from the opinions of former Teachers" is used. This means the Teacher's intention is to make an effort to speak only that which is proven as a hidden correction within the ancient systems; the rest of the meaning is clear.

3. Now he describes whose *Siddhāntas* <note>Established astronomical treatises</note> are being presented here: "The *Pauliśa*, the *Romaka*..."
There are five treatises here: the first composed by Pauliśa, the second by Romaka, the third propounded by Vasiṣṭha, the fourth revealed by the Sun, and the fifth spoken by Brahmā. According to the dialogue between the Sun and Aruṇa, the knowledge spoken by the Great Sage Puliśa to sages like Garga is the *Pauliśa*. That which was spoken by the Sun (who appeared in the city of Rome due to a curse from Brahmā) to Romaka among the Yavana <note>Greek or Western</note> peoples is the *Romaka*. That which was given by Vasiṣṭha to his son Parāśara is the *Vāsiṣṭha*. That which was commanded by the Sun to the demon Maya is the *Saura* <note>The Surya Siddhānta</note>. And that which was given by Brahmā to his own son Vasiṣṭha became the *Paitāmaha* treatise. Such is the statement of the Sun to Aruṇa.

<summary>This page introduces Sudhākara’s commentary on Varāhamihira’s classic astronomical work, identifying the five ancient systems of Indian astronomy and their legendary origins. It emphasizes the importance of the Bīja correction to align mathematical theory with physical observation.</summary>

By these verses, and by the teacher’s auspicious opening which begins with "The Sun, Vasishtha, and the others," it is understood that the first composition was made by Brahma, then by Vasishtha, then by the Sun, then by Pulisha, and then by Romaka. Now, from the phrase "This secret knowledge, situated within the Veda, was remembered by the Grandfather," it is established that Brahma obtained that very knowledge which existed as a limb <note>Vedanga</note> within the boundaries of the Veda; therefore, the composition of the <term>Brahma-siddhanta</term> <note>The system of Brahma</note> occurred at nearly the same time as the composition of the Vedangas. That knowledge was given by Brahma to his son Vasishtha, and published in the world by Vasishtha under his own name. From this, it appears that the composition of the <term>Vasishtha-siddhanta</term> <note>The system of Vasishtha</note> followed shortly after the composition of the Brahma-siddhanta, as is known by a subtle examination of the respective authors. However, the time of the composition of the <term>Surya-siddhanta</term> <note>The system of the Sun</note> is stated by <term>Nityananda</term> <note>A 17th-century astronomer</note>, the author of the <term>Siddhantaraja</term>, to be when 2,600 years of the Kali Age had passed. That time is well-known as the period of the Siddhanta composed by <term>Aryabhata</term> <note>The famous 5th-century Indian mathematician</note>. Therefore, the <term>Surya-siddhanta</term> is established as being contemporary with the Siddhanta of <term>Aryabhata</term>, and this truth is evident.

It also attempts to chronologically place the Surya-siddhanta alongside the era of the astronomer Aryabhata.</summary>

# The Illumination of the Five Treatises

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>The Illumination of the Five Treatises (Pañcasiddhāntikā-prakāśikā)</header>

In the *Aryabhatiya* system propounded by Nityānanda, the views of the *Sūrya Siddhānta* are not established anywhere. The *Sūrya Siddhānta* currently in circulation, which claims to date from the end of the Golden Age <note>Krita Yuga</note>, is clearly a modern reconstruction by someone else; this is evident to calculators <note>astronomers</note> who engage in subtle discernment.

In India, only the treatises <term>Siddhāntas: comprehensive astronomical treatises</term> composed by Sages are considered authoritative, and no others. Therefore, ancient Indian teachers accepted a treatise composed by a Sage, applied corrections <term>Bīja: observational corrections applied to planetary formulas</term> to it, and then established their own systems. For example, Brahmagupta accepted the *Brahma Siddhānta* and composed his own treatise.

> (The planetary calculation spoken by Brahma, which had become decayed over a long period of time, is now clearly expressed by Brahmagupta, the son of Jiṣṇu.)

Bhāskarācārya also accepted that same *Brahma Siddhānta*, and others similarly accept the *Sūrya Siddhānta* and its peers. Because of this, later scholars refer to the treatises composed by those specific teachers by the names of the Sages they adopted. This is precisely why the teacher Varāhamihira says: "Of the five, the first two were explained by Lāṭadeva." This means that the teacher Lāṭa explained the two treatises—the *Pauliśa* and the *Romaka*—and expanded them in his own work after applying corrections to the revolutions of the planets. What is being said here is that Lāṭācārya accepted the *Pauliśa* and *Romaka* treatises and, by making specific corrections, composed a different treatise. Therefore, with the thought that "my handbook <term>Karaṇa: a practical astronomical manual</term> should be accepted by all people," the Teacher <note>Varāhamihira</note> composed this *Pañcasiddhāntikā* by adopting the views of the five treatises. In the same way, Viṣṇucandra and others accepted the *Vasiṣṭha Siddhānta* and others to compose their own works; in my opinion, they are not the direct authors of the original *Vasiṣṭha* and other treatises.

As for the claim some make—based on Brahmagupta's statement "having taken from Śrīṣeṇa"—that the *Romaka Siddhānta* was authored by Śrīṣeṇa, that is not the case. Such an assumption would make the *Romaka Siddhānta* more recent than Lāṭācārya, which contradicts its inclusion in the traditional canon. Thus, in my view, the correct reading of that passage is: "Having taken from Śrīṣeṇa, the Romaka [calculation] of the Sun's apogee was made..." <note>original: "śrīṣeṇena gṛhītvā ravoccaraumakaḥ kṛtaḥ kanyā"</note>.

In my opinion, the *Sūrya*, *Pauliśa*, and *Romaka* treatises are roughly contemporary; I shall elaborate on this further to strengthen this point.

4. Now he describes the agreement between observation and calculation for the five treatises. Regarding the one made by Pauliśa:
->The meaning is clear.<-

5-7. Now he describes his own duty. Regarding "That which is supreme," etc.:
->The meaning is clear.<-

8-10. Now he describes the calculation of the number of elapsed days <term>Ahargaṇa: the count of civil days from a fixed epoch</term>. Regarding "The number seven, horses, and Vedas," etc.:
->The meaning is clear.<-

Here is the mathematical proof: According to the verse stated by the Teacher <note>Varāhamihira</note> regarding the Moon in the Romaka Era, in 2,850 solar years there are:
Intercalary months <term>Adhimāsa</term> = 1,050
Omitted days <term>Kṣayāha</term> = 16,549
From these, Solar months = 34,200
Lunar days = 1,050,500
Civil days <term>Sāvana-dina</term> = 1,040,953
The value of intercalary months in one solar month = $\frac{1050}{34200}$

He also begins the technical calculation of the Romaka system's calendar constants.</summary>
<keywords>Pañcasiddhāntikā, Sūrya Siddhānta, Brahmagupta, Varāhamihira, Pauliśa Siddhānta, Romaka Siddhānta, intercalary month, omitted days, solar months, civil days</keywords>

# Elucidation of the Five Treatises
<page-num>4</page-num>

$= \frac{Desired}{Desired}$ From this, the calculation of intercalary months <note>Adhimāsa: extra months added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar seasons</note> by proportion is established. Then, the measure of the omitted lunar day <note>Kṣayāha or Avama: a lunar day that is skipped in the civil calendar because it begins and ends within the same solar day</note> in one lunar day is:
$= \frac{16549}{4575500} = \frac{11}{303}$ approximately. From this, the calculation of the omitted days by proportion is established. At the beginning of the calculation, the "Manu-Shara" <note>The number 514</note> is the additive constant <term>Kṣepa (additive constant used to adjust calculations to a specific epoch)</term> suitable for multiplication by zero and seven; thus all is established. Here, this should be noted: the Teacher <note>Varāhamihira, the author of the original text</note> has indeed mentioned the intercalary month additive constant for the start of another epoch due to a slight difference, because there, by the rule "From the solar Romaka, from the sum of the cycles..." etc., the absence of an intercalary additive constant is not proven. I shall explain this distinction further in the commentary on that specific verse.

**11–16** Now, he describes the measures of the intercalary months etc., according to the opinions of the other four treatises <note>Siddhāntas</note>, which are useful for calculating the total elapsed days <term>Ahargaṇa (the number of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a given date)</term> belonging to those systems. "Divided by two and seven," etc.

According to the opinion of Bhaṭṭotpala <note>A famous 10th-century commentator on Indian astronomical works</note>, the measure of the solar year in the Pauliśa and Saura systems is the same; they differ only in name. That is to say, the solar measure found in the opinion of Parāśara and others was given the name "civil" <term>Sāvana (a day measured from sunrise to sunrise)</term> by the teacher Puliśa. Similarly, the civil measure was given the name "solar." However, if one accepts this and calculates the intercalary months according to the Pauliśa method, a great discrepancy arises compared to the method stated by the Teacher. Therefore, although the true meaning of verses 11–13 has not yet been fully grasped, the approximate values of solar days in one intercalary month are written here according to Bhaṭṭotpala’s written Pauliśa opinion, for the purpose of correcting verses 11–13.

# The Illumination of the Five Siddhāntas
### Page 3

17–22. Now he describes the method for determining the Lord of the Year and other regents. Starting with the verse "Sages, twins, twins..." <note>original: *muni-yama-yama...* refers to the number 2227 using the Katapayadi system where words represent numbers</note>.
> The remainder for each zodiac sign; "with those attained" means including the current one.
> That is, increased by one. The rest is self-explanatory.

Here is the mathematical proof: Having conceptualized a single year as consisting of 360 civil days <term>savana-dina; a day measured from sunrise to sunrise</term>, the day of the week on which that year begins is designated by the ancients as the Lord of the Year for the purpose of astrological results. In this context, the total count of days <term>ahargana; the number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term> is divided into two parts: one from the beginning of the astronomical calculations to the start of the era, and the second from the start of the text to the current day. Here, the first part is divided by 2520 <note>represented by the code "zero-two-five-twins"</note>. A constant segment equal to 2227 <note>represented by "sages-twins-twins-mountains"</note> is established. Thus, the form of the day-count from the start of calculations = (2520 × quotient) + 2227 + days. Now, this (2227 + days) is also divided by 2520. Let the quotient be *q'* and the remainder be *r*. Then the previous day-count is rewritten as: 2520q + 2520q' + r.

Dividing this by 360 <note>represented by "sky-seasons-fires"</note>, the years obtained = 7q + 7q' + <gloss>r</gloss> / 360. Let the quotient of *r* divided by 360 be <term>elapsed years</term> and the remainder be *r'*. For the sake of the current year, that quotient is increased by one. Therefore, the total years from the start of calculations to the current year = 7q + 7q' + elapsed years + 1. Now, since 360 divided by 7 leaves a remainder of 2, the year-count is multiplied by three <note>to find the shift in weekdays</note>, resulting in: 21q + 21q' + 3(elapsed years + 1). At the start of the calculations, the Lord of the Year was Mercury; to calculate from the Sun onwards, an additive constant of 3 is added from the time of the epoch. The Lord of the Year (starting from Sunday) becomes = 21q + 21q' + 3(elapsed years + 1) + 3. Removing multiples of seven, we get = 3(elapsed years + 1) + 3 - 7 = 3(elapsed years + 1) - 4. If this number exceeds seven, multiples of seven are again removed. Thus, verses 17–18 are proven. Similarly, by dividing the day-count by twenty to find the months, increasing by one for the current month, and multiplying the month-count by two and dividing by seven, the Lord of the Month is derived. By this, the proof of verse 19 becomes clear.

Now, it is well known that the Lord of the Day is found by dividing by seven.
"The Lord of the Hour <term>hora; an astrological hour</term> is the sixth in succession from the Lord of the Day," etc. By this rule, the Lords of the Hours increase by five for each hour. The first hour belongs to the Lord of the Day itself. Therefore, (Hour - 1) multiplied by five and added to the Lord of the Day gives the elapsed Lord of the Hour = Day-Lord + 5(Hour - 1). Since adding any multiple of seven does not change the regent, we add 14 times the Day-Lord: = 14(Day-Lord) + Day-Lord + 5(Hour - 1) = 15(Day-Lord) - 5 + 5(Hour) = 5(3 × Day-Lord - 1 + Hour). Then this number, when divided by seven, gives the Lords of the Hours. The rule "the Lord of the Year is the fourth" etc., is easily understood, and thus everything is proven.

23–25. Now he explains the names and the method for bringing forth the Lords of the degrees of the zodiac signs for the purpose of predicting results.
Starting with the verse "In an even sign, increased by one..."
Here, first the day-count is divided by the number of civil days in a solar year, and the remainder is divided by twenty. From the mean motion, the degrees of the signs are calculated. For the sake of the current degree, the day-count is increased by one. The Lords of these degrees are as follows: The Lotus-Born (Brahma), the Lord of Creatures (Prajapati), the Heavenly One (Indra), the Moon, the Worshipful One, the Dwelling, and Lakshmi.

2-6. Now he describes the calculation of the Moon. "Six, three, nine..." etc.
The "Day-count" <term>Ahargaṇa: the number of days elapsed since a fixed epoch</term> is increased by 1636. Then, divided by 3031, the resulting quotient is known as the **Cube-term** <note>Sanskrit: Ghana-saṃjñā</note>. The remainder is multiplied by nine and divided by 248; the quotient is known as the **Motion-term** <note>Gati-saṃjñā</note> and the remainder is known as the **Step-term** <note>Pada-saṃjñā</note>. The Cube-term is divided by sixteen; the remainder is set aside, multiplied by three, and divided by four; the result is in Signs <note>Rāśi: 30 degrees</note> etc., which is subtracted from the remainder set aside as Revolutions <note>Bhagaṇa</note>. This is to be known as the **First Part**. Then, the Cube-term is doubled and divided by 2971; the result in Signs etc. is the **Second Part**. One hundred and eighty-five (185) is multiplied by the Motion-term, then decreased by one-eighth of the Motion and one-tenth of the Motion; the result in minutes <note>Kalā</note> is the **Third Part**. However, if the Step-term is greater than 124, then half of the Motion-term should be added to those Motion-terms to calculate the Third Part as previously stated. From the Step-term, 124 should be subtracted; the remainder is then known as the Step-term. Then, in the refinement of the three parts, if the Step-term exceeded 124, six Signs <note>half a revolution</note> plus four minutes must be added, and degrees equal to the remaining Step-term must also be added. This means: when the Step-term is greater than 124, one makes a new Step-term from the remainder after subtracting 124 and adds degrees equal to that; otherwise, degrees equal to the original Step-term are added to the Third Part—then the **Mean Moon** is found. Then, from those steps, the following result should be applied. That is to say, the wise should understand for themselves: subtract when the steps are less than 124, and add when they are more. Thus, the remaining Step-term minus one, multiplied by five, and increased by 1094—this sum is subtracted from 2414. The remainder, multiplied by the remaining Step-term and divided by twenty, gives a result in minutes which is applied to the previously calculated Mean Moon; then the **True Mean Moon** is obtained.

Now the derivation: The Teacher has divided the Day-count into three parts. Multiplying these numbers by 3031 gives the first part. Multiplying the Motion-term by 248 and dividing by nine gives the second part. Dividing the Step-term by nine gives the third part. By doing this, the transformed version of the Day-count becomes:
$= \text{Cube} \times 3031 + \frac{248 \times \text{Motion}}{9} + \frac{\text{Step}}{9}$
By multiplying these three parts separately by the Moon's motion and adding them together, the calculation of the Moon is easy. For example, in the first part, the Moon resulting from a group of 3031 days is:
$= 1 - \frac{<gloss>Rev.</gloss> / 3}{4} + \frac{<gloss>Sign</gloss> / 2}{2971}$ <gloss>Rev.</gloss> is Cube-multiplier <gloss>Sign</gloss> is Cube $- \frac{<gloss>Sign</gloss> / 3}{4} + \frac{<gloss>Sign</gloss> / 2}{2971}$

8. Now he describes the length of the day. Starting from Capricorn:

Starting from Capricorn, day by day, [the day length increases] by the measure of "Earth-Heaven-Lunar Day" <note>A Sanskrit numerical code (bhū-svarga-tithi) where Earth=1, Heaven=5, and Tithi=15, representing 1591</note>, which is 1591, increased by three <term>Palas</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> at a time; that becomes the day length. Similarly, starting from Cancer, that same value becomes the <term>Sharvarimana</term> (the length of the night).

**The logic here:** In the city of Ujjain <note>original: "Avantika"</note>, the minimum day length at the start of Capricorn is assumed to be 1591 Palas. From that point, an increase of three Palas per day is calculated for the day length. Since the day length at the start of Capricorn is equal to the night length at the start of Cancer, the Teacher has stated that this same value represents the night length starting from Cancer; thus, the explanation is faultless.

9-10. Now he explains the noon shadow and how to find the Sun's position from the noon shadow. Starting from Cancer:

The measure of the signs traversed by the Sun starting from Cancer, when doubled, becomes the length of the shadow at noon. By this same logic, whatever result is obtained starting from Capricorn should be subtracted from the "Circle" of twelve; that gives the Sun's position at that place. Thus, on a desired day, half of the noon shadow represents the number of signs; when added to three signs, that is the Sun's position during the Southern Solstice <note>original: "Yamya-ayana"</note>. During the Northern Solstice <note>original: "Udaga-ayana"</note>, the previously mentioned half-shadow should be subtracted from fifteen; that gives the Sun's position.

**The logic here:** In Ujjain, according to the ancient system, the latitude is equal to the maximum declination, which is <term>Jina 24</term> <note>The number 24, named after the 24 Jinas of Jainism</note> degrees. Therefore, when the Sun is at the start of Cancer, there is no noon shadow. From that point, sign by sign, the shadow is assumed to increase by two digits <note>Angulas</note> at noon. Therefore, it is said that the signs elapsed from the start of Cancer, doubled, become the noon shadow. By this same logic, when the Sun enters Capricorn, the remaining signs from Cancer are doubled to equal twelve digits, which is the shadow of a twelve-digit <term>Gnomon</term> <note>original: "Shanku," a vertical pillar used to cast shadows for timekeeping</note>. Thereafter, the shadow decreases; for this reason, it is said that it should be subtracted from the "Circle" <note>the number 12</note> starting from Capricorn. Now, the Southern Solstice begins from Cancer; at the start of the Southern Solstice, the Sun's measure is three signs. Thus, the elapsed signs from Cancer doubled is the noon shadow; therefore, half the noon shadow will be the elapsed signs. Adding that to three signs gives the Sun's position by reversing the previous method. Similarly, in the Northern Solstice starting from Capricorn, the Sun's measure is nine signs; then the noon shadow is equal to twelve minus twice the signs elapsed from Capricorn. Therefore:

->$\text{Noon Shadow} = 12 - 2 (\text{Signs elapsed from Capricorn})$<-
->Therefore, $2 (\text{Signs elapsed from Capricorn}) = 12 - \text{Noon Shadow}$<-

Likewise, the signs traversed starting from Capricorn = 6 – <gloss>Capricorn</gloss>/2. Then, this value of the traversed signs, when added to the measure of the sun starting from Capricorn, results in the sun's measure during the northern transit (Uttarayana) = 15 – <gloss>Capricorn</gloss>/2. 11–13 Now, he describes the calculation of the Ascendant <term>Lagna; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> from the shadow, and the calculation of the shadow from the Ascendant. "By twelve with the desired shadows," etc.

The dividend is "flavors and fires" <note>A system of numerical notation where 'flavors' (rasa) equals 6 and 'fires' (hutāśa) equals 3, read right-to-left as 36</note>, i.e., thirty-six. The divisor is the desired shadow plus twelve, with the midday shadow subtracted. When the dividend is divided by this divisor, the quotient obtained is added to the sun's position in signs; that becomes the Ascendant. In the western hemisphere <note>afternoon</note>, however, the first quotient obtained should be subtracted from a half-circle (six signs), and the remainder added to the sun's position; that becomes the Ascendant. 

Now, for calculating the shadow from the Ascendant: subtract the sun's position from the Ascendant. In the eastern hemisphere <note>forenoon</note>, the remainder in minutes of arc <term>liptā; 1/60th of a degree</term> serves as the divisor. In the western hemisphere, those minutes should be subtracted from the minutes of a half-circle <note>10,800 minutes</note> to find the divisor. Of what? Of "zero-sky-atmosphere-cloud-Vedas-sixes" <note>Another numerical code: 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 6, representing 64,800</note>, i.e., 64,800. From the result of that division, twelve should be subtracted, and the midday shadow added to the remainder. Then, according to the *Lesser Vasistha Siddhanta*, the shadow at the desired time is found.

The derivation is as follows: The ancient tradition holds that the point of the ecliptic <term>krāntivṛtta; the sun's path</term> which touches the eastern horizon at a given time is the Ascendant. Therefore, at sunrise, the sun itself is the Ascendant. At midday, it is assumed to be roughly equal to the sun plus three signs. At that time, the difference between midday and the desired time is zero, and the difference between the desired and midday shadows will be = (Desired Shadow – Midday Shadow). By applying an inverse proportion—since the result decreases as the shadow increases—if twelve yields a difference of two signs between the sun and the Ascendant, what is obtained by the difference of the midday and desired shadows plus twelve? This gives the difference between the sun and the Ascendant in signs.

---

-> Thus, the difference = <gloss>12 x 3</gloss> / (12 + Desired Shadow - Midday Shadow) <-

When the sun is in the eastern hemisphere, this [difference] added to the sun is the Ascendant. In the western hemisphere, this difference is the distance from the sun to the seventh Ascendant <note>the setting point</note>; therefore, it must be subtracted from a half-circle (six signs) to find the difference between the sun and the Ascendant. By adding the sun to that difference, the Ascendant is known. Similarly, in calculating the shadow from the Ascendant, the difference between the Ascendant and the sun in the eastern hemisphere is the result of the previous proportion. In the western hemisphere, that difference is subtracted from a half-circle. However, the Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> has used the difference in minutes here. Therefore, the difference in signs from the previous proportion, multiplied by 1,800, is equal to the difference calculated now. By doing so, we get:

-> Diff = <gloss>36 x 1800</gloss> / (12 + Desired Shadow - Midday Shadow) = <gloss>64800</gloss> / (12 + Desired Shadow - Midday Shadow) <-

Therefore, 12 + Desired Shadow - Midday Shadow = <gloss>64800</gloss> / Diff. Then, by rearrangement, Desired Shadow = (64800 / Diff) – 12 + Midday Shadow. Thus, everything is proven.

### Thus ends the section on the division of Nakshatras and other matters.

# 1-6 Now, he describes the calculation of the Sun and Moon according to the Pauliśa system. "Multiplied by the sky and the sun," etc.

When the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The count of elapsed days since the epoch</note> is multiplied by one hundred and twenty <note>original: "khārka-viṃśatyadhika-śatena" (sky=0, sun=12, plus 20 = 120)</note>, and from that product thirty-three <note>original: "agni-hutāśana" (fire=3, fire=3)</note> is subtracted, the remainder is divided by 43,831 <note>original: "rūpāgni-vasu-hutāśa-kṛtaiḥ" (1, 3, 8, 3, 4 in reverse order)</note>. The result gives the mean Sun in revolutions, signs, etc. From that, the <term>Anomaly</term><note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee</note> is found. That Anomaly should be increased by twenty degrees <note>original: "saviṃśāṃśa"</note> to determine the working Anomaly. Then, for the six signs of the Anomaly, the following minutes <note>arc-minutes</note> are to be added as an increase to the mean Sun. Specifically, the minutes arising from the two sets of tabular factors for the first six signs are additive, and for the second six signs, they are subtractive; thus the true Sun is determined. Those minutes are: eleven (11), forty-eight (48), sixty-six (66), sixty-six (66), fifty-four (54), and twenty-five (25).
And also: ten (10), forty-eight (48), seventy (70), seventy-one (71), fifty-four (54), and twenty-five (25).

->Specifically, the First Factors = 11, 48, 66, 66, 54, 25<-
->The Second Factors = 10, 48, 70, 71, 54, 25<-

To demonstrate the application of this method: suppose the Anomaly (increased by 20°) is one sign. Then the result from the first factor for one sign is 11, and from the second factor is 10. Their sum gives the <term>Equation of Center</term><note>The correction needed to find the true position from the mean position</note> as twenty-one. Similarly, if the Anomaly is six signs, the sum of the first factors is 25 and the second factors is 25, resulting in an Equation of Center of fifty minutes.

If the Anomaly (increased by 20°) equals seven signs, one should take the first factors again from the beginning. Or rather, when the Anomaly exceeds six signs, subtract six signs from it and take the corresponding factors from the two sets based on the remainder; the resulting Equation of Center then becomes negative <note>original: "dhanātmakaṃ" here implies the magnitude, but the context of the second half of the circle implies subtraction</note>. The author <note>Varahamihira</note> did not explicitly write how to calculate the Anomaly according to the Pauliśa system here; it is inferred that this was because the Pauliśa method for the Anomaly was extremely well-known during the author's time.

---

->Now, the Mathematical Proof. Let the degrees of Anomaly be: 10°, 40°, 70°, 100°, 130°, 160°<-

Then, with a maximum Equation of Center of 140' according to the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> method, the Equations are:
Anomaly (An) = 10°, 40°, 70°, 100°, 130°, 160°
Sine of An <note>original: "jyā-ke"</note> = 21, 77, 113, 118, 62, 41
Resulting Minutes = 24', 60', 132', 138', 100', 47'

Now, adding twenty degrees to the aforementioned Anomaly degrees (10°, 40°, 70°, 100°, 130°, 160°), we get the signs:
Signs (S) = 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6. The Pauliśa factors related to these signs are:
<margin>When these two are summed, the minutes of the Equation of Center are produced.</margin>
1st Factor = 11, 48, 66, 66, 54, 25 }
2nd Factor = 10, 48, 70, 71, 54, 25 }
Equation = 21 | 96 | 136 | 137 | 108 | 50. These minutes are nearly equal to the previously calculated Equations of Center; therefore, my explanation is correct.

### 10-12 Now he describes the calculation of the ascensional difference <note>The 'ascensional difference' (chara) is the variation in the length of the day compared to the equinox.</note> and related factors. "Twenty, eighteen," and so on.

The numbers are: twenty (20), eighteen and a half (18.5) <note>original: "ashti" usually means 16, but the text specifies "sardha-shodasha" or 16.5; however, the calculation follows the specific parameters of this system</note>, and seven minus a quarter (6.75). These figures are to be multiplied by the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha: the length of a shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</term>. When placed in direct and reverse order, these become the segments of the ascensional difference in breaths <note>Pala: a unit of time equal to 6 seconds</note> for the signs beginning with Aries. In the three signs starting with Aries, the increase in daylight from the equinox is measured by the accumulation of these segments. In the three signs starting with Cancer, the increase decreases by those same segments. Similarly, in the six signs starting with Libra, there is a decrease in the length of the day.

For example, in Ujjain, the equinoctial shadow is 5. Multiplying this by 20, 18.5, and 6.75 in order, we get 100, 42, and 34 <note>Rounded figures</note>. These are the segments for the growth of the signs starting with Aries. In reverse order—34, 42, 100—they are the segments for the signs starting with Cancer. Again, in direct order—100, 42, 34—for the signs starting with Libra. And again, in reverse order—34, 42, 100—for the signs starting with Capricorn. Thus, the segments for the first six signs starting with Aries are:

| Aries | Taurus | Gemini | Cancer | Leo | Virgo |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 100 | 42 | 34 | 34 | 42 | 100 |

For the six signs starting with Libra:

| | Libra | Scorpio | Sagittarius | Capricorn | Aquarius | Pisces |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | 100 | 42 | 34 | 34 | 42 | 100 |

By adding these segments together, the total ascensional difference in breaths for the signs starting with Aries is:

| Aries | Taurus | Gemini |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 100 | 142 | 176 |

For the signs starting with Cancer:

| Cancer | Leo | Virgo |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 176 | 142 | 100 |

And similarly for the signs starting with Libra:

| Libra | Scorpio | Sagitt. | Capric. | Aqua. | Pisces |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 100 | 142 | 176 | 176 | 142 | 100 |

**The Rationale:** If we assume an equinoctial shadow of one digit and calculate the ascensional difference for the Aries group, and then separate them, they are produced by multiplying by specific factors. To calculate the total length of the day, the Teacher <note>Referring to Varahamihira, the author of the original text</note> doubled these and recited "Twenty," etc. By proportion, if these doubled segments are for a one-digit shadow, what would they be for the desired shadow? Thus, the doubled segments for one's own location are established. From the equinox, the increase in day length accumulates through the signs of Aries, then the increase diminishes through the signs of Cancer. Similarly, the decrease in day length accumulates through Libra and diminishes through Capricorn.

This operation for the minutes of ascensional difference is accurate within the "circumference of the Ocean and the Himalayas" <note>Meaning the Indian subcontinent</note>. This means that from the Ocean to the Himalayas, the ascensional difference remains accurate using these segments with very little error. Further away, as the equinoctial shadow increases, a discrepancy in the segments occurs. For that reason, he says, "I shall explain in the graphical representation how this may be made clear elsewhere."

### 13-15 Now he describes the difference in longitude. "The ghatikas arising from the distance to Yavana," and so on.

From the city of the Greeks <note>Yavanapura, often identified as Alexandria</note> to Avanti <note>Modern Ujjain</note>, there are seven and one-third <gloss>7:20</gloss> <term>Ghatikas: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> of longitudinal difference. For Varanasi, the difference is nine ghatikas. Furthermore, the Teacher explains the method for knowing the longitudinal difference in time: From the total distance in *yojanas* <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> between two cities, multiply by nine and divide by eighty <gloss>80</gloss>. From that result, squared... [the text describes a geometric calculation involving the difference in latitudes between the prime meridian and one's own location].

# Light on the Five Treatises (Pañcasiddhāntikā-prakāśikā)

One should subtract or abandon the remainder's square root divided by sixty; then the <term>ghaṭikās</term> <note>units of time equal to 24 minutes</note> of terrestrial longitude are found. From these longitudinal minutes, in the first half of the circle <note>the first 180 degrees of the zodiac</note> during the northern course of the sun, a subtraction must be made from half of the previously calculated ascensional difference. In the latter half of the circle and during the southern course, an addition must be made. Then the "clear" or corrected minutes are obtained. One should also abandon that speed and quickly set aside the ascensional difference.

The proof here is as follows: Let the point *Re* be the location of the prime meridian and its meridian circle. Let the point *De* be one's local position and its meridian circle. The true circumference passing through point *De* is *De-La*. The distance between the prime meridian *Re* and the local position *De* in degrees is known from the distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>an ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly 8-13 km</note> by proportion: If the Earth's circumference corresponds to the degrees of a circle, then what do the *yojanas* of the distance correspond to? The result is *Re-De* = (Degrees of the circle × Distance in *yojanas*) / Earth's circumference. The Teacher <note>Varāhamihira</note> assumed the Earth's circumference to be 3200 *yojanas*. Then *Re-De* = (360 × *yojanas*) / 3200 = (6 × *yojanas*) / 80. Since *Re-La* is equal to the difference in latitude, and considering the small distance, we imagine the triangle *Re-De-La* to be a right-angled triangle.

<margin>
Re
La
Dhru
De
</margin>

The square root of the difference of the squares of *Re-De* and *Re-La* is assumed to be equal to *De-La*. The value obtained for *De-La* in degrees is then divided by six to get the half-minutes. The previously obtained ascensional difference was doubled, then halved, and the remainder here is easy to understand.

### 16. Now he describes the calculation of Lunar Days (Tithis) and Lunar Mansions (Nakṣatras). "A mansion is 800 minutes," etc.

Eight hundred minutes of arc constitute one <term>Nakṣatra</term> <note>Lunar Mansion</note>. Therefore, by proportion, the mansion is calculated from the minutes of the planet's position. This means: the minutes of the planet divided by 800 gives the number of passed mansions. The remaining minutes are the minutes passed in the current mansion. By subtracting these from 800, the remaining minutes to be traversed are found. Similarly, the <term>Tithis</term> <note>Lunar days</note> are found by dividing the distance between the Sun and the Moon by twelve degrees. To find the time of the mansion, a proportion of the daily motion must be made: If sixty <term>ghaṭikās</term> are obtained from the total daily motion, then what is obtained from the passed or remaining minutes? The results are the passed and remaining minutes of time respectively. In calculating the time of the *Tithi*, the difference between the motions of the Sun and Moon should be used in the proportion.

### 17. He describes the Sun's motion month by month. "Multiplied by three, fire," etc.

From sixty (60), sequentially subtracted by: three (3), "fire" (3), three (3), "fire" (3), "twins" (2), and "moon" (1). Then in the first six months, the minutes of motion are 57, 57, 57, 57, 58, and 59. Then that same sixty is increased by one, and by one and one; that is, sixty is placed in four positions and increased by one in each. Then that same sixty is joined with "poet" (6) and "poet" (6) <note>original: "kavi-kavi-yutā", where kavi represents the number 6</note>, and in one place decreased by "sky" (0) and in another by one. Then the minutes are 61, 61, 61, 61, 60, and 59. This is the sequential daily motion of the Sun in the other six months.

The proof here: By treating each zodiac sign as the anomaly and calculating the gross correction for motion, the minutes of motion for the twelve months are established through that refinement.

### 18-19. Now he describes the calculation of the Karana. "Of the bright and dark halves," etc.

From the Moon's position minus the Sun's position, the minutes are divided by "sky-seasons-fires" (360). The result is the <term>Karana</term> <note>half of a lunar day</note>. However, in the bright and dark fortnights, six degrees must be subtracted or added respectively. This means: subtract six degrees from the difference between the Sun and Moon in the bright fortnight and convert the remainder to minutes. In the dark fortnight, add six degrees to the difference and convert to minutes. Then divide by "sky-six-Rama" (360)...
