Because the bottom of the vessel is small, the piercing <note>the hole for water flow</note> should be made such that in a full day and night, sixty units of water are added; meaning, if the immersion happens sixty times, that constitutes one *ghatika* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. Because the sixty piercings are curved, crooked, and long, there is another verse. Or, one *nadi* <note>synonym for ghatika</note> is equal to the time taken to recite sixty verses. The meaning is that the time it takes to read sixty verses is one *nadi*.

<margin>
Water measure for a day and night
---
60

Now for the explanation: There are sixty *ghatikas* in a day and night. Therefore, by proportion, if the amount of water that flows out in sixty *ghatikas* (a full day) is known, then what is obtained in one *ghatika*? That is the measure of water for one *ghatika*. Furthermore, the time between one breath and the second breath is considered two *asus* <note>a unit of time based on respiration</note>. Three of these make one *pala*, and sixty *palas* make one *nadi*. Thus, one *nadi* is also equal to 180 breaths. The time to pronounce ten long syllables is one *asu*; therefore, six *asus* or sixty long syllables make one *pala*. This is the same as the time to recite a verse; hence, it is proven that sixty verses make one *nadi*. Here, the Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> has described the *ghati* vessel using the meter of the verse itself, starting with "A vessel shaped like a jar..."

33. Now, he speaks regarding the conjunction of stars and the Moon: *“Having understood the Moon’s deviation...”*

Having understood or known the *vikshepa* <note>celestial latitude</note> or "arrow" of the Moon, and having observed the distance between the star and the Moon, one should first determine everything through observation. Then, having calculated everything using mathematical methods for the desired time, the conjunction of the star with the Moon should be announced.

34--38. Now, for the purpose of conjunction, he states the suitability of certain stars for observation: *“At the end of the sixth part of Krittika...”*

At the end of the sixth part of *Bahula* (Krittika), at a distance of three and a half *hastas* <note>a "cubit" or hand-length, used here as an angular measure</note> north of the ecliptic circle, lies the junction-star of Krittika. At the end of the eighth part of Rohini, five and a half *hastas* south of the ecliptic, is the junction-star of Rohini. In the eighth part of Punarvasu, at a distance of eight *hastas*, there are two junction-stars on both sides of the ecliptic, south and north. In the fourth part of Pushya, three and a half *hastas* north of the ecliptic, is its junction-star. In the first part of *Sarpa* (Ashlesha), one *hasta* south of the ecliptic is one junction-star, and another is to the north. In the sixth part of its own field in *Pitya* (Magha), the conjunction of the Moon occurs exactly on the ecliptic; thus, that is the junction-star of Magha. In the seven-and-a-half part of Chitra, the junction-star is three *hastas* south of the ecliptic. Now, the "arrow" (*shara*) in the form of *angulas* <note>finger-breadths</note> is made from the minutes of latitude from the center of the Moon. The author writes the method for how the latitude should be converted into *angulas*: Subtract seventeen from the latitude (*shara*), multiply the remainder by fifteen, and know that the result in thirty-fourths is the measure in *angulas*. Likewise, one should know the time by the difference in daily motion. This means, knowing the distance between the Moon and the star on the desired day, the time of conjunction should be known by the Moon's daily speed.

Now for the explanation: This is based on observation. The minutes of latitude of the junction-stars found by observation are converted to *angulas* using the method in verse 38, and then converted to *hastas* by the rule that twenty-four *angulas* make one *hasta*.

In calculating *angulas*, one subtracts 17 (the semi-diameter of the Moon's disk) from the observed latitude minutes of the stars to find the minutes of distance between the edge of the Moon's disk and the star's disk. Then the proportion is: if 34 minutes give 15 *angulas*, what do the remaining minutes give? By this proportion, the conversion to *angulas* is clearly established.

Regarding the calculation: Even when calculating the time of conjunction, the Moon, moving by its own velocity, approaches a lunar mansion <note>nakṣatra</note> from the west. Since the stars do not have a daily motion of their own, one must determine the minutes of arc <note>kalā</note> separating the Moon and the star at the desired time. A proportion is then calculated: if the Moon's daily motion in minutes corresponds to sixty ghatikās <note>a unit of 24 minutes; 60 ghatikās equal 24 hours</note>, then what time corresponds to the minutes of separation? However, because the Moon's velocity changes every moment, one must recalculate the Moon's true position for that specific instant. By repeating this process <note>iteration</note>, the precise time of conjunction is established.

## 36-41. Now, the rising of Agastya is described. "Half the equinoctial shadow," etc.

**Twenty-five** <note>original: pañcakṛti, literally 'five squared'</note> is multiplied by half of the equinoctial shadow <note>palabhā; the shadow of a gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>. From this, the arc should be determined. That arc is increased by fifteen and then multiplied by ten. The result is added to the product of the equinoctial shadow and thirty-three. The resulting numbers are the vināḍīs <note>units of 24 seconds</note> and vipals. When the Sun is at the sign of the zodiac corresponding to these vināḍīs—calculated from the start of Cancer to the end of Gemini for one's local latitude—then the sage Agastya <note>the star Canopus</note> becomes visible, or rises, according to the calculations and the observational instruments <note>chedyaka-yantra</note> previously described. How is Agastya described? As the "ornamental mark <note>tilaka</note> on the face of the lady of the Southern Quarter." The Southern Quarter <note>direction</note> is personified as a woman, and the star is the beautiful mark on her forehead. This divine knowledge concerning time and the stars gladdens the hearts and minds of men.

The mathematical proof is as follows: According to the current *Sūrya Siddhānta* <note>a foundational Sanskrit astronomical treatise</note>, Agastya is located at eighty degrees south at the end of Gemini.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of the visibility of the star Canopus (Agastya) based on its celestial coordinates and the observer's latitude, following the principles of the Panchasiddhantika.</meta>

<header>-> Elucidation of the Panchasiddhantika <-</header>

**Mi** represents the point of the summer solstice <note>literally: the end of Gemini</note> on the ecliptic. **A$_1$Mi** = the declination of the summer solstice = 24°. **AMi** = the celestial latitude of Canopus <note>Agastya</note> = 80°. **AA$_1$** = the rectified declination of Canopus = **AMi** - **A$_1$Mi** = 80° - 24° = 56°. **Akra** represents the arc of the earth-sine <term>Kujya: the distance between the rising-setting line and the diurnal circle</term> on the diurnal circle of Canopus. The corresponding ascensional difference <term>Chara: the difference between the celestial equator and the horizon</term> in degrees = **A$_1$Sam**. The diurnal circle of the summer solstice is **MiMi$_1$**. **GMi$_1$** is its corresponding earth-sine arc. Its ascensional difference is measured as **SamMi$_1$**. Therefore, when Canopus rises on the horizon, the degrees of the elevated time of the summer solstice point = **A$_1$Mi$_2$** = the sum of the two ascensional differences. At that time, when the Sun reaches the point on the eastern horizon where the ecliptic rises (marked as **L$_1$**), Canopus and the Sun rise together; thus, Canopus is hidden by the Sun's brilliance and becomes invisible.

The ancients determined through observation that if the Sun rises two and a half ghatikas <note>one ghatika is 24 minutes; 2.5 ghatikas equals 1 hour</note> after the rising of Canopus, then Canopus is visible to the human eye on that day. Therefore, it is assumed that on the celestial equator, the arc of two and a half ghatikas equals fifteen degrees = **Mi$_1$Ra$_1$**. On the point marked **Ra$_1$**, the pole-prolongation <note>meridian</note> meets the ecliptic at point **Ra**; the remaining Sun will arrive there two and a half ghatikas after the rising of Canopus. Now, the distance of point **Ra** from the summer solstice on the time-circle is equal to the arc degrees of **A$_1$Ra$_1$**. Degrees divided by six are ghatikas. Ghatikas multiplied by sixty are palas; therefore, degrees multiplied by ten become vinadiyas <note>units of time</note>. Now, by projecting the Sun at the end of Gemini or the beginning of Cancer, the position of point **Ra** on the ecliptic is determined by the rising of the local place in the desired ghatikas **A$_1$Ra$_1$**.

According to the calculation in the "Chapter on the Three Problems" <note>Triprashna: dealing with time, place, and direction</note>, for a place where the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> is one digit, the ascensional difference of the summer solstice in palas is twenty-one. From this, the proportion is: if a one-digit equinoctial shadow yields twenty-one palas of ascensional difference, then what is produced by the desired equinoctial shadow? The ascensional difference in palas = 21 × Palabha. Now, for the proportion to find the ascensional difference related to the rectified declination of Canopus: if a base of twelve <note>the gnomon height</note> yields the equinoctial shadow as the side, then what does the sine of the rectified declination of Canopus yield? This produces the earth-sine:

---

$\frac{\text{Sine (AA}_1\text{)} \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12} = \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times \text{Sine 56}^\circ}{12} = \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times 66}{12}.$ 

Again, by proportion: if the cosine of the declination yields the earth-sine, then what does the radius yield? This produces the sine of the ascensional difference $= \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow} \times 66 \times 120}{12 \times \text{Cosine (AA}_1\text{)}} = \frac{66 \times 120 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12 \times \text{Cosine 56}^\circ}$

$= \frac{66 \times 120 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12 \times \text{Sine 34}^\circ} = \frac{66 \times 120 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{12 \times 67} = \frac{660 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{67} = \frac{2 \times 660 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{67 \times 2} = \frac{1860 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{67 \times 2}$

$= \frac{\frac{1860}{67} \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{2} = \frac{1860}{67} \times \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{2} = \frac{30 \times \text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{2}$ 

Thus, using the eighty degrees of celestial latitude for the planet <note>Canopus</note> as taught in the currently famous *Surya Siddhanta*, the value comes to thirty instead of twenty-five.

---

It is inferred that in the *Surya Siddhanta* used during the Teacher's <note>Varahamihira's</note> time, the degrees of celestial latitude were less. If the degrees of latitude are calculated by the inverse method, assuming twenty-five instead of twenty, they come to 55° 30' with a slight difference. However, in the opinion of Bhaskaracharya, the celestial latitude of Canopus is 77 degrees. Now, the sine of the ascensional difference in minutes is $21 \times \frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow}}{2}$; the arc resulting from this is measured as **SamVre$_1$**. From that, the arc degrees of **A$_1$Ra$_1$** = **A$_1$Sam** + **SamMi$_1$** + **MiRa$_1$** = Arc + $\frac{21}{10}$ Palabha + 15. These degrees multiplied by ten become vinadiyas = 10 (Arc + $\frac{21}{10}$ Palabha + 15) = 10 (Arc + 15) + 21 Palabha. The method for calculating the rising sign was explained previously, so everything is faultless.

# Elucidation of the Five Treatises
<note>original: "Panchasiddhantika-prakashika"</note>

The start of the weekday is not the same everywhere, even during a common festival, nor is the beginning of the day simultaneous in all places. As to why the start of the day is not simultaneous—since the underlying cause has not been stated—therefore, the calculators <note>astronomers/mathematicians</note> disagree and engage in debate on this matter.

**18-20. Now he states the various opinions regarding the start of the day. "From the heap of days, the weekday is obtained," etc.**

Indeed, because the weekday is obtained from the "heap of days" <term>Ahargana; the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term>, and that heap of days is established through the relationship between place and time. For instance:
* **Latacharya** stated the day-count at the time of sunset in **Yavanapura** <note>literally "City of the Greeks," likely Alexandria</note>.
* **Simhacharya** stated it at sunrise in **Lanka** <note>the astronomical equator, not necessarily modern Sri Lanka</note>.
* Among the **Yavanas** <note>Greeks/Westerners</note>, the day-count was declared by **Yavanacharya** to begin when ten *muhurtas* <note>units of 48 minutes</note> of the night had passed.
* **Aryabhata**, however, in one place declared the start of the day to be at the time of midnight in Lanka, yet elsewhere the same Aryabhata says the start is from sunrise in Lanka.

**21-23. Now he states the specific details. "The correction for terrestrial longitude," etc.**

If, in various countries, the synchronization of time does not occur even after applying the correction for terrestrial longitude <term>Deshantara; the difference in longitude between two places</term>, then for the sake of reconciling the time, those very teachers have stated how time is synchronized according to the scriptures. To explain what that synchronization is, he says: "At midday among the Bhadrashvas," etc.

When the Sun is rising in **Bharatavarsha** <note>India</note>, it simultaneously creates:
* Midday for the people living in **Bhadrashva-varsha**.
* Sunset for the people in **Kuru-varsha**.
* Midnight for the people of **Ketumala-varsha**.

Similarly, the sunrise in **Lanka** is the same moment as sunset in **Siddhapura**, midday in **Yamakoti**, and midnight in the **Romaka** region <note>the Roman/Byzantine West</note>. Thus, astronomers, having understood the geographical positions, calculate the day-count for the desired time of a desired place. The planets derived from that calculation are all accurate for their respective times; therefore, the teacher’s view is that there is no harm caused by the difference in the start of the day.

**24. Now he states the time of the beginning of the Age. "By the intercalary months," etc.**

At the very beginning of the *Yuga* <note>a vast cosmic cycle of time</note>, the intercalary months, the omitted days, the planets, the solar days, the lunar days, the signs of the zodiac (Aries, etc.), the Moon, the Sun, the solstices, the seasons, and the lunar mansions—all these commenced simultaneously. That is to say, the teacher does not explicitly state *where* the intercalary months and the rest began simultaneously at sunset, but according to almost all astronomical treatises <term>Siddhantas</term>, the beginning of the Age is fixed at **Lanka**.

**25. Now he states a specific detail regarding longitude. "Other than the Romaka region," etc.**

The longitude of other places is different from the Romaka region. Likewise, the longitude of other places is also different from Yavanapura.

**25-27. Now he states another opinion regarding the Lord of the Day. "From the time of midnight in Lanka," etc.**

One opinion is that the weekday begins from the time of midnight in Lanka; likewise, there is another opinion that the weekday begins from sunrise. Now, if we were to declare the "Lord of the Day" <note>the ruling planet of the day</note> or the start of the weekday based on the sunset of the Sun every day, there is no authoritative statement <term>Apta-vakya; testimony of a reliable authority</term> for that, nor is there any other logical argument. Because of the Sun, the "Lord of the Day," it is twilight in one place, day in another, and night in another. Thus, even across small distances, the concept of "Day-Lordship" would become confused and inconsistent.

It explains how global synchronization works by showing that sunrise in India corresponds to different times of day in other mythical and geographical regions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Panchasiddhantika, specifically concluding the fifteenth chapter which deals with the philosophical and mathematical foundations of time-keeping.</meta>

->**Illumination of the Five Siddhantas**<-

28. Now, he explains a specific detail regarding the lore of the *Hora* <note>The term 'Hora' refers to a planetary hour, a unit of time roughly equal to one hour, used in astrology</note>. Regarding the lore of the *Hora*:

Just as the account of the Lord of the Day <note>original: "Dinapati"; refers to the planet ruling the specific day of the week</note> was previously established starting from sunrise, the lore of the *Hora* functions in the same way, because the first *Hora* of any day belongs to that Day-Lord. Therefore, if there is uncertainty or a lack of determination regarding that Day-Lord, how can there be a determined Lord of the *Hora*? This means it should be understood that if the Day-Lord is uncertain, the *Hora* Lord is also necessarily uncertain.

29. Now, he states the established conclusion. Regarding "without deliberation":

In this way, this populace or country generally follows the day of the week based on tradition, without any critical deliberation, accepting whatever day is heard through lineage. In other words, what day it is today is known only through tradition; there is no mathematical or logical reasoning applied there by which the knowledge of the day could be independently verified. However, the Teachers <note>referring to the ancient masters of astronomy</note> declare that only that calculation which is consistent with the analysis of the "True Lunar Day" <note>original: "Sphuta-tithi"; the actual astronomical position of the moon relative to the sun</note> is proper and correct. This means that whatever calculation brings the planets into "visual correspondence" <note>term: <term>Drktulyata</term> (The state where mathematical calculation matches observed reality through the eyes)</note> should be known as the correct calculation. One should not be dogmatic about who the Day-Lord is <insert>if it contradicts observation</insert>.

## Thus ends the Fifteenth Chapter, titled the Secret Doctrine of Astrology.

Just as the *Upanishads* <note>sacred philosophical texts</note> in the Vedas are dedicated to defining the Supreme Brahman, this chapter is dedicated solely to defining the essential principles of Astrology; for that reason, this chapter is designated as an "Upanishad." Thus, the fifteenth chapter, which serves as the Secret Doctrine of Astrology, is completed.

It justifies calling this section an 'Upanishad' because it deals with the core essence of astrological science.</summary>

### Now, the Chapter on Mean Motion for Mars and the other planets according to the Surya Siddhanta.

1-3. Here, he speaks of Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. "This is at midnight in Avanti," and so forth.

In Avanti <note>modern-day Ujjain, the prime meridian of ancient Indian astronomy</note>, at the time of midnight according to the Sun-Siddhanta <note>Surya Siddhanta</note>, there is the following determination of the "star-planets" <note>the five visible planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>. In that determination, the "Son of the Moon" (Mercury) and Venus are known to have a mean motion equal to that of the Sun. Thus, the mean Mercury and Venus should be understood as exactly equal to the mean Sun. 

The calculator should multiply the *Ahargana* <note>the number of elapsed days since the beginning of the epoch</note> by one hundred and divide by 433,232. The quotient obtained will be the revolutions of Jupiter. From the remainder, the parts such as signs, degrees, etc., should be calculated in order. 

Similarly, multiply the *Ahargana* by one and divide by 687. The quotient will be the revolutions of Mars. From the remainder, the parts such as signs, degrees, etc., should be calculated in order. 

From the *Ahargana* multiplied by one thousand, divide by 10,766,066. The quotient will be the revolutions of Saturn. From the remainder, here too, the parts such as signs, degrees, etc., should be calculated in order. Thus, in this sequence, all the mean planets are determined.

$= \frac{1000 \times \text{Planet}}{90766066} = \frac{102776 \times \text{Planet}}{90766066 \times 1577919800}$ Here too, the Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> states that the result arising from the first part is the mean Saturn in terms of revolutions, and he will describe the correction arising from the second part later; thus, everything is consistent.

4. Now, he describes the correction arising from the second part for the mean positions of Mars and the others. **"Ten-ten," etc.** <note>This refers to the opening words of a specific verse in the source text.</note>

For the mean Jupiter, which is produced from the result of the first part in revolutions and so on: for every revolution, ten <term>tatparas</term> <note>A tatpara is a "third" or 1/60th of a second of arc (sixtieths of a vikala).</note> should be subtracted from each <term>vikala</term> <note>A vikala is an arc-second.</note>; then it becomes the true Jupiter, the Teacher of the Gods. Similarly, for every revolution of the mean Mars, fourteen <term>tatparas</term> should be added to each <term>vikala</term>. And in the mean of Saturn, five <term>tatparas</term> should be subtracted from each <term>vikala</term>; then those two, Mars and Saturn, become true.

Here is the proof. By the previous method, the true Jupiter $= \frac{100 \times \text{Planet}}{433232} = \frac{2066 \times \text{Planet}}{433232 \times 1577919800}$. When the number of days elapsed $= \frac{433232}{100}$, then exactly one revolution is obtained in the result of the first part. The result of the second part is in revolutions, then $\frac{2066 \times 433232}{100 \times 433232 \times 1577919800} = \frac{2066}{100 \times 1577919800}$. This is the value; its <term>tatparas</term> are:
$= \frac{2066 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60 \times 60 \times 60}{100 \times 1577919800} = \frac{2066 \times 12 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 60}{15779198} = \frac{2066 \times 4 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 60}{5259736}$
$= \frac{2066 \times 4 \times 6 \times 6 \times 60}{1753245} = \frac{2066 \times 4 \times 6 \times 6}{292209} = \frac{3018240}{292209} = 10^{'''}$ <note>The notation $'''$ denotes thirds or tatparas.</note> Therefore, the calculation for Jupiter's correction is proven.

By the previous method, the true Mars in revolutions $= \frac{\text{Planet}}{687} + \frac{288 \times \text{Planet}}{687 \times 1577919800}$. Here, when the number of days elapsed $= 687$, then exactly one revolution is obtained in the first part. In the second part, $\frac{288 \times 687}{687 \times 1577919800}$ is obtained in revolutions. Its <term>tatparas</term> are $= \frac{288 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60 \times 60 \times 60}{1577919800}$
$= \frac{288 \times 12 \times 3 \times 6 \times 60 \times 60}{15779198} = \frac{288 \times 4 \times 3 \times 6 \times 60 \times 60}{5259736} = \frac{288 \times 4 \times 3 \times 60 \times 60}{876629}$
$= \frac{288 \times 4 \times 60 \times 60}{292209} = \frac{4147200}{292209} = 14^{'''}$ Therefore, the calculation for Mars's correction is proven. Now, similarly by the previous method, the true Saturn in revolutions $= \frac{1000 \times \text{Planet}}{90766066} = \frac{102776 \times \text{Planet}}{90766066 \times 1577919800}$. Here too, when the number of days elapsed $= \frac{90766066}{1000}$, then exactly one revolution is obtained in the first part, and in the second part, the value $\frac{102776 \times 90766066}{1000 \times 90766066 \times 1577919800} = \frac{102776}{1000 \times 1577919800}$ is obtained in revolutions. Its <term>tatparas</term> are:
$= \frac{102776 \times 12 \times 30 \times 60 \times 60 \times 60}{1000 \times 1577919800} = \frac{102776 \times 12 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6}{157791980} = \frac{102776 \times 4 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6}{525973260}$
$= \frac{102776 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6}{131493315} = \frac{102776 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6}{4383105} = \frac{102776 \times 2 \times 6 \times 6}{1461035} = \frac{7399872}{1461035} = 5^{'''}$

Thus, the calculation for Saturn's correction is proven. By this, it is inferred that for all planets, the revolutions and civil days of a Great Age according to the *Surya Siddhanta* of Varahamihira's time are generally equal to the revolutions and civil days of the *Aryabhatiya*, because the method for the revolutions etc. of the *Aryabhatiya* is proven in this manner.

### Page 60

5-6. Now he states the epochs <note>The starting positions of planets at a specific point in time</note> for Mars and the others. Beginning with "Four signs..."

In the mean motion of **Saturn**, one should apply an additive correction <note>Sanskrit: *dhana*, meaning positive or additive</note> of four signs, twenty-two degrees, twenty-eight minutes, and forty-nine seconds. For **Jupiter**, the correction to be added is eight degrees, six minutes, and twenty seconds. The text uses the word *maccha* <note>original: "मच्च"</note> which, through the etymology "that which destroys or gathers together," refers to Yama <note>The god of death, associated with the number 2</note>; thus, that specific number 2 is used for the seconds. Alternatively, in place of the phrase "khamaccha," the reading "khapaksha" <note>referring to the number 20</note> should be applied. For **Mars**, the epoch is: two signs, fifteen degrees, and twenty-five minutes.

**The Proof:** If the total revolutions of a planet in a Great Age <term>Mahayuga: a vast cosmic cycle of 4,320,000 years</term> are obtained using the civil days <term>Savana-divasa: solar days from sunrise to sunrise</term> of a Great Age, then what would be obtained by the elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the count of days since the epoch</term> at the start of this text, which is 1,577,917,800? By this proportion, the stated epochs of the planets are produced.

7. Now he states the "Fast Motion" <term>Shighrocca: the apex of quick motion, used to calculate the anomaly for inner planets</term> of **Mercury**. Beginning with "Multiplied by one hundred..."

When the elapsed days are multiplied by one hundred and divided by 8,797, the result is the Fast Motion of Mercury starting from the revolutions. However, here, half of a fifth-order unit <note>original: "tatpara"</note>—that is, 4.5 <gloss>1/2</gloss>—multiplied by the revolutions must be added; then the true Fast Motion is obtained.

**The Proof:** Here, by the inverse method, we assume the value of the revolutions of Mercury's Fast Motion in a Great Age = *y*. Then, by the method stated by the Teacher, the Fast Motion of Mercury = (100 × *A* / 8797) + (*y* × *A* / 1,577,917,800).

- 100 × *A* / 8797 = In this first part, if we substitute the value 8797 / 100 for the elapsed days, one revolution is obtained. In the second part, the result per second of arc is:

= ( (8797 / 100) - (*y* / 1,577,917,800) ) × 12 × 30 × 60³ = ( (8797*y* / 1,577,917,800,000) - 1 ) × 12 × 30 × 60 × 60 × 60

= ( (12 × 30 × 60 × 60 × 60 × 8797) / 1,577,917,800,000 ) *y* - 77,760,000 = ( (12 × 3 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 8797) / 15,779,178 ) *y* - 77,760,000

= ( (4 × 3 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 8797) / 5,259,726 ) *y* - 77,760,000 = ( (4 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 8797) / 1,753,242 ) *y* - 77,760,000

= ( (4 × 6 × 6 × 8,797) / 292,207 ) *y* - 77,760,000 = Multiplying by 6/6 gives ( (6 × 6 × 6 × 8,797) / 292,207 ) *y* - (77,760,000 × 2) = 6

Or, ( (288 × 8,797) / 292,207 ) *y* - 15,552,000 = 6

Or, ( 2,533,536 / 292,207 ) *y* = 15,552,006

Therefore, *y* = (292,207 × 15,552,006) / 2,533,536 = 4,544,403,526,863 / 2,533,536 = 17,939,000.

By this same algebraic method, the Great Age revolutions of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn mentioned previously should be understood. These 17,939,000 revolutions for Mercury's Fast Motion are different from the revolutions found in the modern *Surya Siddhanta* and the *Aryabhatiya*. The proof of the previous method is very easy to understand through this inverse logic of calculating revolutions.

# Light on the Five Treatises (Pancha-siddhantika-prakashika)

### 8. Now he describes the fast anomaly <note>shighrochcha: the point of highest speed, used in Indian astronomy to calculate the planet's position relative to the Sun</note> of Venus. "The fast [anomaly] of Venus..."

When the sum of days <note>ahargana: the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</note> is multiplied by ten and divided by "Svara-Adyo-Vashi-Yama" (2247), the result is the revolutions and remaining parts of the fast anomaly of Venus. However, ten and a half seconds <note>vilitpika/vikala: 1/3600th of a degree</note> multiplied by the number of revolutions should be added; that is, an addition equal to ten and a half times the revolutions makes it the true fast anomaly.

The derivation here: By the previously mentioned method of equations, the revolutions of the Venusian fast anomaly are known to be 7,022,388. From these and the civil days in a Great Age <note>Mahayuga: a vast cycle of 4,320,000 years</note> (1,577,917,800), the proportion is: if these revolutions occur in a Great Age of days, what occurs in the current sum of days? The resulting fast anomaly of Venus = $\frac{10 \times \text{days}}{2247} + \text{days} \left( \frac{7022388}{1577917800} - \frac{10}{2247} \right)$
$= \frac{10 \times \text{days}}{2247} + \text{days} \left( \frac{1577930536 - 1577917800}{2247 \times 1577917800} \right) = \frac{10 \times \text{days}}{2247} + \frac{12736 \times \text{days}}{2247 \times 1577917800}$. Here also,
if the sum of days $= \frac{2247}{10}$, then in the first part there is exactly one revolution, and in the second part the result in seconds is:
$= \frac{12 \times 30 \times 60 \times 60 \times 12736 \times 2247}{10 \times 2247 \times 1577917800} = \frac{12 \times 3 \times 6 \times 6 \times 12736}{15779178} = \frac{4 \times 3 \times 6 \times 4 \times 12736}{5259726}$
$= \frac{4 \times 6 \times 4 \times 12736}{1753242} = \frac{4 \times 6 \times 12736}{292207} = \frac{305854}{292207} = 10'' \frac{2}{3}$ approximately. Thus, it is proven.

### 9. Now he describes the additive constants <note>kshepa: the initial position at the start of the epoch</note> for the fast anomalies of Mercury and Venus. "Of the Lion..."

For the Lion (the sign of Leo), the "Vasu-Yama" degrees—meaning 4 signs and 28 degrees—and "Svara-Indu" (17) minutes should be added to the fast anomaly of Mercury as its specific additive constant. Similarly, for Venus, from the fast anomaly of Venus, "Shashi-Rasa-Shad-Dvi-Guna-Dahana" (332,661) seconds should be subtracted, meaning they are negative.

The derivation here: If the revolutions of a Great Age are obtained by the civil days of a Great Age, then by the sum of days at the start of this work (1,893,440), what is the proportion? The additive constant for Mercury's fast anomaly in signs etc. comes to $4^s \text{ } 28^\circ \text{ } 17' \text{ } 6''$. The Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> omitted the six seconds due to the small difference. For the fast anomaly of Venus, by the aforementioned proportion, the constant in signs $= 8^s \text{ } 29^\circ \text{ } 30' \text{ } 35''$. By subtracting this from a full circle <note>mandala: 12 signs</note>, the negative constant $= 3^s \text{ } 2^\circ \text{ } 26' \text{ } 25'' = 332,661$ [seconds]. The constant mentioned by the Teacher differs by only four seconds, which is inferred to be due to a small difference or a variation in the manuscript reading.

### 10-11. Now he describes the correction <note>bijakarma: "seed-action," a corrective factor applied to mean positions to match observations</note> for Mars and the others. "Seventeen seconds are to be added..."

Every year, 17 seconds ("Svara-Indu") should be added to the mean position of Mars. From Jupiter, 15 seconds should be subtracted. For Saturn, 7.5 seconds should be added. For the fast anomaly of Venus, 45 seconds ("Pancha-Abhrayah") should be subtracted. For the fast anomaly of Mercury, 120 seconds ("Kha-Ashvi-Chandra") should be added. Furthermore, from the mean of Jupiter ("the one worshiped by the gods"), 1400 seconds ("Kha-Kha-Veda-Indu") should be subtracted. By doing this, the planets become suitable for observation <note>i.e., the calculated positions will match the actual sky</note>.

Now, the observation itself is the underlying impression <note>original: "vasana"; the conceptual understanding or mental model derived from observation</note>; no other cause can be stated. Therefore, it is impossible to even refine the previous verses. In this same way, the astronomer Lalla also spoke of the "Seed-Correction" <term>Bija-karma: a corrective factor applied to astronomical formulas to align calculated positions with observed reality</term> in his work, *The Increase of the Intellect of Students*. His statement is as follows:

> When the Shaka year is diminished by 420, and multiplied by 28 for the Moon; when divided by 1114, and by 66 for the Rahu <note>the ascending node of the moon</note>;
> When multiplied by 47 for Jupiter, it should be subtracted from the Moon’s apogee; when divided by 153 and then by 350;
> When multiplied by 48 for Mars, and for Saturn multiplied by 20;
> When multiplied by 430, one should apply the resulting increase to the minutes of Mercury, Mars, and Saturn.

# 83
### The Illumination of the Five Treatises

->## Now, the Correction of Mars and Other Planets According to the Surya Siddhanta ##<-

**1-2.** First, he states the circumferences of the apsides <note>manda-paridhi: the epicycle used to account for the planet's varying speed</note> and the degrees of the highest points <note>mandocca: apogee or aphelion</note>. **The Sun is called the "Swift One," and so on.**

For the other planets—Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—the Sun itself is designated as the "Swift One" <note>shighra: the "fast" point, referring here to the solar motion which drives the synodic cycle of the outer planets</note>. The numbers are: thirty-five (35), Manu (14), the sky and the mountains (16), the arrows (5), and thirty minus six (24). When these numbers are doubled, they become the circumferences of the apsides for Mars and the others. Thus, the degrees of the circumferences for Mars and the others are:

| <gloss>Mars</gloss> | <gloss>Merc.</gloss> | <gloss>Jup.</gloss> | <gloss>Ven.</gloss> | <gloss>Sat.</gloss> |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 70 | 28 | 32 | 50 | 60 |

Similarly, the numbers are: flavors (6), Bhava (11), Vasus (8), Vedas (4), and the Sun (12). These numbers, multiplied by twenty, and in the case of Mars, reduced by ten parts, become the degrees of the highest points <note>mandocca</note> for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. Thus, the highest points for Mars and the others are: **Mars = 6 × 20 - 10 = 110°; Mercury = 11 × 20 = 220°; Jupiter = 8 × 20 = 160°; Venus = 4 × 20 = 80°; Saturn = 12 × 20 = 240°.**

**3.** Now he states the circumferences of the fast epicycles <note>shighra-paridhi: the epicycle used to account for the Earth's motion relative to the planet</note>. **In the fast circumference, etc.**

Now, for Mars and the others, the degrees of the fast circumferences are: the hands, qualities, and wings (**234**); the two, the fires, and the moon (**132**); the five and the notes (**72**); the void, the six, and the twins (**260**); and the void and the hands (**40**).

**4.** Now he states the base and the perpendicular <note>bhuja and koti: the sine and cosine components of the planet's position</note>. **From the "Swift One" minus the mean, etc.**

When the mean planet is subtracted from the "Swift One" <note>the shighrocca or fast anomaly</note>, whatever remains within the three signs <note>90 degrees</note>—the elapsed portion and the portion yet to be reached—their sines become the base and the perpendicular respectively. Beyond that, if the remainder exceeds three signs, it should be subtracted from six signs, and the same method applied to the remainder. Here, the Teacher has shown the base and perpendicular in brief. In reality, in one circle of the constellations, there are four quadrants of three signs each. In the first quadrant, the elapsed is the base and the remaining is the perpendicular. In the second, the remaining degrees are the base and the elapsed are the perpendicular. In the third, the elapsed is the base and the remaining is the perpendicular. In the fourth, the remaining is the base and the elapsed is the perpendicular. This is the well-known traditional method, though not explicitly stated by the Teacher here.

**5-6.** Now he states the "fast result" <note>shighra-phala: the equation of center or correction</note>. **Multiplied by its own circumference, etc.**

The previously calculated base and perpendicular sines are multiplied by their own fast circumference and divided by the "sky-season-qualities" <term>360</term> <note>the total degrees in a circle</note>. Then those two are transformed; that is, they become the "base-result" and "perpendicular-result" in the fast circumference. Then, that perpendicular-result should be added to or subtracted from the radius <term>120</term> depending on whether the center is in the signs beginning with Capricorn or Cancer. Specifically, in the center beginning with Capricorn, the perpendicular-result is added to the radius; in Cancer and others, it is subtracted. The result of this is known as the <term>corrected perpendicular</term> <note>sphuta-koti</note>. Then, the base-result multiplied by the "sky-suns" or radius <term>120</term> should be divided by the square root of the sum of the squares of the corrected perpendicular and the base-result. Half of the resulting arc, depending on the fast center, should be added to or subtracted from the highest point <note>mandocca</note>. That is, in the center beginning with Aries, half should be subtracted from the highest point, and in Libra and others, it should be added. Then the corrected highest point is obtained.

# The Illumination of the Five Treatises
<page-num>94</page-num>
<header>The Illumination of the Five Treatises (Pañcasiddhāntikā-prakāśikā)</header>

Here is the mathematical proof: The sine of the base and the sine of the perpendicular <note>original: bhujajyā and koṭijyā</note> in the radius of the standard circle <note>tri-jyā, literally 'three-sine' or the radius of a circle where the circumference is divided into 360 degrees</note>, when transformed into the radius of the final epicycle of the fast motion <note>śīghra-antyaphala-jyā</note>, become the base and perpendicular sines of the fast anomaly <note>śīghra-kendra</note> on the fast circumference. These are respectively designated as the "base-result" <note>bhujaphala</note> and "perpendicular-result" <note>koṭiphala</note>.

Now, let it be assumed that:
**Earth** (bhū) is the center of the Earth.
**Orbit** (sphu-ma-sphu') is the true-mean orbit circle.
**M** (ma) is the position of the mean planet.
With **M** as the center, the fast circumference <note>śīghra-paridhi</note> is designated as **Gra-U-Gra'**.
**U** is the position of the apex <note>ucca</note>. From that point, moving backwards by the distance of the arc, the anomaly beginning with Capricorn <note>makarādi-kendra</note> is formed, and the other is the anomaly beginning with Cancer <note>karkyādi-kendra</note>.
**Gra** is the position of the planet in the Capricorn-starting anomaly.
**Gra'** is the position of the planet in the Cancer-starting anomaly.
**Gra-La** is the base-result <note>bhujaphala</note>.
**La-Ma** is the perpendicular-result <note>koṭiphala</note>.
**Bhū-Ma** is the radius. In the Capricorn anomaly, the true perpendicular **Bhū-La** is the sum of the radius and the perpendicular-result. In the Cancer anomaly, the true perpendicular **Bhū-La'** is the difference between them.
The square root of the sum of the squares of that [true perpendicular] and the base-result is the hypotenuse <note>karṇa</note>, equal to **Bhū-Gra** or **Bhū-Gra'**. Then, by proportion:

If for this hypotenuse the base-result is obtained, then for the radius **Bhū-Sphu**, what is obtained? The result is the sine of the fast correction <note>śīghraphala</note> of the arc **Ma-Sphu**. Half of that arc is added to the mean planet in the anomaly beginning with Aries <note>meṣādi-kendra</note> and subtracted in the anomaly beginning with Libra <note>tulādi-kendra</note>, following the current *Sūrya Siddhānta* <note>A foundational text of Indian astronomy, likely the 11th-century version</note>. Then, the slow apex <note>mandocca</note> is subtracted from this to find the slow anomaly. Thus, the mean planet, corrected by half the fast correction, is used for both:

->Anomalies = Mean Planet ± $\frac{Fast Correction}{2}$. And Slow Anomaly = (Mean Planet ± $\frac{Fast Correction}{2}$) - Slow Apex = Mean Planet ± $\frac{Fast Correction}{2}$ - Slow Apex<-
->= Mean Planet - (Slow Apex ∓ $\frac{Fast Correction}{2}$). Thus, everything is proven.<-

7-8. Now he describes the slow correction <note>mandaphala</note>. "Having thus clarified," etc.

In the manner previously described, having clarified the slow apex <note>mandocca</note>—that is, having made it "true"—the base <note>bāhu</note> of that true slow apex, subtracted from the mean planet, is transformed into the slow circumference. In other words, the sine of the base <note>bhujajyā</note> is multiplied by the slow circumference and divided by the degrees of the circle (360). Half of the resulting arc should be added to or subtracted from the slow apex according to the slow anomaly. Specifically, in the Aries-starting anomaly, it is added; in the Libra-starting anomaly, the difference is taken. Thus, the true slow apex is formed again. This is again subtracted from the mean planet, the base is calculated from that, and as before, it is transformed into the slow circumference to find its arc. That arc, according to the slow anomaly, should be added to or subtracted from the mean planet: subtracted in the Aries anomaly and added in the Libra anomaly.

The proof here is: By subtracting the slow apex from the mean, the slow anomaly is found. Its sine, transformed by the slow circumference, is the slow base-result. Since there is no hypotenuse-proportion <note>karṇānupāta</note> in the slow process <note>manda-karma</note>, the arc of the slow base-result itself becomes the slow correction. <insert>As Bhāskarācārya <note>The famous 12th-century mathematician-astronomer</note> also said: "The wise call the arc of the result of the slow base the slow correction."</insert> Half of that should be applied as a correction to the mean planet. Here, the slow anomaly is the opposite of the fast anomaly; because in the fast process, the apex is subtracted from the planet to get the anomaly, but here the slow apex itself is subtracted from the mean planet. Therefore, in the Libra anomaly, the slow correction is additive, and in Aries, it is subtractive. By this method, the mean planet corrected by half the slow correction = Mean Planet ∓ $\frac{Slow Correction}{2}$. From this again, the slow apex...

# Page 95
## The Illumination of the Five Treatises

By calculation, the <term>anomaly of the apsis</term> <note>original: mandakendra; the angular distance of a planet from its slowest point</note> = Mean Longitude $\mp \frac{\text{Equation of Center}}{2}$ - Longitude of Apsis = Mean Longitude - (Longitude of Apsis $\pm \frac{\text{Equation of Center}}{2}$). Having calculated the <term>equation of center</term> <note>original: mandaphala; the correction needed to account for elliptical motion</note> from this anomaly, the mean planet corrected by that becomes the "slow-corrected" planet <note>original: mandasphuṭa</note>. This is the method of the ancients.

8. Now he describes the calculation of the true planet. "Thus, those called the true-mean," and so on.
By the previous method, those planets established as "true-mean" (the slow-corrected planets) should be subtracted from the <term>apex of quick motion</term> <note>original: śīghrocca; the point corresponding to the Earth's or the planet's orbital motion</note>. Having calculated the "quick hypotenuse" and other values by the same previous method, the arc obtained—just like the first—should be added to or subtracted from the slow-corrected "true-mean" planet. This means in the half-circle starting with Aries, it is an addition, and in the half-circle starting with Libra, it is a subtraction. In this way, all planets become "true" <note>sphuṭa</note>; this is the connection to the following.

The logic here: Having brought the <term>equation of conjunction</term> <note>original: śīghraphala</note> from the slow-corrected position, that result should be applied to the slow-corrected position. The planets then exist on their own eccentric circles; this is clear through the method of geometric projection.

10-11. Now he describes a specific correction for Mercury and Venus. "All shall be true," and so on.
For this Mercury, subtract the longitude of the Sun’s apsis from its <term>apex of quick motion</term>. The <term>sine</term> <note>original: bhujajyā</note> of the remainder is reduced by the Sun's circumference—meaning the sine is multiplied by the Sun's slow circumference and divided by the degrees in a circle (360). That resulting arc should be added to Mercury like a "Mercury-correction." If the new anomaly established by the apex of quick motion (minus the Sun's apsis) is in the half-circle starting with Aries, it is an addition; if in Libra, it is a subtraction. By doing this, Mercury becomes "true." Now, for Venus, which has been made "true" by the two previous corrections, 67 minutes should be subtracted from its mean position; then Venus becomes truly "true." In this way, the time of retrograde and "re-retrograde" motion should be known by the specific daily motion. When the motion is negative, it is retrograde. When the negative motion increases further, it is known as "re-retrograde."

The logic here is simply based on observation; no other cause can be stated.

12. Now he describes the "degrees of time" <note>original: kālāṃśa; the degrees of separation from the Sun required for a planet to become visible</note>. "The true Sun," and so on.
Twenty should be reduced by eight, one (1), three (3), seven (7), nine (9), and five (5) respectively. Then these are the degrees of difference from the true Sun for the appearance of the planets starting with the Moon. This means when the difference in degrees between the Sun and Moon is twelve, the Moon becomes visible. When the difference between the Sun and Mars is nineteen, Mars becomes visible at night. These are the degrees of difference for the Moon and others:

| 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 8 | 1 | 3 | 7 | 9 | 5 |
| **12** | **19** | **17** | **13** | **11** | **15** |
<note>The bottom row represents the resulting degrees of visibility for the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn respectively.</note>

The logic here: When a planet comes into conjunction with the Sun, the body of the planet is overpowered by the Sun's brilliance and is not visible to the eye at night for some days. Thus, because of its distance from the Sun, on the day its body becomes visible, the difference between the Sun and the planet is determined by observation. Although these degrees of difference are not fixed—due to the varying sizes of the planetary bodies and their proximity or distance—the Teacher has stated them here for the sake of convenience.

13-14. Now he describes the calculation of the celestial latitude <note>shara; literally 'arrow', referring to the perpendicular distance from the ecliptic</note> of Mars and the other planets. **"The sine of the difference of the slow planet..." and so forth.**

The sine of the difference between the planet and its node <note>the point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> is increased by its own eighth part. Based on that difference between the node and the corrected "slow" planet <note>manda-spashta; the planet's position corrected for its elliptical orbit</note>, the celestial latitude <note>vikshepa</note> of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn occurs in the north or south directions. There is also a latitude produced by the "fast" motion <note>shighra; referring to the correction for the Earth's motion</note>. That is to say, in the case of Mercury and Venus, one should take their "fast apex" <note>shighrocca</note> and apply the previously mentioned method to the difference between the node and that fast apex. From this, the other latitude is produced. The meaning is that the sine of the difference between the node and the fast apex, increased by its own eighth part, becomes the latitude for Mercury and Venus.

Furthermore, for the sine thus established (increased by its eighth part), a reduction of one-quarter <note>subtracting 1/4th of the value</note> should be made for Jupiter, Mars, and Venus. For Mercury and Saturn, the sine increased by its eighth part should be kept exactly as it is. The resulting number should be multiplied by the radius <note>trijya</note> and divided by the hypotenuse <note>karna; the distance from the Earth to the planet</note>. Then the latitude of Mars and the others, arising from the difference and directed according to the node-planet interval, is obtained.

Here is the proof: The Teacher <note>Varahamihira</note> has assumed the maximum mean latitude minutes <note>shara-kala</note> for Mars and the others to be, in order: 101', 135', 101', 101', and 135'. From this, the proportion is: if for the radius we get the maximum latitude minutes, then for the desired sine of the node-planet difference, what do we get? Thus the mean latitude minutes for Mars etc. are produced. Then, if these are the mean latitude minutes for the hypotenuse distance, what are they for the radius? Thus the true latitude minutes on the celestial sphere are produced.

| | |
|---|---|
| **For Mars** = | $\frac{101 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{(135 - 34) \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{135 \times \text{Radius}}{120} - \frac{34 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8} - \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8 \times 4}$ |
| **For Mercury** = | $\frac{135 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8}$ |
| **For Jupiter** = | $\frac{101 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8} - \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8 \times 4}$ |
| **For Venus** = | $\frac{101 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8} - \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8 \times 4}$ |
| **For Saturn** = | $\frac{135 \times \text{Radius}}{120} = \frac{9 \times \text{Radius}}{8}$ |

By this sequence, the calculation of latitude for all is proven. The proof of the proportion involving the hypotenuse is very simple. When the planet (relative to its node) is in the northern hemisphere, the latitude is north of the ecliptic; in the south, it is the opposite. Thus, everything is faultless.

### Thus ends the Sixteenth Chapter, named "The Correction of the Star-Planets."

The sixteenth chapter, which consists of the correction of those planets that appear in the form of stars (Mars and the others), is completed.

## Now he describes the chapter on the rising and setting of planets.

1.-2. First, he describes the motion of Venus according to the school of Vasiṣṭha. Starting with "Having left the sages, water..." and so on.

From the sum of days <note>Sanskrit: *dyugaṇa* or *ahargaṇa*; the total number of days elapsed since the epoch</note>, subtract 147 <note>original: "sages" (7), "water" (4), "moon" (1) read right-to-left as 147</note>. Divide the remainder by 584 <note>original: "Vedas" (4), "eight" (8), "elements" (5) read right-to-left</note>. The quotient obtained represents the number of "risings." The remaining days and fractions should be set aside separately. Now, at every rising of Venus, the measure is 5 degrees of Scorpio <note>original: *ali*, the Scorpion</note> along with the fractional parts of Venus's motion. Now, the position is 7 signs, 5 degrees, and 28 minutes. After the calculated rising, Venus travels for 36 days to reach its "interval of rising" and then it rises in the west. Thus, 36 days after the initial rising-point, the western rising of Venus occurs. Now, take the number of risings obtained earlier, divide it by eleven, and add that quotient to the previously set-aside remaining days. From this, the "wanderings" or motions of Venus are to be known according to the method described hereafter.

Here is the mathematical proof <note>Sanskrit: *upapatti*</note>. According to Āryabhaṭa, the revolutions of Venus in a Kalpa <note>an eon of 4.32 billion years</note> are 4,320,000. The revolutions of Venus's "fast anomaly" <note>term: *śīghrocca* — the apex of quick motion, used in Indian astronomy to account for heliocentric motion from a geocentric perspective</note> are 7,022,388. The difference between these equals the revolutions of the "conjunctional anomaly" <note>term: *śīghrakendra*</note>, which is 2,702,388. Then the proportion is: if these revolutions of the anomaly occur in the total civil days of a Kalpa (1,577,917,800), then how much for one revolution?

-> Time for one revolution = $\frac{1577917800}{2702388}$ = 584 - $\frac{1}{9}$ (approximately). Here, Vasiṣṭha has taken 584 - $\frac{1}{11}$. <-

Therefore, if the sum of days is divided by this 584 - $\frac{1}{11}$, the revolutions of the anomaly are obtained, and the remainder is days. For the sake of division, it is first assumed that the sum of days is divided by 584 to get the risings; then the true remainder is:

-> Value = Days - Risings $\times$ ($584 - \frac{1}{11}$) = Days - 584 $\times$ Risings + $\frac{Risings}{11} = Remainder + \frac{Risings}{11}$. <-

Here, Days - (584 $\times$ Risings) = the remaining days. Therefore, if one-eleventh of the number of risings is added to the previous remaining days, the true remainder is found. Now, when Venus is equal to its fast anomaly, the revolution of the conjunctional anomaly is complete; 36 days after that, the rising of Venus occurs in the west—this is the observation-based understanding of the Teacher <note>Varāhamihira</note>. Now, to find the position of Venus in the time of one revolution (584 - $\frac{1}{11}$ days), the proportion is: if 12 signs are obtained in the civil days of one solar year (365 $\frac{1}{4}$), then what is obtained in 584 - $\frac{1}{11}$ days? The result is the value of Venus's position at one rising = 7 signs, 5 degrees, 28 minutes. Thus, all is proven.

In this text, we have taken the word "water" <note>Sanskrit: *jala*</note> to mean the number 4 by inference. In the currently available astronomical treatises <note>Sanskrit: *Siddhāntas*</note>, the word "water" is not used anywhere to represent a number. In astrological works, "water" refers to the fourth house among the twelve houses of the zodiac.

Then, in 85 days (calculated by groups of eight), it moves 77 degrees. Then in three days...

# Clarification of the Pañcasiddhāntikā
<note>This title refers to the "Light on the Five Treatises," a commentary on Varāhamihira’s astronomical work.</note>

The value for the first section of Jupiter’s position in signs and degrees is 5 signs, 6 degrees, and 30 minutes. In the second section, it is half a circle, which is six signs. In the final section, however, it is ten plus three, totaling thirteen degrees. When Jupiter is equal to its <term>apex of quick motion<note>Sanskrit: śīghrocca; the point in a planet's orbit where its apparent speed is greatest, used in ancient Indian astronomy to calculate planetary positions.</note></term>, it then travels 12 degrees in sixty days. With forty days, it travels four degrees. With twenty-four days, it travels two degrees. Then, in fifteen days, it becomes retrograde. From that sixty-day point, Jupiter moves in retrograde for six degrees over sixty days, and again six degrees over another sixty days. After this, it becomes "after-retrograde" <note>prograde or direct motion</note> and follows its path. It travels nine degrees in eighty days, and another nine degrees in forty-five days before it reaches its setting <note>heliacal setting, disappearing in the sun's glare</note>. After remaining there for one month, in the following month, the "clear rising" <note>heliacal rising</note> of this Jupiter occurs.

### The Mathematical Proof

Here is the derivation: According to the modern *Sūrya Siddhānta*, the solar revolutions in an eon are 4,320,000, and the revolutions of Jupiter are 364,220. Therefore, the revolutions of the <term>anomaly of conjunction<note>Sanskrit: śīghrakendra; the difference between the mean longitude of the Sun and the planet.</note></term> = Solar revolutions - Jupiter's revolutions = 3,955,780. The number of conjunctions of the Sun and Jupiter in 1,577,919,800 <term>civil days<note>Sanskrit: kudina; terrestrial days in a Kalpa or great cycle.</note></term> is equal to these revolutions of the anomaly.

By proportion: If 3,955,780 conjunctions occur in 1,577,919,800 civil days, then how much time for one conjunction?
The time for one conjunction = $\frac{1577919800}{3955780}$ = 396 - $\frac{1}{9}$ days (approximately).

Then, another proportion: If one conjunction occurs in 396 - $\frac{1}{9}$ days, then what is the value of the conjunctions for a given <term>count of days<note>Sanskrit: ahargaṇa; the number of days elapsed since the start of an epoch.</note></term>?
Value of conjunctions = $\frac{Days}{396 - \frac{1}{9}}$

If we divide the total days by 396 and call the quotient "Risings," then by the method of division, the actual remainder = Days - Risings $\times$ (396 - $\frac{1}{9}$) = Days - 396 $\times$ Risings + $\frac{Risings}{9}$ = Remaining days + $\frac{Risings}{9}$.
Now, in one rising there are 399 days, so in 391 risings there will be 399 $\times$ 391 days.
By proportion: If in 1,577,919,800 days there are 364,220 revolutions of Jupiter, then in 399 $\times$ 391 days, how many?
Jupiter's revolutions in 391 risings = $\frac{364220 \times 399 \times 391}{1577919800}$ = 36 revolutions, 0 signs, 4 degrees (approximately).

Another proportion: If 36 revolutions are obtained in 391 risings, then how many revolutions for a desired number of risings? These are discarded as they are not needed for the current purpose, and the remainder is designated as "Steps" <note>Sanskrit: padasaṃjñā</note>.
Again, if 4 degrees (or 240 minutes) are obtained in 391 risings, then for a desired number of risings, the minutes = $\frac{5 \times Risings}{8}$ (approximately).

The initial additive constant <note>Sanskrit: kṣepa</note> at the start of the text is 18.
Now, when the "Step" is 187, by the previous logic, Jupiter's position in revolutions etc. = $\frac{187}{391}$ = 0 revolutions, 5 signs, 15 degrees, 43 minutes. Here, in the first section, the Teacher <note>referring to the author Varāhamihira</note> has taken 5 signs, 6 degrees, and 30 minutes.
In the second section of 165, Jupiter's value = $\frac{165}{391}$ = 6 signs, 0 degrees, -27 minutes; the Teacher took 6 signs.
In the third section, Jupiter's value = $\frac{16}{391}$ = 0 signs, 14 degrees, 44 minutes; the Teacher took 13 degrees.

It is inferred that to account for the variation caused by Jupiter's <term>slow-equation<note>Sanskrit: mandaphala; the correction for the eccentricity of the orbit.</note></term>, the Teacher sometimes used values like "nine and a half degrees of Virgo" etc., resulting from corrections like "the moon, the Vedas, the arrows, the flavors" <note>A mnemonic code (Kaṭapayādi system) for numbers used in calculations</note>. If Jupiter is equal to its apex of quick motion, then following that, by calculation with slight difference—

# 14-20. Now he describes the movement of Saturn. **One hundred and a half** etc.
<note>original: *Śanaiścara* (Saturn)</note>

From the days of the total count of days <term>Ahargana</term><note>The number of elapsed days since the start of an epoch</note>, one should subtract **one hundred and a half (150)** along with one-third part and twenty <term>Ghatis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. Subtract it. Then, from the quotient obtained by dividing by the "Vasu-Muni-Gunas" **378** <note>Vasu=8, Muni=7, Guna=3; read right-to-left in the Katapayadi system</note>, those are the "Rising-names" <note>The number of synodic cycles</note> of the Sun-knower <note>Saturn</note> as before. The remainder represents the days etc. situated after the rising. Then, from the remaining days, one should abandon—meaning discard—one-tenth of the Rising-name. The remaining days are to be placed separately for the purpose of knowing the movement. Now, from the Rising-name multiplied by nine and divided by the "Subject-Senses" **256**, the remainder becomes the "Step-number" <term>Pada-sankhya</term>. That should be added to eighty-nine **89**. Through verses 16-17, a certain special correction arising from the <term>Manda-phala</term> <note>The equation of center, correcting for elliptical orbits</note> is given by the Teacher. Nevertheless, by the latter half of verse 17, the correction which is calculated from the Rising-name is as follows: Saturn's rising, the Rising-name multiplied by twenty-one and divided by "Double-Senses" **32**, the result is the increase to be made in the "Accumulation-name" <term>Caya</term>. That is to say, by this method, the correction produced is an increase of minutes <term>Kalas</term> equal to the twenty-second part of the Rising-name multiplied by twenty-one. By verse 16 and the first half of verse 17, the correction is calculated based on three "Steps" <term>Padas</term>: the first segment up to **30** steps, the second segment up to **129** steps, and the third segment up to **66** steps. In the first segment, the measure of Saturn is sixteen degrees of Taurus minus ninety. In the second, five signs, three times twenty-seven degrees, and thirty-four minutes. In the third segment, it is seven degrees of Leo and twenty-eight minutes—this is the measure of Saturn in sequence. Now, when Saturn is at its <term>Shighrochcha</term> <note>Apex of fast motion/perigee in ancient models</note>, thereafter in sixteen days it covers three degrees; in fifty-six days it covers double—meaning it moves three degrees and fifty-two minutes. Then, in fifty-five days, it becomes retrograde <term>Vakri</term>. Then, the retrograde Saturn, having moved three degrees in sixty-eight days and four degrees in sixty days, becomes direct <term>Margi</term>. Then, "half and a hundred"—the sum of these is "one hundred and a half" <note>original: *adhyardha-śata*</note>—by the derivation of "one hundred and a half," it moves through the eighth parts of one hundred and five **105** and goes to its setting <term>Asta</term>. Then, the set Saturn, having moved three degrees in thirty-six days, goes to its rising.

Here is the proof <term>Upapatti</term>. According to the contemporary *Surya Siddhanta*:
Solar revolutions = **4,320,000**
Saturn's revolutions = **146,568**
Revolutions of Saturn's conjunction = Solar revs - Saturn revs = **4,173,432**
Then the proportion: if **4,173,432** revolutions take **1,577,917,800** days, then how many for one revolution? This gives the time of the Sun-Saturn conjunction:
= $\frac{1,577,917,800}{4,173,432}$ = 378 $\frac{11}{93}$
The Teacher has taken $\frac{10}{84}$ in place of this $\frac{11}{93}$. Then another proportion...

If one revolution of the <term>anomaly (shighrakendra)</term> occurs in 378 $\frac{1}{10}$ days, then what are the revolutions for the given <term>total days (ahargana)</term>? ### 21-35. Now he describes the motion of Mars and others. "From the total days," etc.

Subtracting two-five-six (256) <note>read as 256 using the 'ankanam vamato gatih' rule where digits are read right to left</note> and forty (40) <term>nadi (60 nadi = 1 day)</term> from the total days, and dividing the remainder by eight-seven (78), the risings of Mars are obtained as before. To the remaining days, add the number of risings multiplied by one hundred and sixty-one (157 + 4 = 161) in <term>vinadi (1/60 of a nadi)</term>; then the true remaining days are found—this should be understood. The number of risings multiplied by eighteen and divided by fifteen gives the remaining value from this division. Then, making each remaining sign less by its own fifth part, the mean Mars is to be calculated according to the zodiacal proportions. That is, the remainder minus its fifth part is the mean Mars in signs and degrees.

From this, the calculator should determine the true course of Mars according to the sequence of its clear motion. Based on the true position of Mars, one should calculate its rising, retrograde motion, and other movements. The degrees representing the difference between the mean and true Mars—if the mean is greater—should be added to the previously established corrected days. If the mean is less, those degrees of difference should be subtracted; then the actual days for knowing the true motion are obtained. Now, the Teacher <note>Varāhamihira, the author of the original text</note> speaks of the motion through its course in verses 25–26. Among them, the knowledge of the numbers in verse 25 is not possible due to extreme corruption in the text. Mars, having gone thirteen degrees from its setting <note>heliacal setting</note>, becomes zero-degrees <note>conjunction</note> with the Sun. Then, after passing twenty degrees beyond the zero-point, it reaches its rising <note>heliacal rising</note>. Therefore, the Teacher says, "I shall describe the sequence of days based on the velocity of the course." In verses 27–28, what kind of sequence of days or sequence of motion he describes is not understood until now.

When Mars is situated in Pisces, Scorpio, Aries, or Sagittarius and becomes retrograde—that is, starts moving in the reverse direction—then in six times seven, which is forty-two (42) days, it covers nine degrees. Again, in forty-two (42) days, it covers seven (7) degrees. Then, having traversed sixteen degrees in sixty days, it enters "following motion" <term>Anugati: a specific stage of planetary speed</term>. It is inferred that the Teacher uses the word *Anugati* to mean the mean motion of Mars. If *Anugati* is taken to mean direct motion, then the start of direct motion after retrogradation would come after 144 days; however, in actual calculation, the start of direct motion after retrogradation usually occurs within 60 days. Therefore, in my opinion, the word *Anugati* does not mean direct motion.

Mars situated in Taurus, Gemini, Libra, or Virgo covers seven degrees in 40 days, then ten degrees in 40 days, and seventeen degrees in 60 days, respectively, after the start of retrogradation as before. Mars (the "Forward-Moving One") situated in Cancer or Leo similarly covers seven degrees in 44 days, six degrees in 40 days, and eighteen degrees in 60 days respectively during the stages of retrogradation. Likewise, Mars situated in Aquarius or Capricorn, in that same reduction, covers six degrees in 32 days, nine degrees in 36 days, and fifteen degrees in 57 days.

In verse 33, the Teacher describes the measure for the motions of retrograde, extreme retrograde, and post-retrograde, but that is not understood due to the corruption of the verse. The numbers 1, 5, 8, 11, 14, 11, 6, when combined with two fortnights <note>adding 2 to each</note>, result in the seven types of motion for Mars: 3, 7, 10, 13, 16, 13, 11. Thus, the eighth motion, named "Fast Motion," is of three types: 36, 36, 36, by subtracting Moon (1), Squares (4), and Vedas (4) from forty. He then states the days for the previously established motions. When 36 is increased by the numbers Fire (3), Fire (3), Nine (9), Sun (12), Square (4), Fire (3), and Zero (0), the days for the seven previously established motions become: 38, 36, 45, 48, 45, 36, 36. The days of travel stated for these seven motions are to be understood as the same (thirty-six) for the eighth motion and the Fast Motion.

->**Now, the Rationale:** According to the modern *Sūrya Siddhānta*, the Sun's revolutions = 4,320,000. The revolutions of Mars<-
= 2,296,832. The revolutions of the <term>Śīghrakendra: the anomaly of conjunction</term> = 2,023,168. The resulting synodic period of Mars and the Sun = $\frac{1577919800}{2023168}$ = 780 days and 277 <term>Vighaṭikās: units of time equal to 24 seconds</term>. According to the Teacher's view, 161 of these Vighaṭikās are arrived at. Now, another proportion: if one synodic period is 780 days and 161 Vighaṭikās (including fractions), then what is obtained from the total elapsed days <note>Ahargaṇa</note>? These are called the "Heart-values" produced from the first part as before. From that, the actual remainder = Total Days - Rising (780 days - 161 Vighaṭikās) = Total Days - (780 × Rising) + (161 × Rising Vighaṭikās) = Remainder + (161 Vighaṭikās × Rising).

Following the previous logic, eighteen revolutions of <term>Mars</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Bhauma*</note> occur in fifteen so-called "risings." From this, a proportion is made: if eighteen revolutions are obtained from fifteen risings, then what is obtained from the desired rising? Since the resulting full revolutions are not needed here, they are discarded. The remainder is multiplied by twelve and divided by fifteen, resulting in the signs and degrees of the <term>Mean Mars</term> <note>The average position of the planet without corrections</note> $= \frac{12 \times \text{remainder}}{15} = \frac{4 \times \text{remainder}}{5}$. Thus, the calculation for <term>Mars</term> is established. Since one day is obtained by the motion of the <term>Mars anomaly</term> <note>Sanskrit: *śīghrakendra*</note>, then how many days are produced by the difference in degrees multiplied by sixty? The days $= \frac{60 \times \text{difference degrees}}{28} = 2 \times \text{difference degrees}$. Due to the small difference, a correction of days equal to twice the difference in degrees is appropriate to add to the previously established days; then the days elapsed after the conjunction of the <term>Apex of Quick Motion</term> <note>Sanskrit: *śīghrocca*</note> and Mars will be found. If the method of the Teacher <note>Referring to Varāhamihira</note> for the true calculation of <term>Mars</term>—the reason for which does not currently occur to the mind—is distinct, then the previously stated correction is fitting. Now, even without the <term>correction for the equation of center</term> <note>Sanskrit: *mandaphala-saṃskāra*</note>, by a rough calculation after retrogradation, <term>Mars</term> moves 6 degrees in 42 days, then 5 degrees in 40 days in reverse; then it moves 20 degrees sequentially in 60 days. However, when <term>Mars</term> is in a different sign, it will certainly move different degrees due to the difference in motion caused by the <term>equation of center</term> and other factors. These were written by the Teacher after confirming them through observation. Thus, the days available for all eight types of motion were recited by the Teacher.

## 36-56. Now he describes the movement and other details of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Budha*</note>. Beginning with "Add seven times four..."

The fractional parts of the remaining days, or the remaining days themselves, are to be known as the real days. From these, subtract minutes equal to the risings divided by four; then the real days for the purpose of knowing the movement are known. The risings are multiplied by four and three <note>43</note>, then one should subtract three and three <note>33</note>. Divide the remainder by nine, eight, and three <note>389</note>; then the <term>Mean Mercury</term> starting from revolutions will be found. Now, from the remainder after dividing by 389, the <term>True Mercury</term> and the <term>Apex of Quick Motion</term> are to be known by the method to be described. **Here is the mathematical proof:** According to the modern <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, the revolutions of Mercury = 4,320,000. $= 8 \text{ days} - 3 (629 \text{ days} + 2 \text{ ghatikas}) = 8 \text{ days} - 629 \text{ risings} - 2 \text{ ghatikas per rising} = \text{remainder} - 2 \text{ ghatikas per rising}$. This remainder relates to eight risings; therefore, by dividing by eight, the remainder for a single rising is produced $= \frac{\text{rem}}{8} - \frac{3 \text{ ghatikas}}{4}$. By this, verse 36 and the first part of verse 37 are proven. Thus, from these 286 risings <note>likely typo for 'udayaih'</note>, 123 revolutions of Mercury are derived. The true position of Mercury has been calculated using the correction for the equation of the center <note>original: *mandaphala-saṃskāra*</note>. Following this, the movements of Mercury through the twelve signs of the zodiac, starting with Aries, are described. Just as with Mars, there is a cause arising from the equation of the center which depends on the specific calculation of true positions; however, we do not yet fully understand this. This matter should be deeply contemplated by the wise.

### 57. Now, the visibility correction related to latitude is described. "By the method of sines..."

By the previously mentioned method of sines, the latitude <note>original: *vikṣepa*, specifically the sine of the latitude or *śarajyā*</note> is multiplied by the ascensional difference <note>original: *carākālāṃśa*</note> and divided by 480. Depending on whether the latitude is North or South, one should subtract from or add to the planet's position as appropriate. 

In other words, the result obtained by multiplying the sine of the latitude by the ascensional difference (in minutes) and dividing by 480 <note>original: *śūnyāṣṭavedaiḥ*</note> gives the degrees to be added to the planet for the purpose of calculating its rising if the latitude is Southern, or subtracted if Northern. For calculating the setting of the planet, the opposite must be done: subtract for Southern latitude and add for Northern. Thus, the planet becomes "corrected for visibility latitude" <note>term: *akṣadṛkkarmasaṃskṛta* — a correction to find the point on the ecliptic that rises or sets simultaneously with the planet</note>. Then, based on the rules to be mentioned regarding the distance between the Sun and the planet, the astronomer should declare the planet's visibility or disappearance.

**Here is the geometric proof:** Let *kha-saṃ* be the prime vertical. *me-saṃ* is the celestial equator. *ya-khaṃ* is the horizon. *me-dṛ-stha* is the ecliptic. *ya* is the planetary disk on the horizon. *syā* is the position of the planet on the ecliptic. *syā-sthā'* is the diurnal circle at the planet's position. *dṛ* is the point on the ecliptic on the horizon when the planetary disk is on the horizon. *syā-dhra* is the latitude of the planet along the polar longitude circle. *saṃ-ca'* is the ascensional difference based on the planetary disk. *saṃ-ca* is the ascensional difference based on the ecliptic position. Their difference is *ca-ca'*. *syā-sthā'* is approximately equal to *syā-dṛ* due to the small difference; calculating this is our goal. This arises from the latitude *syā-dhra* and the ecliptic segment. For this, the Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> has provided a rough proportion: If by the maximum declination sine 48...

[Calculation:] $\frac{\text{Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Sine of Latitude}}{48}$ 
This results in the visibility correction in degrees = $\frac{\text{Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Sine of Latitude}}{480}$

Thus, what was stated is proven. When the latitude is South, the planet's position on the ecliptic goes above the horizon; therefore, at rising, the planetary disk is at the eastern horizon, and the value must be added to the ecliptic position. When the latitude is North, as in my diagram, when the planetary disk is at the eastern horizon, the ecliptic position is below it; therefore, it must be subtracted from the ecliptic position. At setting, the opposite occurs. Everything is thus consistent.

### 58-60. Now, the degrees of time and their correction are described. "Having done this..."

After performing the visibility correction, one should declare the disappearance or appearance of the planets based on their distance from the Sun. These "degrees of time" <note>term: *kālāṃśa* — the arc of separation from the Sun required for a planet to be visible</note> are respectively: 12 for the Moon, 14 for Mars, 12 for Jupiter, 15 for Venus, 8 for Saturn, and 15 for Mercury. At these degrees, the rising or setting of the Moon and others occurs. Now, for the correction of these degrees: the aforementioned degrees are multiplied by 20 and divided by the rising time (in *vināḍikās*) of the zodiac sign occupied by the planet. This gives the true degrees for the rising or setting of those planets.
