It should be said: Thus, by those degrees of the planet—the degrees of time relating to the planet—when Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are <note>original: "averunāstada"</note> less than the Sun, they rise in the East; this is the remaining sense. Similarly, for the Moon: when the Moon is greater than the Sun by the degrees of time, it becomes visible. Thus, having known all the latitudes <term>vixepa: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</term> from the <term>shara: literally 'arrow', referring to the sine of the latitude</term>, the calculator should then make predictions of the future, such as the risings and settings of those planets to come.

In this matter, the proof is simply observation. The clarification of the degrees of time <note>original: "kālāṃśa"</note> is done by the Rule of Three: if the degrees of time mentioned in the text are obtained by twenty, then what are they by the rising minutes of the zodiac sign occupied by the planet? By an inverse proportion, the corrected degrees of time are produced = $\frac{Mean\ Degrees\ of\ Time \times 300}{Rising\ Minutes\ of\ the\ Sign}$. In this inverse Rule of Three, the reasoning is also based on observation. Everything else is easy to understand.

61-65. Now he states the conclusion of the book. "The one from Avanti, having attained..." and so on.

The teacher named Varāhamihira, residing in the city of Avanti <note>modern Ujjain</note>, composed this <term>karika-tantra: a concise astronomical treatise</term> of the star-planets from the Five Siddhāntas in a summarized form for the benefit of his students, making it consistent with observed calculations and clear figures. Whether regarding the Mars <note>literally: "son of the earth"</note> of the teacher Pradyumna, or the Jupiter of Vijayanandin, or the Saturn and Mercury of the Sūrya Siddhānta—any calculator whose enthusiasm is broken because of a lack of unity between calculation and observation should now devote himself to this clear <term>karana: a practical astronomical manual</term> of mine. Three quarters of verse 62 are damaged. Now he praises the virtuous man: He who does not speak of the faults of an absent person even when the occasion arises—that is, during a discussion of such faults—and who proclaims their virtues even when there is no specific occasion, spreading them extensively; salutations to such a virtuous man who acts for the welfare of others. Now, the envy-free Varāhamihira gives this excellent path of the planets, this manual in the form of a system for the star-planets, to his students in eighteen *āryā* verses.

66. Now he states a specific rule regarding risings and settings. "From the calculation..." and so on.

For the sake of perfect calculation, first, the degrees of the Sun should be known when the planet is equal to its <term>shighrochcha: the 'fast apex' or anomaly, used to calculate the planet's position relative to the Sun</term>. Then, the days related to the degrees of motion should be added to the Sun; thus the Sun at the time of the desired motion is found. Thus, when the degrees of the Sun are calculated from the days according to the previous method, those degrees of the *shighrochcha* should be known from the time of the completion of the cycle.

The proof here is very easy. Since, if by a rough method the daily motion of the Sun is assumed to be one degree, then the Sun at the time of the planet's *shighrochcha*, plus the degrees equal to the days of motion, becomes the Sun at the time of motion from the completion of the *shighrochcha* cycle.

67. Now, wishing to explain the rising of the planets according to the school of Puliśa, he first describes the rising of Mars. "Nine, two, three, six..." and so on.

Generally, the teacher Puliśa does not mention the name of the <term>ahargana: the count of elapsed days since the start of an epoch</term> (the calculation of the mean positions should be observed). Therefore, the term *ahargana* must be supplied here. When the *ahargana* is diminished by 6329 <note>original: "navayamaguṇartu"</note>, then multiplied by four, and divided by 3075 <note>original: "viṣayasaptakhāgni"</note>, and the remainder is again divided by four, the result is the "degree-less days" of Mars—meaning the days since the time of the Sun-Mars conjunction.

Here is the rationale: The teacher Pulisa <note>Pulisa-acharya, a renowned astronomer often associated with the Paulisa Siddhanta</note> assumed the period of the conjunction of the Sun and Mars to be $768 \frac{3}{4}$ days (calculated as $\frac{3075}{4}$). However, by the previous method, these days come to 780. Therefore, the proportion is: if 4 conjunctions are obtained in 3075 days, then how many are obtained from the *Ahargana* <note>The total count of elapsed civil days since the epoch</note>? Since the resulting quotients are of no use here, they are discarded; the remainder is divided by four to determine how many days have passed since the last conjunction.

### 68-69. Now, he describes the motion [of Mars]. "By six-mountains" etc.

By "six-mountains" (26) days, Mars is seen separated from the Sun by "lunar days" (15) degrees. Then, by "eight-eighteen" (188) days, it is separated by sixty degrees; by "eight-hundred" (108) days, by sixty degrees; by "two-increased-by-seventy" (72) days, by ninety degrees; by "eight-joined-with-sixty" (68) days, by "half-a-hundred" (50) degrees; and by "sky-oceans-twins" (240) days, it is separated by "seven-times-ten" (70) degrees. After this, it sets. After setting, in "seven-eights" (56) days, there is a decrease equal to the degrees of the Sun-Mars interval at the time of setting (15 degrees), and Mars reaches "zero-motion" <note>original: "niranshagati"</note> when Mars becomes equal to the Sun.

| Days | Intervals of Sun-Mars Separation |
|----------|----------|
| 26 | 15° |
| 188 | 60° |
| 108 | 60° |
| 72 | 90° |
| 68 | 50° |
| 240 | 70° |
| 56 | 15° |
| **767** | **360°** |

The rationale here: The teacher Pulisa has stated these intervals of separation as they were obtained through observation or calculation for those specific days in a simplified manner.

### 70-72. Now, he describes the rising and other phases of Mercury. "Moon-Vasu-Rasas" etc.

When the *Ahargana* is reduced by "Moon-Vasu-Rasa-Indra" (14,681) and then multiplied by "nine-twins" (29) and divided by "Sun-Rama-Guna" (3,312), the remainder—when divided by the multiplier "nine-twins" (29)—gives the days of the "Son of the Moon" (Mercury). From these days, the following motions are described: When the conjunction of the Sun and Mercury occurs, ten days later, being 12 degrees from the Sun, Mercury becomes a visible riser in the East. Then, in "Manu" (14) days, the distance decreases by ten degrees. Then, in eighteen days, Mercury is within nine degrees of the Sun. Then, in thirty days, having increased by thirteen degrees from the Sun, it rises in the West. Then, in eighteen days, it moves forward by nine degrees. Then, in sixteen days, it decreases by eight degrees and sets in the West. Finally, in eight days, Mercury, decreasing by another nine degrees, becomes "degree-less" <note>original: "niransha"</note>, meaning equal to the Sun.

73-75. Now he describes the rising and other phenomena of Jupiter, beginning with the phrase "Subtracting two-eights," etc.

Here, the first quarter of verse 73 is corrupt; therefore, the actual value of the epoch-constant <term>Kshepa: a value added to the calculation to account for the starting position at the beginning of an era</term> is not known. When the <term>Ahargana: the total count of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term> is multiplied by seven and divided by 2752 <note>The text uses the word-numeral "two-senses-tones-horses" where senses=5, tones=7, horses=2, read right-to-left as 2752</note>, the remainder is again divided by seven. From these days, the motions of Jupiter occur according to the rule to be stated. When those motions are subtracted from the position of the Sun, Jupiter's position at the desired time is found—this is the remainder of the calculation. This means those motions are the degrees of separation between the Sun and Jupiter.

Sixteen days after the time of conjunction, having reached a separation of twelve degrees from the Sun, Jupiter rises in the east. Then, in 54 days <note>original: "kṛta-viṣayai" (4 and 5)</note>, it moves 44 degrees <note>original: "kṛta-vedāḥ" (4 and 4)</note>. In 70 days, it moves 64 and a half degrees. In 109 days, it moves a number equal to 120. In 88 days, it moves a number equal to 76. In 40 days, it moves 32. These are the segments of separation in order. After Jupiter has traversed these degrees of separation, it then goes to its setting <note>Heliacal setting, becoming invisible due to the Sun's glare</note>. Sixteen days after setting, with a separation of twelve degrees again, Jupiter becomes "degree-less"—meaning it reaches a conjunction with the Sun.

# Page 109 of the Illumination of the Panchasiddhantika

He describes the motion and other characteristics [of Venus] with the phrase **"By the senses (5) and minus nine,"** meaning that when Venus is five days and nine degrees away from the Sun, it rises in the east. Then, in fifteen days <note>Sanskrit: *tithi*, a lunar day</note>, it becomes twenty-one degrees less than the Sun. By two hundred and eight days (*vasu-krtya*) <note>Vasu = 8, Krtya = 20; a poetic way to say 208</note>, it is fifteen degrees less. Again, by twelve days (*krta* plus *asta*), it increases by five degrees; that is, it moves five degrees toward the Sun and sets in the east. Then, in forty-eight days (*sastha-astaka*), it moves ten degrees toward the Sun and becomes "degree-less" <term>niransha: the point of conjunction where the planet's longitude matches the Sun's</term>, equal to the Sun. From this degree-less position, moving in reverse <note>retrograde motion</note>, it appears ahead of the Sun in the west after a period of forty-eight days, and then, moving in reverse, it sets. That is, Venus sets in the west while in retrograde.

->Days of the Degree-less Period $\qquad$ Intervals of Degrees<-

| Days of the Degree-less Period | Intervals of Degrees |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|
| 5                              | — 6                  |
| 15                             | — 21                 |
| 208                            | — 15                 |
| 12                             | + 5                  |
| 48                             | + 10                 |
| ---                            | ---                  |
| 288                            | 0                    |

Thus, in 288 days, it becomes degree-less again in the west. By doubling this to 576 days, the time of conjunction in that direction is determined.

Now for the proof: As before, the teacher Pulisha <note>A famous astronomer often associated with Greek-influenced Indian astronomy</note> has taken the time of the Sun-Venus conjunction to be equal to the period of the revolution of the anomaly, which is $579 \frac{1}{2}$ (from $\frac{1159}{2}$). Therefore, all calculations follow the previous logic, and the reasoning is easy to understand. It is inferred that after describing the rising in the west, the duration of the setting etc. was not mentioned because it is already well-known.

***

78-81. Now he describes the rising and other motions of Saturn. **"By the *vidhuti*, *shara*, and *rasa*..."**

Here, the word in brackets in the first quarter of verse 78 appears incorrect because it breaks the meter. When the total count of days <term>ahargana: the number of days elapsed since a fixed epoch</term> is reduced by 16,518 (*dhrti-shara-rasa-shashanka*), and the remainder is multiplied by three and divided by 1,118 (*dhrti-rudra*), the result divided by three gives the "degree-less" days of Saturn <note>Sanskrit: *saura*, referring here to the son of the Sun, Saturn</note> as before. Then, the extent of its motion should be known by the following rules: In eighteen days (*dhrti*), Saturn rises in the east when it is 16° 30' (sixteen and a half degrees) from the Sun. Then, in 88 days, it is 90° 30' (ninety and a half degrees) from the Sun. Then, in fourteen days (*manu*), it is thirteen degrees less; in 113 days (*guna-rudra*), it is 120 degrees less; in 98 days, it is nine degrees less; and in thirteen days (*ati-jagati*), it becomes 12° 30' less and sets. Then, for the duration of its invisibility, Saturn moves 16° 30' in nineteen days (*ati-dhrti*) to reach the degree-less conjunction with the Sun. Thus, Saturn always moves while being "less" <note>behind in longitude</note> than the Sun.

# CHAPTER I.

---

### INTRODUCTORY.

---

1. Having at the outset done devout reverence to the various most excellent <term>Sages</term> <note>original: "Munis"; refers to ancient inspired seers or holy men</note> among whom the <term>Sun-God</term> <note>original: "Sûrya"</note> and <term>Vasishṭha</term> <note>One of the seven great Vedic seers</note> are foremost, and to my father and teacher by whom I was instructed in this <term>Scientific Treatise</term> <note>original: "Śâstra"</note>,

2. I shall endeavour to state in its entirety, according to the opinions of earlier teachers, that correction of the planetary motions (<term>seed-correction</term>) <note>original: "bîja"</note> which is most excellent, easy, clear and a wonderful mystery.

The term <term>seed-correction</term> <note>original: "bîja"</note> signifies any correction applied to astronomical elements which aims at bringing about an agreement between the celestial phenomena such as calculated and such as actually observed. <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>The 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath who authored this text</note> seems anxious to show that the <term>seed-correction</term> applied by him is not his own invention but bases on the authority of former teachers.

3. There are the following <term>Astronomical Systems</term> <note>original: "Siddhântas"; established scientific traditions or conclusions</note>: The <term>Paulisha</term>, the <term>Romaka</term> <note>Likely influenced by Greek or Roman/Alexandrian astronomy</note>, the <term>Vasishṭha</term>, the <term>Solar</term> <note>original: "Saura"</note> and the <term>Ancestral</term> <note>original: "Paitâmaha"; referring to the god Brahma</note>. Out of these five the first two have been explained by <term>Lâṭadeva</term>.

4. The <term>System</term> made by <term>Paulisha</term> is accurate, near to it stands the <term>System</term> proclaimed by <term>Romaka</term>; more accurate is the <term>Solar System</term> <note>original: "Sâvitra" or "Saura"</note>; the two remaining ones are far from the truth.

5. That subject which is the greatest mystery, which perplexes the minds of the writers of astronomical works, namely, the eclipses of the sun, I am going to explain in this work, dismissing all jealousy.

6. Moreover, there are contained in this work the (rules for the calculation of the) direction, the duration, the period of total obscuration,

The three preceding stanzas contain a concisely stated rule for the calculation of the civil day-count <note>original: "sâvana ahargaṇa"</note> <note>i.e., the number of civil days which have elapsed from a certain epoch up to a given date</note>, according to the Roman Doctrine. ### Rules for finding the so-called Lords of the year, month, day and hour.—

The rule for finding the Lord of the year bases on the assumption of years of 360 days; the Lord of the year so constituted is that planet which rules over the first day. In order to facilitate the calculation, the rule directs us to divide the whole given <term>ahargana</term> into periods of 2520 = 7 x 360 days; as during each of these periods the <term>Lord of the year</term> <note>original: "varshapati"</note> revolves through the whole series of seven, they may be disregarded in the calculation. The <term>additive quantity</term> <note>original: "kshepa-quantity"</note> is manifestly added to the end that the calculation may start from the epoch of the <term>astronomical manual</term> <note>original: "karana"</note>. The days remaining—after the periods of 2520 days have been rejected—are divided by 360; to the resulting years one is added for the current year, they are multiplied by three because in the series of the planets arranged in the order of the days of the week the Lords of the years follow one another at intervals of three, and finally four are deducted (which is the same as adding three) in order to enable us to count the <term>Lords of the years</term> <note>original: "varshapatis"</note> from the sun, instead of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Budha"</note> who is the Lord of the year of the epoch. We finally divide by seven when the remainder shows the <term>Lord of the year</term> of the current year.—The Lord of the month is found in an analogous manner. The resulting number of months of thirty days each is multiplied by two because the Lords of the months follow one another at intervals of two places.—The Lord of the day is found by a simple division of the <term>ahargana</term> by seven.—The formula for the elapsed Lords of the hours would be: Lord of the day + 5 (elapsed hours — 1)—for the Lord of the first hour is the Lord of the

Stanza 2 directs us to add a <term>kshepa</term> <note>an additive constant or "interpolated" value used to align a calculation with a specific epoch</note> quantity of 1936 to the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>the count of elapsed days since the beginning of a specific era</note> and thereupon to divide the latter into periods of 3031 days each which are called <term>ghana</term> <note>literally "solid" or "cube," here used as a technical term for a specific large time cycle</note>. The remainder is to be multiplied by 9 and divided by 248, *i. e.*, it is to be divided into periods of <sup>248</sup>/<sub>9</sub> days each which are called <term>gati</term> <note>literally "motion" or "gait," representing a smaller time unit</note>. The remainder of the last division is called <term>pada</term> <note>literally "step" or "quarter"</note>. The whole given <term>ahargaṇa</term> is thus subdivided into a certain number of <term>ghana</term>s plus a certain number of <term>gati</term>s plus a <term>pada</term>. The rationale of this subdivision is, that the period of <sup>248</sup>/<sub>9</sub> days very nearly represents one anomalistic month <note>the time it takes the moon to travel from perigee to perigee, roughly 27.55 days</note>, while the <term>ghana</term> period of 3031 days is nearly equal to one hundred and ten such months. Hence in any integral number of <term>ghana</term>s and <term>gati</term>s the moon returns to her apogee <note>the point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> (from which the calculation must be supposed to start) and thus no equation of the centre <note>the correction required to account for the elliptical shape of an orbit</note> need be applied to it. The latter in fact depends solely on the remainder which is here called <term>pada</term>.

While the division of the <term>ahargaṇa</term> into <term>ghana</term>s and <term>gati</term>s furnishes us at once, without any further calculation being required, with information as to the position of the moon with regard to her apogee, special calculations have to be performed to the end of finding her mean place. We have at first to ascertain how many revolutions the moon performs in one <term>ghana</term>. As we are so far ignorant of the moon's mean motion according to that <term>Siddhānta</term> <note>a traditional Indian astronomical treatise</note> whose teaching the text here summarizes, we employ the rate of motion as determined by the <term>Sūrya Siddhānta</term> <note>one of the most influential early Sanskrit astronomical texts</note>, when we find that the moon's motion in 3031 days amounts to 110<sup>rev</sup> 11<sup>s</sup> 7° 31' 23''. Rejecting the whole revolutions we might express the above as one revolution minus three quarters of a sign plus about <sup>1</sup>/<sub>1285</sub> of a sign. The reason for this is apparent; during $\frac{124}{9}$ days = half a <term>gati</term> the moon advances from her apogee <note>The point in the orbit farthest from Earth.</note> to the perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth.</note> where the equation of the centre <note>The correction applied to the mean position to find the true position due to the orbit's eccentricity.</note> again is equal to zero, and any calculation of the moon's true place may with advantage start from the last place at which the equation had been equal to zero. Only it is in that case not apparent why stanza 5 directs us to add, for that half <term>gati</term>, six signs plus four minutes to the moon's mean place; for the moon's mean motion in one half <term>gati</term> amounts to considerably more, *viz.*, six signs plus about ninety-two minutes. Nor are we at present able to throw light upon the meaning of the processes prescribed in stanza 6. They possibly refer to the operation of finding the moon's true place, although we are more inclined to think that this latter point is treated in stanzas 4—9 of the next chapter. But as those stanzas themselves have, on the whole, remained obscure to us, no definite conclusion can for the present be arrived at.—Some further remarks on the point under discussion are to be found in the Introduction to this work.

7. One-fourth of the moon’s longitude multiplied by nine gives the <term>nakshatra</term><note>A lunar mansion or segment of the ecliptic; there are 27 in total.</note> in which the moon is currently located; the remaining degrees represent <term>muhûrtas</term><note>A traditional unit of time equal to 48 minutes; there are 30 in a full day.</note>. Half the difference in longitude between the sun and the moon multiplied by five gives the <term>tithi</term><note>A lunar day, defined by the longitudinal angle between the sun and moon.</note>, which is interpreted in the same manner (*namely*, with the degrees corresponding to the muhûrtas).

The verse above explains how to determine the current lunar mansion and lunar day based on the moon's position. For the first calculation, we must remember that since 12 zodiac signs are equal to 27 lunar mansions, 1 sign equals 9/4 mansions. Therefore, divide the signs of the moon's longitude by 4 and multiply by 9. Since the moon remains in one mansion for 30 muhûrtas (by average measure), the degrees of the moon's longitude divided by 4 and multiplied by 9 provide the elapsed time in muhûrtas of the current mansion. For the second calculation, we note that one lunar day passes for every 12 degrees of difference between the sun and moon. Thus, each sign of difference corresponds to 2.5 (or 5/2) lunar days, and each degree corresponds to 5/2 muhûrtas.

8. At the start of Capricorn, the <term>solar day</term><note>original: "sâvana day"; a natural day measured from sunrise to sunrise.</note> measures 1591 <term>palas</term><note>A unit of time; 60 palas make one nâḍikâ (24 minutes).</note>, to which three palas must be added for each passing day; in the six signs starting with Cancer, three sets of three (added daily) provide the measurement of the night.

This is a very simplified rule for calculating the length of day and night throughout the year. The shortest day at <term>Avanti</term><note>An ancient Indian city (modern Ujjain) used as the prime meridian by early astronomers.</note> is assumed to be 1591 palas (equivalent to 26 <term>nâḍikâs</term> and 31 palas). Between the shortest and longest days, the daylight is assumed to increase by a steady three palas daily, and then decrease by the same amount during the other half of the year. The day length in one half of the year corresponds to the night length in the other.

9. In the six signs starting with Cancer, multiply the sun's progress (*that is*, the sun's position in signs) by two; the result is the length of the shadow at noon. In the six signs starting with Capricorn, multiply in the same way and subtract the result from twelve.

10. Take half of the midday shadow of any given day and, treating the value as signs, add three signs; this reveals the sun's longitude during its southern journey. During its northern journey, subtract half of the midday shadow from fifteen.

# Page 12

Two very rough rules for finding the length of the gnomon’s shadow from the sun’s mean longitude, and *vice versâ* the latter from the former. — The latitude of Avanti <note>Modern Ujjain, a city of central importance in Indian astronomy as it sits on the ancient prime meridian</note> being supposed equal to the inclination of the ecliptic, the gnomon <note>The vertical rod of a sundial that casts a shadow</note> throws no shadow on the noon of the day on which the sun enters Cancer. The supposition then is that, when the sun has passed through Cancer and is at the first point of Leo, the shadow has reached the length of two <term>angulis</term> <note>A traditional unit of measure, literally "fingers"</note>, and that each further sign adds two more <term>angulis</term> until the sun has reached the first point of Capricorn when the shadow will be 12 <term>angulis</term> long. Each further sign then takes away two <term>angulis</term> until the shadow will again have become zero at the moment when the sun again enters Cancer. — In order to find, by the reverse process, the longitude of the sun from the shadow, we, on any day during the sun's southern progress, divide the midday shadow by two and add three to the quotient, because at the moment when the sun enters on his southern progress his longitude already amounts to 3 signs.

During the six signs of the sun's northern progress the midday shadow is equal to twelve minus double the number of the signs passed through; therefore 2 multiplied by the signs passed through = 12 — shadow; therefore signs = 6 — <sup>shadow</sup>/<sub>2</sub>. But as at the beginning of the northern progress the sun's longitude already amounted to 9 signs, we have to add 9 to the 6 of the above formula and we therefore have in conclusion : Sun's longitude in signs = 15 — <sup>shadow</sup>/<sub>2</sub>.

> 11. Divide 36 by the sum of twelve and of the given shadow minus the midday shadow, and add the longitude of the sun; the result is the <term>lagna</term> <note>The ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, *i. e.*, the ecliptic point on the eastern horizon. If the <term>lagna</term> is required for any time in the afternoon the result is to be deducted from six signs, and the remainder to be added to the sun's longitude.
>
> 12. (In order to calculate the shadow from the given <term>lagna</term>) deduct the longitude of the sun from the <term>lagna</term>; the resulting minutes are to be used as the divisor of 64800. Thus in the eastern hemisphere; in the western hemisphere those minutes have (before being used as divisor) to be deducted from the minutes of six signs.
>
> 13. From the result (in both cases,) 12 has to be deducted and the midday shadow has to be added; this is the calculation of the shadow according to the concise <term>Vâsishṭha Siddhânta</term> <note>One of the five early systems of Indian astronomy, attributed to the sage Vashistha</note>.

The above three stanzas contain rough rules, 1. for the calculation of the <term>lagna</term> (*i. e.*, that point of the ecliptic which at a given moment is on the

The following proportion is now established : When the difference of the given shadow and the midday shadow amounts to zero, the longitude of the <term>lagna</term> amounts to the longitude of the sun plus three signs; to how much will it amount when the difference of the given shadow (whether in the forenoon or afternoon) and the midday shadow amounts to so and so much. In order to establish a workable proportion (for so far we only have a proportion one of whose members is zero) twelve is added to the first and to the third member of the proportion, so that it assumes the following form : When the difference of the given shadow and the midday shadow amounts to 12, the <term>lagna</term> amounts to longitude of sun plus three signs; to how much will the <term>lagna</term> amount when the difference of the given shadow and the midday shadow amounts to so and so much plus 12. Considering that the greater the difference between the given shadow and the midday shadow is (*i. e.*, the nearer the sun is to the eastern horizon), the lesser the interval between sun and <term>lagna</term> will be; the formula for that interval assumes the form stated in stanza 11 :

->12 x 3<-
->I = ---------------------------<-
->12 + given shadow — midday shadow<-

Adding to this the longitude of the sun we have the longitude of the <term>lagna</term>, for any time between sunrise and noon.—For any time in the afternoon the above formula gives, not the interval between the sun and the eastern ecliptic point, but the interval between the sun and the ecliptic point on the western horizon; the result has therefore to be deducted from 6 signs whereby it is transformed into the interval between the sun and the eastern ecliptic point.

Stanzas 12 and 13 contain the rule for finding the length of the shadow from the given <term>lagna</term>; it is simply the reverse of the preceding rule. Instead of signs the calculation is however carried on with minutes, so that the above formula for the interval between sun and <term>lagna</term> assumes the following form :

# CHAPTER III.

---

## THE TREATISE OF PAULIŚA. <note>original: "Pauliśa Siddhānta." One of the five early systems of Indian astronomy, often associated with Greek influences.</note>

---

1. Multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The total count of elapsed days since a specific epoch.</note> by 120, subtract 33, and divide by 43,831; the result is the mean longitude of the sun in the proper order (that is, in full revolutions, signs, and degrees). Add twenty degrees to the sun’s mean anomaly;

2—3. Corresponding to the signs of the anomaly, we have the following sets of minutes which must be subtracted from or added to the sun’s mean longitude; namely:

->11, 48, 69, 69, 54, 25;<-
->and again:<-
->10, 48, 70, 71, 54, 25.<-

Through these adjustments, the mean longitude of the sun is converted into the true longitude.

The three verses above contain the rules for determining the mean and true longitudes of the sun. The first rule is straightforward (if we set aside the <term>kshepa-quantity</term> <note>A constant value or "additive" used to align a calculation with a specific starting point in time.</note> of 33) and is based on the assumption of a <term>sidereal year</term> <note>The time it takes for the sun to return to the same position relative to the fixed stars.</note> consisting of 365 days, 6 hours, and 12 minutes. On the other hand, the method for determining the true position of the sun is stated very obscurely. However, it appears it should be understood as follows:

To determine the sun’s true position, the <term>kendra</term> <note>The mean anomaly, or the angular distance of a planet from its point of closest approach (perigee) or furthest distance (apogee).</note>—that is, the mean anomaly—must be calculated first; however, the text fails to explain how to do this.

Once the <term>kendra</term> is found, we are instructed to increase it by twenty degrees; the reason for this becomes clear from what follows. There is no doubt that the quantities listed in verses 2 and 3 represent different <term>equations of the centre</term> <note>The angular difference between the actual position of a planet in its elliptical orbit and the position it would have if its motion were perfectly circular and uniform.</note>; for it is stated at the end of verse 3 that through them the mean

<page-num>15</page-num>

sun is rendered true. There are two series, each containing six such quantities; but as stanza 2 says that those quantities correspond to signs of anomaly <note>Anomaly refers to the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point from Earth, used to calculate its irregular motion.</note>, we must conclude that only six different equations are intended to be stated, and that hence the corresponding terms of the two series have to be added to each other. On doing this we obtain the following series of equations

->21', 96', 139', 140', 108', 50';<-

and a nearer investigation leaves hardly any doubt that these values represent the sun's equations of the centre <note>The "equation of the centre" is the correction needed to account for the elliptical shape of an orbit when calculating a planet's position.</note> for the mean anomalies of 10°, 40°, 70°, 100°, 130°, 160°. According to the modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, likely dating to the 4th or 5th century CE.</note> the equations of the centre for the mentioned anomalies would amount to

->24', 90', 132', 138', 107', 48';<-

a series not very widely differing from the one given above.

It now appears that the direction given above to add 20° to each anomaly aims at enabling the writer to state his equations of the centres—nominally at least—for entire signs of anomaly; for 10° + 20° = 30° = one sign; 40° + 20° = 60° = two signs and so on.

Another question is why the author prefers to state the equations of the centre for 10°, 40° etc. of anomaly, instead of giving, from the outset, the equations for 30°, 60° and so on.

The reason probably is that he originally intended to state the equations of the centre for whole signs reckoned not from the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit of the sun or a planet where it is farthest from the Earth.</note> of the sun, but from the beginning of the sphere, *i. e.*, the first point of <term>Aries</term>. For stating the sun's equations of the centre for 10° 40° etc. of anomaly is the same as stating them for 90° 120° etc. reckoned from the beginning of the sphere, if only the longitude of the <term>apogee</term> amounts to 80°. But it is well known that the different <term>Siddhântas</term> <note>General term for Indian astronomical texts.</note> teach the longitude of the <term>apogee</term> to amount to so much or about so much.

4—9. Six stanzas referring to the moon and most probably teaching how to find her true position. The details however are obscure. Compare the Introduction.

10—11. Twenty, sixteen and a half, seven minus one quarter multiplied by the equinoctial shadow (of a given place) and taken in direct as well as in reverse order give the <term>vinâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time in ancient Indian astronomy, equal to 24 seconds.</note> of ascensional difference <note>The difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude.</note>.

Beginning from the day of the spring equinox, there is an increase in the length of the day. This increase is determined for the first three zodiac signs starting with Aries by adding the specific numerical quantities (<term>khanda</term> <note>Sanskrit: "parts" or "segments" used in trigonometric calculations</note>). Conversely, these quantities are subtracted successively for the three signs starting with Cancer. A decrease in day length, calculated in a similar manner, occurs during the six signs starting with Libra.

12. This method for finding the <term>vinâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 seconds; 60 vinâdikâs make one nâdikâ</note> of the "ascensional difference" <note>The difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude</note> provides accurate results for the region located between the ocean and the Himalaya mountains. I shall explain how to find accurate results for other locations in the <term>chedyaka</term>-chapter <note>The section dealing with graphical representation or "cutting" of diagrams</note>.

### A rough rule for finding the length of the day during the different seasons of the year in a given latitude.

The author first—using a method not detailed here—calculates the <term>vinâdikâs</term> of the ascensional difference for the first three signs for locations where the shadow cast at noon on the equinox is equal to one unit. He then doubles these results to prepare the quantities that must be added to the length of the equinoctial day in any specific case. He then instructs us to simply multiply these doubled results by the actual equinoctial shadow of the given location to find the ascensional difference for that latitude. The subsequent steps follow the standard procedure and are further explained in the Sanskrit Commentary.

13. The <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> resulting from the difference in longitude from Yavana (<insert>that is, Yavanapura</insert> <note>Literally "City of the Greeks," referring here to Alexandria in Egypt</note>) are seven and one-third in Avanti <note>Another name for the city of Ujjain</note>, and nine in Varanasi (Benares). I will now explain the calculation of the difference in longitude for other places.

14. Take the total distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian measure of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note>, multiply by nine, divide by eighty, and then square the result. From this, subtract the square of the difference between the two latitudes. The square root of the remainder, divided by six, gives the desired <term>nâdikâs</term> of longitude.

The two verses above teach how to calculate the longitude of any given place. Verse 13 states the longitudinal distance of Ujjain and Benares from Yavanapura—which undoubtedly refers to Alexandria. Verse 14 explains how to calculate the longitudinal distance of any place from a chosen prime meridian. If we take the meridian of Ujjain as the base and know the distance in <term>yojanas</term> from Ujjain to the target location, the first task is to convert this distance into degrees. Assuming the earth's circumference at the equator is 3,200 <term>yojanas</term>, we use the following proportion:

We then take the right-angled spherical triangle which has the distance of <term>Ujjayinî</term><note>A city in central India used as the prime meridian (0° longitude) in ancient Indian astronomy.</note> and the given place for its hypotenuse, and for its two sides: 1. that part of the parallel of latitude of the given place which lies between that place and the prime meridian and 2. that part of the prime meridian which lies between <term>Ujjayinî</term> and the mentioned circle of latitude. The latter side is known, for it is equal to the difference of latitude of <term>Ujjayinî</term> and the given place. The triangle is now treated as a plane one, and from the hypotenuse and the given side the third side—which represents the desired distance in longitude—is deduced. The result which comes out in degrees is turned into <term>nâḍikâs</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; there are 60 nâḍikâs in a day.</note> by being divided by six.

15. Half the <term>nâḍikâs</term> of ascensional difference<note>The difference between the time of rising of a celestial body and its rising at the equator.</note> have to be subtracted from the <term>nâḍikâs</term> of difference of longitude in the northern hemisphere, and in the southern hemisphere they have to be added; reject the remaining ascensional difference.

16. One <term>nakshatra</term><note>A lunar mansion or segment of the ecliptic; there are 27 or 28 in total.</note> comprises eight hundred minutes of arc. The <term>tithi</term><note>A lunar day, or the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and the sun to increase by 12°.</note> is to be calculated from (the longitude of) the moon lessened by (the longitude of) the sun, by means of twelve degrees (being used as the divisor). The time (past and to come of the moon’s conjunction with a <term>nakshatra</term>) is to be calculated by a proportion founded on the motion (of the moon); the time of the current <term>tithi</term> is to be found from a proportion founded upon the difference of motion of sun and moon.

17. The (daily) motion of the sun amounts to sixty (minutes) minus three, three, three, three, two, one; plus one, one, one, one; minus nought, one, in turn.

A rough statement of the daily amount of motion of the sun during the twelve months of the year beginning with <term>Chaitra</term><note>The first month of the Hindu calendar, beginning in March/April.</note>. The amounts stand as follows:

->57', 57', 57', 57', 58', 59';<-
->61', 61', 61', 61', 60', 59'.<-

18. In the light half of the month<note>The waxing phase of the moon.</note> six degrees have to be subtracted and in the dark half<note>The waning phase of the moon.</note> as many have to be added; the minutes of the longitude

of the moon lessened by the longitude of the sun have to be divided by 360; the result is the <term>karana</term> <note>A karana is half of a tithi, or lunar day; there are 60 karanas in a lunar month.</note>. The remaining operations are to be performed as in the case of the <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, calculated by the longitudinal separation of the sun and moon.</note>.

19. The fixed karanas begin from the middle of the fourteenth tithi of the dark half; they are called **Sakuni**, **Chatushpada**, **Nâga** and **Kimstughna**. The other karanas are moveable. (All) karanas occupy half (of a tithi).

The above two stanzas teach how to calculate the *karanas*, *i. e.*, half lunar days. Four of the sixty *karanas* of the month—whose names are given in the text—are fixed, *i. e.*, the four names are bound to the second half of the fourteenth tithi of the dark half <note>The waning phase of the moon.</note>, to the two halves of the fifteenth of the same half and to the first half of the first tithi of the light half <note>The waxing phase of the moon.</note>. The other *karanas* are *chara*, moveable, *i. e.*, they recur, eight times each, at different places of the lunar month.—In order to find the current *karana*, we divide the difference in longitude of sun and moon by 360, *i. e.*, the number of minutes of arc constituting one *karana*; the quotient then indicates the number of the elapsed *karanas*. In order however that the counting of the *karanas* may uniformly begin from *Bava* the first moveable *karana*, we, before division, deduct from the difference of longitude six degrees in the case of the light half of the month and add six degrees to it in the case of the dark half. Compare the table of the *karanas* given in *Burgess-Whitney’s Sûrya Siddhânta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit text on Indian astronomy, translated by Burgess and Whitney in 1860.</note>, p. 287.—The calculation of the elapsed <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> of the *karana* is analogous to that of the *tithis*.

20. When the sum of the longitudes of the sun and the moon plus ten <term>nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions or sectors of the sky.</note> amounts to six signs, it is called *Vaidhrita*; when it amounts to a complete circle it is called *Vyatipâta*; the time (of those conjunctions) is to be ascertained by means of the degrees passed through by the sun and the moon.

21. When the return of the sun towards the south (*i. e.*, the summer solstice) took place from the middle of *Âshleshâ* <note>A specific nakshatra or star cluster.</note>, then the <term>ayana</term> <note>The solar journey or solstice point.</note> was right; at the present time the *ayana* begins from *Punarvasu*.

22. When the degrees of the *ayana* are in the opposite direction (*i. e.*, when the <term>precession</term> <note>The slow movement of the axis of a spinning body; here, the shift in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis.</note> is retrograde), and the quantity to be added to the longitudes of sun and moon amounts to (as much as) the degrees of the sun’s greatest declination (*i. e.*, when the degrees of precession amount to 24); then the *Vyatipâta* takes place when the sum of the longitudes of sun and moon amounts to half a circle.

The <term>Vyatipâta</term> <note>A specific astronomical aspect or "yoga" occurring when the sun and moon are in opposite declination but have the same magnitude.</note>—aspect takes place when the sum of the longitudes of sun and moon amounts to 180°; the <term>vaidhṛiti</term>-aspect <note>A similar astronomical aspect occurring when the sun and moon are on the same side of the equator with equal declination.</note> when it amounts to 360°. This definition, without any qualification, applies to the time of the <term>Siddhântas</term> <note>Ancient Indian astronomical treatises.</note> when there was no precession, or when—as stanza 22 expresses it—the <term>ayana</term> <note>The solar journey or the precession of the equinoxes.</note> had retrograded 24 degrees from the point which it formerly occupied, *viz.*, the middle of <term>Âśleśhâ</term> <note>The 9th lunar mansion or nakshatra.</note>. At the time however when the solstice occurred at this latter point, there were 24°—or more strictly—23° 20' precession (reckoned from the beginning of <term>nirayana mesha</term> <note>The sidereal or "fixed" sign of Aries.</note>) and hence, in order to express the condition of <term>Vaidhṛita</term> and <term>Vyatipâta</term>, we should have to say : <term>Vaidhṛita</term> occurs when

->longit. sun — 23° 20' + longit. moon — 23° 20' = 12^s ; <note>12^s represents 12 signs, or a full 360-degree circle.</note><-
->and <term>Vyatipâta</term> when<-
->longit. sun — 23° 20' + longit. moon — 23° 20' = 6^s . <note>6^s represents 6 signs, or 180 degrees.</note><-

Rearranging the terms of these two equations of condition we have
->longit. sun + longit. moon = 12^s + 46° 40'<-
->and<-
->longit. sun + longit. moon = 6^s + 46° 40'.<-

Substituting <term>nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions; the ecliptic is divided into 27 of these segments.</note> for signs, the right side of the former equation = 3 1/2 <term>nakshatras</term> (the whole revolution being rejected) ; and the right side of the latter equation = 17 <term>naksh</term>. Now we may write for the former equation
->longit. sun + longit. moon + 10 <term>naksh.</term> = 3 1/2 <term>naksh.</term> + 10 <term>naksh.</term> = 6^s ;<-
->and for the latter one<-
->longit. sun + longit. moon + 10 <term>naksh.</term> = 17 <term>naksh.</term> + 10 <term>naksh.</term> = 12^s .<-

Thereby the rule given in stanza 20 explains itself. When that rule applied, then the <term>ayana</term> was right, *i. e.*, agreed with the rule given in stanza 20 for the determination of <term>Vaidhṛita</term> and <term>Vyatipâta</term>.

23. The equinox (<term>vishuvat</term>) occurs at the beginning of Aries and Libra ; the <term>Shaḍaśitimukha</term> <note>A solar period occurring every 86 days, used for specific ritual or astronomical calculations.</note> within the degrees of that sign which precedes Libra (*i. e.* Virgo) ; those (degrees or) solar (days) which remain from the <term>Shaḍaśitimukhas</term> are the days of the fathers <note>Refers to the Pitris or ancestral spirits, indicating days set aside for ancestral rites.</note>.

24. The <term>Shaḍaśitimukha</term> is placed at the fourteenth degree of Virgo, the eighteenth degree of Gemini, the twenty-second degree of Pisces and the twenty-sixth degree of Sagittarius.

The <term>Shaḍaśîtimukhas</term> <note>Literally "eighty-six-mouthed" divisions</note> are divisions of the ecliptic into arcs of 86°, beginning from the first point of Libra. — The sixteen degrees or solar days remaining between the fourth <term>shaḍaśîtimukha</term> and the first point of Libra are said to belong to the fathers <note>The Pitṛs or ancestral spirits</note>, because whatever is given in them to the fathers is imperishable (*Sûrya Siddhânta* XIV. 6).

25. The northern progress of the sun begins from the first point of Capricorn, so also the solar seasons beginning with <term>Śiśira</term> <note>The cool or dewy season</note>. Each season extends in time over two signs. The southern progress of the sun begins from Cancer.

26. The minutes of (the diameter of) the sun’s disc, multiplied by sixty and divided by the sun’s daily motion, give the number of <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> which constitute the holy time on the occasion of the sun entering a new sign; half before (the sun’s actual entrance) and half afterwards.

The <term>saṃkrânti</term> <note>The passage of the sun from one zodiacal sign to another</note> actually takes place at the moment when the sun’s centre enters the new sign; but the whole time from the entrance of the sun’s eastern limb to the entrance of the western limb is considered holy. The proportion employed for the calculation of the length of that time is easily intelligible.

27. When the sun rises touching the end of a <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, or 1/30th of a lunar month</note> and another day, the conjunction is the one, ‘which touches three days’; while in the case of one day touching three <term>tithis</term> (we have the conjunction touching three <term>tithis</term>).

An explanation of two terms connected with <term>tithivṛiddhi</term> <note>Expansion or increase of a lunar day</note> and <term>tithihrâsa</term> <note>Decrease or omission of a lunar day</note>. The former term refers to the case of a <term>tithi</term> beginning before the sunrise of a certain day and terminating after sunrise on the next day, so that it ‘touches’ three <term>sâvana</term> <note>Civil or terrestrial</note> days. The latter term applies to the opposite case of one <term>sâvana</term> day touching three <term>tithis</term>.

# CHAPTER IV.

1. The square root of the tenth part of the square of the circumference—which comprises 360 parts—is the diameter <note>This refers to the common ancient approximation that the square of the circumference is roughly ten times the square of the diameter, implying a value for Pi as the square root of 10 (approx. 3.16).</note>. Having assumed the four parts of the circle <note>Dividing the circle into four quadrants of 90 degrees each.</note> the sine of the eighth part of a sign <note>A "sign" is 30 degrees or 1800 minutes; an eighth part is 225 minutes or 3.75 degrees.</note> (has to be ascertained).

2. Take the square of the Radius and call it the 'constant' (<term>dhruva</term> <note>original: "dhruva"; a Sanskrit term meaning fixed, polar, or constant</note>); the fourth part of it is (the square) of Aries <note>In this context, "Aries" represents the first sign of the zodiac, or 30 degrees.</note> (*i. e.* of the sine of one sign.) The 'constant' square is to be lessened by the square of Aries (*i. e.* one sign). The square roots of the two quantities (*i. e.* the square of Aries and the 'constant' lessened by the square of Aries) are the sines (*viz.* of 30° and 60° respectively).

3. In order to find the remaining desired (sines), take the double of the arc (whose sine you wish to find), deduct it from the quarter (of the circle), diminish the Radius by the sine of the remainder, and add to the square of half of that (*viz.* the Radius so diminished) the square of half the sine of double (the original) arc.

4. The square root of that sum is the desired sine. The 'constant' square lessened by that sum (is the square) of the remaining quantity (*i. e.* of the cosine of the given arc). Half of the 'constant' square is called (the square of) one and a half (*viz.* signs *i. e.* 45°).—Another method also is taught here.

5. Lessen the Radius by the sine of three signs (*i. e.* Radius) from which (three signs) double the required arc has been previously deducted, and multiply the remainder by sixty; the result is the square (of the desired sine). By deducting that square from the square of the Radius you obtain the square of the cosine.

The above four stanzas teach how to calculate the sines generally employed in Indian astronomy.—The formula expressing the relation of the diameter to the circumference is the usual one.—The sine of 30° is half of the chord of 60° which is equal to Radius; the sine of 60° is found by taking <unclear>the square root of the remainder</unclear>.

Of the arc the sine of which is required — let us say *ab* — double is taken = *ac*. The sine of this double arc = *cf* and the sine of the complementary arc <note>The arc required to complete a 90-degree quadrant</note> (*cd*) = *ef*. By deducting *ef* from the Radius we get *af* and by drawing from *h* (i. e., the point marking the centre of the chord *ac*) the line *hg* parallel to *cf* we halve the line *af* and thus obtain the value of *ag*. The line *hg* again is half of *cf*, and *ah* i. e., the desired sine = $\sqrt{hg^2 + ag^2}$. — The sines of 60° and 30° being given, the above method can of course be employed for finding the sine of 15° and so on. — The cosine of the given arc — Stanza 4 goes on to say — is found by deducting the square of the sine from the square of the Radius and taking the square root of the remainder. The sine of 45° is equal to $\sqrt{\frac{R^2}{2}}$ (the square of the chord of 90° being 2R² and consequently the square of half that chord i. e., the sine of 45° being equal to $\frac{2R^2}{4} = \frac{R^2}{2}$).

20. To the square of the midday shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical rod of a sundial that casts a shadow</note> on the day of the equinox add 144 and take the square root of the sum. By this square root divide the product of 120 and the equinoctial shadow;

21. The quotient is the sine of latitude; the arc corresponding to that sine is the latitude.—Or else on any given day (after having gone through the process described) add to the result the sun's declination in the six signs beginning with Aries, and deduct it in the six signs beginning with Libra. The result is the latitude of the given place.

The two well known methods for ascertaining the latitude of a given place.—The first method avails itself of the equinoctial shadow and of the proportion

->Equinoctial hypotenuse : equinoctial shadow = 120 *that is* Radius : sine of latitude.<-

The second method dispenses with the knowledge of the equinoctial shadow and starts directly from the midday shadow of any given day. It thus ascertains the sun's zenith distance (the <term>natâṁśas</term> <note>Sanskrit term for zenith distance, literally "degrees of bowing"</note>), and by adding to it—or subtracting from it in the southern hemisphere—the sun's declination obtains the desired latitude.

22. Deduct the sun's declination from the latitude (in the northern hemisphere), and add it (in the southern hemisphere); divide the sine of (the remainder or the sum) by the square root of the difference of the squares of the sine (found by the above subtraction or addition) and the Radius, and multiply by twelve. The result is the length of the shadow at noon.

A rule for finding the length of the shadow at noon on any given day from the latitude of the place and the sun's declination. By either deducting the sun's declination from the latitude or adding it to the latter we obtain the sun's zenith-distance. We then establish the proportion

->Square root of difference of squares of Radius and sine of zenith-distance : Sine of zenith-distance = 12 (*that is* length of <term>gnomon</term>) : *x* (*that is* length of shadow).<-

For this purpose the so-called earth-sine (<term>kujyâ</term> <note>original: "kujyâ"; a specific trigonometric value used in Indian astronomy to calculate the difference between the local and equatorial horizon</note>) has to be found, which is done by dividing the product of the sine of latitude and the sine of declination by the sine of colatitude <note>The complement of the latitude, found by subtracting the latitude from 90 degrees</note>. Thereupon the sine of the ascensional difference <note>The difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude</note> is found by dividing the product of the earth-sine and the Radius by the day-radius, *i. e.*, half of the day-diameter found previously. Of this sine of the ascensional difference the arc is taken. As six minutes of arc go to one <term>vinâdikâ</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> of time, the minutes, in order to be turned into *vinâdikâs*, would have to be divided by six, but as, in order to determine the true length of the day, the double ascensional difference has to be added or deducted (according to circumstances), the divisor three is substituted for the divisor six.

27—28. Multiply the day-diameter by the sine of half the ascensional difference and divide by two hundred and forty ; the result is the earth-sine (*kujyâ*). Take the square root of the sum of the squares of the earth-sine and the sine of declination, and divide by that square root the product of earth-sine and Radius. The quotient is the sine of latitude. Deduct the degrees of latitude from ninety ; the sine of the remainder is the sine of colatitude.

A rule for finding the latitude and colatitude from the given ascensional difference. At first the earth-sine is found from the ascensional difference ; the divisor is 240 *i. e.* 2 × 120 = 2 R <note>R represents the Radius of the celestial sphere</note>, since the multiplier is not the day-radius but the day-diameter. The earth-sine and the sine of declination are the two sides of a right-angled triangle whose hypothenuse (the measure of amplitude ; <term>agrâ</term> <note>original: "agrâ"; the distance along the horizon between the east point and the point where the sun rises</note>) is therefore known. A proportion is then established

->Measure of amplitude : earth-sine = Radius : sine of latitude.<-

->The complementary sine of the sine of latitude is the sine of colatitude.<-

29. Of the signs beginning with Aries take the square of the sine and of the sine of declination ; by the square root of the difference of those squares multiply the diameter and divide by the day-diameter. Multiply the arc (of the sine thus found) by ten ; the result are the *vinâdikâs* of the rising of the signs.

Stanza 29 gives the rule for finding the times occupied by the individual signs of the ecliptic in rising in the right sphere <note>The "right sphere" refers to the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon.</note>. At first there is found—from the sine of the sign of the ecliptic (reckoning from the beginning of Aries) and the sine of declination of the end point of the sign—the sine of that arc of the day-circle described by that end point, which, if reduced to terms of a great circle, furnishes the ascensional equivalent of the sign on the equator. In order to effect the reduction, the sine is multiplied by the diameter (instead of the Radius) and hence divided by the day-diameter (instead of the day-radius). The degrees of the arc thus found are divided by 6 in order to ascertain the <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 nâḍikâs make one sidereal day.</note> (360° = 60 <term>nâḍikâs</term>), and then multiplied by 60 in order to give the <term>vinâḍikâs</term> <note>A smaller unit of time, 1/60th of a nâḍikâ, equal to 24 seconds.</note> of rising; hence the text directs us to multiply the arc by ten.—Stanza 30 states the numerical results of the preceding rule for each sign of the ecliptic.

31. Three (*i. e.*, the times of rising in the right sphere of the three first signs) are to be lessened by half the time of ascensional difference; three (*i. e.*, the corresponding times for Cancer, Leo, Virgo) are to be increased by the same (amounts of ascensional difference) in the reverse order. In the same time which a sign of the ecliptic occupies in rising, the seventh sign from it goes to its setting.

->A rule for calculating the time occupied by the signs of the ecliptic rising in the oblique sphere, *i. e.*, in any given latitude.<-

32—33. Multiply the sine of the given degrees of northern declination by one hundred and twenty, *i. e.*, Radius and divide by the sine of latitude. The time resulting from the arc corresponding to the sine (found by the above process) indicates the moment when the sun reaches, after sunrise, the prime vertical <note>The vertical circle passing through the east and west points of the horizon.</note>. The same time being deducted from half a day indicates when the sun in the western hemisphere (again reaches the prime vertical). The rule does not apply when the sun is in the six signs beginning with Libra.

The rule has of course no application in the case of the sun having south-declination.

34. Multiply the sine of declination by 240 and by the sine of latitude, and divide by the sine of colatitude <note>Colatitude is the complement of latitude, or 90 degrees minus the latitude</note>. Divide thereupon by the day-diameter. The entire sixth part of the corresponding arc is the quantity by which the day is to be increased.

->A rule for finding the ascensional difference, basing on the proportion<-
->sine of colatitude : sine of latitude = sine of declination : <term>kujyā</term> <note>The earth-sine, a specific chord used in Indian trigonometry to calculate the difference between the length of a day and a night</note>.<-

The result is thereupon reduced to terms of Radius by another proportion.

->A rule for finding the sine of the altitude of the sun when the latter is on the prime vertical.—The first step is to find the sun’s declination for the given time; this is done by means of the proportion<-

->Radius : sine of greatest declination = sine of sun’s longitude : sine of declination.<-

Thereupon the <term>śaṅku</term> is found by comparing the two similar triangles of which the one is formed by the Radius, the sine of latitude and the sine of colatitude; and the other by the <term>śaṅku</term>, the sine of declination and that part of the sun’s day circle which is intercepted by the prime vertical and the six o’clock circle.

->The proportion established is :<-
->sine of latitude : Radius = sine of declination : <term>śaṅku</term>.<-

Combining the two proportions we get

->The gnomon <note>original: "śanku"</note> = (Radius x sine of greatest declination x sine of longitude) / (sine of latitude x Radius) = (sine of greatest declination x sine of longitude) / (sine of latitude).<-

Therefrom the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>A vertical pillar or rod used in sundials to cast a shadow.</note> at the moment when the sun is on the <term>prime vertical</term> <note>The vertical circle passing through the east and west points of the horizon.</note> may be found without difficulty.

36. That person, who determines the moment at which the sun crosses the prime vertical and who is able to produce general confidence in his calculations, thoroughly understands the theory of the sun.

37. > “If the sun performs one complete revolution in a year, how much does he accomplish in a given number of days?”

Such like calculations even an ignorant fellow can easily perform by means of lines drawn with a piece of chalk.

38. When the shadow of the gnomon completely coincides with the east-west line in a circle in which the directions have been marked, then the sun is on the prime vertical.

40. Multiply the sine of declination by 120 and divide by that (*i. e.* by the sine of amplitude as found in 114); the result is the sine of colatitude. Deduct the arc corresponding to that sine from 90; the remainder are the degrees of terrestrial latitude.

->sine of amplitude : sine of declination = Radius : sine of colatitude<-

-> **A rule for finding the length of the shadow at a given time.** <-

The first step is to find the degrees of the ascensional difference <note>The difference between the time of sunrise/sunset and 6:00 AM/PM.</note> which above was determined in terms of <term>vinâḍikâs</term> <note>A smaller unit of time; 1/60th of a nâḍikâ, or 24 seconds.</note>. Six degrees going to one <term>nâḍikâ</term>, the final expression for the degrees of the ascensional difference is:

-> Vinâḍ. x 6 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Vinâḍ. <-
-> —————— = —————— <-
-> 2 x 60 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 20   <-

The given <term>nâḍikâs</term> (*i. e.* the <term>nâḍikâs</term> which have elapsed from sunrise) are thereupon multiplied by six, whereby the number of corresponding degrees is found, and the degrees of ascensional difference as found above are deducted from them in the case of northern declination, and added in the case of southern declination.

The sine of the arc so determined is technically called ‘<term>sûtra</term>’ <note>Literally "thread" or "chord"; here a specific trigonometric line.</note> (compare *Siddhânta Śiromaṇi, Tripraśnâdhikâra*, 54 <note>A reference to a famous 12th-century Indian astronomical treatise by Bhāskara II, specifically the chapter on the three problems of direction, place, and time.</note>). This <term>sûtra</term> increased by the sine of ascensional difference in the northern hemisphere—and diminished by it in the southern hemisphere—gives the sine technically called <term>ishṭa antyâ</term> <note>The "desired last" sine, used in calculating the sun's position.</note>. From it is found the so-called <term>ishṭa hṛiti</term> <note>The "desired divisor" or "desired hypotenuse."</note>, *i. e.*, the perpendicular from the sun to the <term>udayâsta sûtra</term> <note>The rising-setting line; the line connecting the points of sunrise and sunset on the horizon.</note>, *i. e.*, the line joining the points in which the sun rises and sets. The proportion employed is as follows:

->Radius : <term>antyâ</term> <note>The "last sine," specifically the sine of the ascensional difference plus the radius of the diurnal circle.</note> = Radius of day circle : <term>hṛiti</term> <note>The hypotenuse of the sun's altitude at a given time.</note>.<-

->$\therefore$ <term>hṛiti</term> = $\frac{anty\hat{a} \times dyujy\hat{a}}{120}$ = $\frac{anty\hat{a} \times 2\text{ dyujy\hat{a}}}{240}$.<-

In order to find therefrom the sine of the sun's altitude the following proportion is employed:

->Radius : sine of colatitude = <term>hṛiti</term> : sine of altitude.<-

->$\therefore$ sine of altitude = $\frac{anty\hat{a} \times 2\text{ dyujy\hat{a}} \times \text{sine of colatitude}}{120 \times 240 = 28800}$.<-

Taking the right-angled triangle of which the Radius is the hypotenuse and the sine of altitude one side, we find the other side which is equal to the sine of the zenith-distance, the so-called <term>dṛigjyâ</term> <note>Literally "the sine of seeing," representing the horizontal distance from the observer to the sun's position.</note>:

-><term>dṛigjyâ</term> = $\sqrt{\text{Radius}^2 - \text{sine of altitude}^2}$ = $\sqrt{14400 - \text{sine of altitude}^2}$<-

We then finally establish on two similar triangles the proportion:

->sine of altitude : sine of zenith distance = 12 *that is*, gnomon : shadow.<-

45. Take the square root of the sum of the squares of the shadow and of twelve <note>Twelve digits is the standard height for a gnomon or vertical pillar in Indian astronomy.</note>; multiply it by the sine of colatitude, and by the product divide 172800; the quotient is called the first sine (<term>prathama-jîvâ</term>).

46. Multiply the sine of latitude by the (sun's) sine of declination of that day and divide by the sine of colatitude; put the result down separately. Deduct it from the first-sine, if the sun has northern declination; add it, if he has southern declination.

47. Multiply the first sine so modified, and the sine which had been put down separately, by 240, and divide by the double day-radius; the two corresponding arcs have to be added to each other if the sun has northern declination; while they have to be deducted in the case of southern declination. The resulting degrees divided by six give the <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; there are 60 nâḍikâs in a full day.</note>.

A rule for finding the time of the day from the length of the shadow. The hypotenuse of the shadow having been found, the following proportion is established:

->hypotenuse of the shadow : 12 = Radius : sine of altitude<-

Thereupon the following proportion:

->sine of co-latitude : Radius = sine of altitude : hṛiti<-

The sine which commonly is called <term>hṛiti</term> <note>A specific technical term in Indian astronomy representing a portion of the diurnal sine</note> (see above) is by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and mathematician</note> called <term>prathamajyâ</term> <note>Literally "the first sine"</note>. Its value is expressed by the following formula:

->                     12 Radius²              12 × (120)²               172800               <-
-> prathamajyâ = ----------------------- = ----------------------- = ----------------------- <-
->               hyp. shad. × sin colat.   hyp. shad. × sin colat.   hyp. shad. × sin colat.   <-

Next the earth-sine is calculated by the following proportion:

->sine of co-latitude : sine of latitude = sine of declination : earth-sine<-

By deducting the earth-sine from the <term>prathama jîvâ</term> <note>Another term for the first sine</note> in the northern hemisphere—and adding it in the southern hemisphere—we get the sine of that arc of the day circle which intervenes between the <term>unmaṇḍala</term>-circle <note>The equatorial horizon</note> and the place of the sun (which sine is commonly called <term>kalâ</term>; compare <term>Siddhânta Śiromaṇi</term> <note>The "Crown of Treatises," a major work by Bhāskara II</note> as above). The so-called <term>kalâ</term> and the earth-sine are thereupon reduced, in the ordinary way, to the dimensions of a great circle, and we thus obtain the so-called <term>sûtra</term>-sine (see above) and the sine of ascensional difference. We take the arcs of both these sines and add them to each other in the northern hemisphere; while we deduct the latter from the former in the southern hemisphere. By dividing the sum—or difference—by six, we obtain the <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> during which the sun has been above the horizon.

48. Or else multiply the measure of the day by six, and divide by the <term>aṅgulis</term> <note>A unit of measure roughly equal to a finger's breadth</note> of the shadow, after having added to them 12 and subtracted from them the <term>aṅgulis</term> of the midday-shadow. The result are, in the eastern hemisphere, the <term>nâḍikâs</term> which have elapsed since sunrise, in the western hemisphere, the <term>nâḍikâs</term> remaining till sunset.

->given shadow + 12 — noon shadow = 12, holds good, the time is midday.<-

Mihira called this the <term>koṭi</term> <note>The vertical side of a right-angled triangle, often translated as the 'complementary side'.</note>. It being here defined as the interval between the base of the gnomon <note>A gnomon is the upright rod of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> and the east-west line, the presupposition is that the gnomon is so placed that the end of the shadow falls on the central point formed by the intersection of the east-west and the north-south line. If on the other hand the gnomon occupies the central point, the <term>koṭi</term> (or <term>bhujā</term> <note>The 'arm' or horizontal side of the triangle</note>) is the interval between the end of the shadow and the east-west line.

55. Multiply the Radius by the interval between the shadow and the east-west line (*i. e.* by the <term>koṭi</term> = <term>bhujā</term> found above), and divide by the hypothenuse of the shadow. Of this result there has to be taken the difference (from the result found above, *viz.*, the base of the sun's altitude), if there is sameness (*i. e.*, if the <term>bhujā</term> of the <term>śaṅku</term> <note>The gnomon or its shadow-cast altitude</note> and the base of the sun's altitude are both measured in the same direction); while the sum has to be taken, if there is difference (*i. e.*, if one of the mentioned quantities is to be measured from the north to the south, and the other from the south to the north). The result is the sine of the sun's amplitude <note>The angular distance of a celestial body from the east or west point of the horizon.</note>.

56. Multiply the latter sine by the sine of colatitude <note>The complement of the latitude, or 90 degrees minus the latitude.</note>, and divide by the sine of greatest declination <note>The maximum angle between the celestial equator and the ecliptic, roughly 23.5 degrees.</note>; the result is the sine of the sun's longitude.—According to the rules here given for the sun the corresponding calculations have to be made for the other planets also.

The above rule for calculating the sun's longitude from the observed <term>koṭi</term> (=<term>bhujā</term>) *i. e.*, the distance of the point of the shadow from the east-west line at a given moment is simply the reverse of the preceding rule.—The expression for the sine of the sun's longitude is as follows:

->sine of *longitude* = $\frac{\text{sine of } \textit{amplitude } \times \text{ sine of } \textit{colatitude}}{\text{Radius}} \times \frac{\text{Radius}}{\text{sine of } \textit{greatest declination}} = \frac{\text{sine of } \textit{amplitude } \times \text{ sine of } \textit{colatitude}}{\text{sine of } \textit{greatest declination}}$<-

It provides the specific mathematical formula for deriving the sine of the sun's longitude from its amplitude, colatitude, and declination.</summary>

# CHAPTER V.

## ON THE MOON'S BECOMING VISIBLE.

---

1. Take on the one hand the sum, and on the other hand the difference, of the distance of sun and moon and the difference of their <term>declinations</term><note>Declination: The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note>; multiply the two quantities thus obtained and take the square root of the product. Divide by that product the difference of the <term>declinations</term>, which previously has been multiplied by the <term>latitude</term><note>Celestial latitude: The angular distance of a body north or south of the ecliptic (the sun's path).</note> of the moon.

2. The result has to be deducted from the interval of sun and moon, if the moon's <term>latitude</term> has the same direction as the difference of the <term>declinations</term>; in the opposite case the result has to be added. In the case of the morning-twilight the directions as to adding and subtracting have to be reversed.

3. If that (corrected interval of sun and moon) rises in two <term>nâḍikâs</term><note>Nâḍikâ: A traditional Indian unit of time equal to 24 minutes; two nâḍikâs equal 48 minutes.</note>, which we infer from the seventh sign of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the sun across the sky throughout the year.</note>—counting from the sun—; then, the sky being clear, the moon is seen by men.

A rule for determining the distance from the sun at which the moon becomes visible after new moon. Let (fig. 2) E S represent a segment of the <term>Ecliptic</term>, in which S is the place of the sun and E the point in which the moon's circle of <term>latitude</term> cuts the <term>ecliptic</term>. The moon's place is m. E B is a segment of the day circle—parallel to the Equator—described by the point E of the <term>Ecliptic</term>; B S a segment of the sun's circle of <term>declination</term>; md a segment of the moon's circle of <term>declination</term>. Treating all the arcs as straight lines, we have in the right angled triangle E B S

->EB = $\sqrt{\text{ES}^2 - \text{BS}^2} = \sqrt{(\text{ES} + \text{BS})(\text{ES} - \text{BS})}$<-

Now BS and md being parallel, the angles ESB and md E are equal, and hence the two right angled triangles are similar. We thence find by proportion

->Ed = $\frac{\text{B S} \times \text{E m}}{\text{E B}}$.<-

By the amount of Ed so found the distance of the moon from the sun in the ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> has to be corrected. Ed has to be deducted in case of the moon's latitude and the difference of the declinations <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the two bodies having the same direction; while it has to be added in the opposite case.— The moon is first seen when her corrected distance from the sun amounts to so much that it sets—or, what is the same, that an equally large piece of that sign of the Ecliptic, that is seventh from the sign in which the sun is at the time, rises—in two <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time, approximately 24 minutes</note>.

4. (The text and meaning of the first half of this stanza is doubtful; it possibly contains a remark of an astrological character, as explained in the <term>Sanskrit</term> <note>The ancient Indo-Aryan language of India</note>—Commentary).

The twelfth part of the <term>hypothenuse</term> <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle</note> represents the illumined part of the moon; it is to be laid off in the direction of the base.

By the <term>hypothenuse</term> we have to understand the interval between sun and moon as in figure 2. The moon's diameter is supposed to be divided into fifteen <term>angulis</term> <note>A traditional unit of measure, literally "fingers"</note> all of which are illumined when the moon is in opposition, *i. e.*, at the distance of 180° from the sun. Hence the formula

->Illumined part = $\frac{15 \times \text{hyp.}}{180} = \frac{\text{hyp.}}{12}.$<-

5. The perpendicular is constituted by the difference of the declinations (of sun and moon) and of the latitude; of which two quantities the sum has to be taken if their direction is the same, otherwise the difference. The <term>hypothenuse</term> is the interval between sun and moon. The square root of the difference of the squares of those two sides is the base.

6. Let the perpendicular be laid off in that direction in which the sun is with regard to the moon, one degree being supposed equal to one <term>anguli</term>; in the same way the base and the <term>hypothenuse</term> are to be laid off with <term>angulis</term>.

7. First lay off the hypothenuse from the centre of the moon; then from the hypothenuse the perpendicular; then the base in the direction of the moon's centre. This base is called <term>aksha</term> <note>axis</note> on the moon's circumference. Measure out the illumined part from the middle (*i. e.*, the hypothenuse which divides the moon into two halves); it has the shape of a bow.

->Directions how to draw a diagram of the illumined part of the moon,<-

which are immediately intelligible from figure 3, in which S represents the sun's place and m the centre of the moon. The line mh, which ordinarily is called <term>koṭi</term> <note>the vertical side of a right-angled triangle</note>, Varâha Mihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and mathematician</note> calls <term>bhuja</term> <note>the horizontal side or 'arm' of a triangle</note>, and h S which ordinarily is called <term>bhuja</term> he calls <term>koṭi</term>.
