8. Multiply (the moon's) southern or northern latitude by the equinoctial shadow, and divide by 12. The resulting degrees are, in the case of the moon's rising, to be added (if the latitude is southern), and to be deducted (if the latitude is northern); the reverse has to be done at the time of setting.

9. From the longitude of the sun lessened by that of the moon (ascertain the number of the intervening signs); according as they are less or more than six, the rising of the moon has to be determined as taking place during the day or during the night, owing to the rising of the sun.

10. Having thus (*i. e.* in the way indicated in stanza 8) performed the subtraction or addition, deduct the moon's longitude, lessened by that of the sun, from half the circle; in the time (reckoned from sunrise) equal to the time of the rising of the remaining signs the moon goes to her setting.

The above are rules for finding the time of the moon's rising and setting. — First there is given a rule for the so-called <term>dṛik-karman</term> <note>visibility correction or 'aspect-operation'</note>, which however neglects the <term>áyana-dṛik-karman</term> <note>visibility correction for the ecliptic's obliquity</note>, and limits itself to the <term>aksha-dṛik-karman</term> <note>visibility correction for the observer's latitude</note>.

( 41 )

<term>karman</term> <note>Sanskrit for "action" or "operation"; here referring to a specific astronomical correction</note>, *that is*, that operation by which there is determined that point of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>, together with which a planet having latitude rises in a given terrestrial latitude. In figure 4 E L B represents an arc of the Ecliptic, L m H the horizon, m the moon's true place, E its place in the Ecliptic to which it is referred—in the Indian fashion—by means of a circle of declination, L that point of the Ecliptic which rises together with the moon. In order to determine E L, we look upon the triangle E m L as a plane one, in which the angle E m L is equal to the terrestrial latitude, and its complement m L E to the colatitude <note>90 degrees minus the latitude</note>. We then establish the proportion

->E L : sine of latitude = E m : sine of colatitude<-

->$\therefore$ E L = (sine of latitude $\times$ E m) / sine of colatitude<-

Substituting (Equinoctial shadow) / (12 (=gnomon <note>the vertical rod of a sundial used to measure shadows</note>)) for (sine of latitude) / (sine of colatitude),

we finally obtain

->E L = (moon's latitude $\times$ equinoctial shadow) / 12<-

The amount so found is added to, or deducted from, the moon's longitude, according as the moon has southern or northern declination <note>the angular distance north or south of the celestial equator</note>.—Stanzas 9 and 10 present no difficulties.

# CHAPTER VI.

---

## LUNAR ECLIPSES (ACCORDING TO THE PAULIŚA SIDDHÂNTA.)

---

1. From the <term>nâḍikâs</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 nâḍikâs make a full day.</note> of the <term>tithi</term><note>A lunar day, or the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note>, which, taking sunrise as the starting point, have elapsed or are yet to come, the corresponding minutes of motion of the moon have to be calculated. They are to be deducted from the moon's place (in case of the full moon <term>tithi</term> having terminated before sunrise), and we thus obtain the place of the moon at that time (*i. e.*, the time of the termination of the full moon <term>tithi</term>, *i. e.*, the time of opposition); while in the opposite case the minutes have to be added.

There is some corruption in the last line of the text of the stanza; but there can be no doubt about the general meaning. The longitude of the moon had hitherto been calculated for sunrise; now, when the discussion of lunar eclipses begins, it becomes requisite to find it for the moment of opposition, *i. e.*, the end of the <term>tithi</term> of full moon. According as that moment precedes or follows the sunrise for which the moon's longitude had been found, the latter has to be diminished or increased by the amount of the moon's motion during the interval.

2. Deduct from the longitude of <term>Râhu</term><note>The ascending lunar node, personified in mythology as a demon who swallows the moon to cause an eclipse.</note> twenty-six minutes, and thereupon take the degrees intervening between <term>Râhu</term> and the moon. If these degrees are within thirteen, there is an eclipse; if within fifteen, there is the shadow of an eclipse.

3. Deduct the square of the minutes of the moon's latitude from the square of fifty-five, and take the square root of the remainder. Doubling it and operating upon it in the manner of the <term>tithi</term>, we find the time of the duration of the eclipse.

4. Lessen thirteen by the degrees of the interval between the moon and <term>Râhu</term>, and multiply by five; the result taken as <term>vinâḍikâs</term><note>A smaller unit of time; 1/60th of a nâḍikâ, equivalent to 24 seconds.</note> is to be added to the duration of the eclipse in the case of <term>Râhu</term> being more advanced in longitude than the moon; otherwise it is to be deducted.

The former half of stanza 2 refers back to the rule given in III. 29 concerning the place of the moon’s node <note>The point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic, or the sun's apparent path</note>. Its latter half states the lunar ecliptic limits. By the expression ‘shadow of an eclipse’ we apparently have to understand a quasi-eclipse, *i. e.*, the diminution of the moon’s light by the penumbra <note>The partial outer shadow where the light source is only partially blocked</note> ( ? )

Stanza 3 calculates the duration of the eclipse from the line l C (fig. 5) which itself is determined as one of the sides of a right angled triangle of which m l *i. e.*, the latitude of the moon at the moment of contact with the shadow is the other side, and m C *i. e.*, the sum of the radii of the moon and the shadow the hypothenuse <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle</note>. Seventeen minutes are taken for the mean value of the moon’s radius, and thirty-eight for the mean value of the radius of the shadow; the sum of these two quantities amounts to fifty-five. The time which the moon takes in passing—by means of the difference of the motions of sun and moon—along l C is half of the total duration of the eclipse. This time is found by a proportion similar to that employed for finding the <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, past and to come, of a <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, or the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and the sun to increase by 12 degrees</note>, *viz.*

->Minutes of difference of motions : 60 <term>nâdikâs</term> = double the minutes of l C : duration of eclipse.<-

To the duration so found stanza 4 directs us to apply a correction whose rationale we are however unable to assign.

5. By five, diminished by the degrees of interval (between the moon and her node), let ten be diminished and multiplied, then multiply by four, take the square root and multiply the latter by twenty-one; the fifth part of the result indicates the minutes of total obscuration <note>The period during which the moon is completely covered by the Earth's darkest shadow</note>.

A rule for calculating the time of complete obscuration during a total eclipse of the moon.—The quantity to be calculated first is the latitude of the moon at the moment when complete obscuration begins. For this purpose

The sine of the degrees intervening between the moon and the node <note>The node is the point where the moon's orbit crosses the path of the sun; an eclipse can only occur near these points.</note> is calculated according to the formula: sine = $\frac{\text{21} \times \text{degrees}}{\text{10}}$ (21 being the sine of 10 degrees if the Radius = 120, and ten degrees being introduced into the formula, because in the case of a total eclipse the interval between moon and node must be less than 10 degrees.) The sine of latitude is then calculated on the assumption of the moon’s greatest latitude amounting to 240', whence the proportion:

->Radius : sine of greatest latitude = $\frac{\text{21} \times \text{degrees}}{\text{10}}$ : sine of latitude<-

->$\therefore$ sine of latitude = $\frac{\text{240} \times \text{21} \times \text{degrees}}{\text{120} \times \text{10}} = \frac{\text{21} \times \text{degrees}}{\text{5}}$.<-

Having thus found $m'l'$ (fig. 5) we have:

->$l'C = \sqrt{m'C^2 - m'l'^2} = \sqrt{(Ct - tm')^2 - \frac{(21)^2}{25} \times \text{degrees}^2}$<-

->$= \sqrt{(38 - 17)^2 - \frac{(21)^2}{25} \times \text{degrees}^2} = \frac{21}{5} \sqrt{25 - \text{degrees}^2}$<-

->$= \frac{21}{5} \sqrt{(5 - \text{degrees})(5 + \text{degrees})} = \frac{21}{5} \sqrt{[5 - \text{degrees}] [10 - (5 - \text{degrees})]}$<-

Multiplying this last expression by two, in order to find the whole duration of total obscuration <note>The period during which the moon is completely covered by the Earth's shadow.</note>, we finally have:

Minutes of total obscuration

->$= \frac{21}{5} \times 2 \sqrt{[5 - \text{degrees}] [10 - (5 - \text{degrees})]}$<-

->$= \frac{21}{5} \sqrt{4 [5 - \text{degrees}] [10 - (5 - \text{degrees})]}$<-

6. Within a time equal to the difference of half the duration of the eclipse and half the period of total obscuration the shadow swallows the whole moon. The direction of the contact and the separation is to be determined by means of the degrees of the interval between the moon and the node.

7. That direction is opposite to the direction of the moon’s latitude. Divide the quadrant of the moon’s circumference into thirteen parts, and from the east-point lay off the degrees of the direction of the eclipse (*i. e.*, the degrees of the <term>valana</term> <note>Sanskrit: deflection or variation; the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial circle.</note> or deflection). At the point thus determined the <term>parvan</term> <note>Sanskrit: a festival or significant time, here referring to the moment of syzygy or the start of the eclipse.</note>, *i. e.*, the beginning of the eclipse takes place.

8. Multiply the degrees of terrestrial latitude by a quarter of the moon’s circumference, and again by the degrees intervening between the moon and the zenith, and divide by 8100; the result is the deflection (<term>valana</term>) which is north in the eastern hemisphere, south in the western one.

# Calculation of Deflection and Eclipse Projection

A rule for calculating the so-called <term>âksha valana</term> <note>original: "âksha valana"; the deflection or variation in the moon's position caused by the observer's latitude</note>, *i. e.*, the deflection due to latitude (the <term>ayana valana</term> <note>original: "ayana valana"; the deflection due to the obliquity of the ecliptic</note> being altogether neglected). The rule given in stanza 8 for the latitude-based deflection is based on the proportion: If 90° zenith-distance give a deflection equal to the terrestrial latitude, how much do the given degrees of zenith distance give?—This is combined with the further proportion: If 90° give an arc equal to one quarter of the moon’s circumference, how much do the calculated degrees of deflection give?—The resulting formula for the arc of deflection to be laid off on the moon’s circumference is

->Arc = <u>zenith distance x latitude x ¼ circumference of moon</u><-
->90 x 90 = 8100.<-

We do not know the reason for the direction—given in stanza 7—to divide each quarter of the circumference into thirteen parts.

9. During a total eclipse dark yellow is to be declared the peculiar colour of the moon; her colour is dusky in the case of eclipses taking place during the rising or setting of the moon; and waterish in the case of partial eclipses.

10. <note>A stanza of doubtful import; see the Sanskrit Commentary.</note>

11. Describe in one place (*i. e.* from one centre) three circles, one, *viz.*, the moon’s circle with a string measured by seventeen minutes, a second one, *viz.*, the circle of the shadow with a string of thirty-eight minutes, and a third one, *viz.*, the circle of duration with a string equal in length to the sum of the two quantities.

12. (Ascertain) by means of the degrees (of deflection) to be laid off in the direction stated above the east and west-line of <term>Laṅkâ</term> <note>A mythical city on the equator used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note>, and draw on both sides of it thirteen long lines, at equal distances from one another.

13. This is a concise description of the projection of a lunar eclipse, the details of which are to be known from explanation. The first contact, the complete obscuration and the duration are there seen through appropriate constructions.

14. In a lunar eclipse the moon is seen to touch the shadow of the earth from the west-side; in the same way she touches, in a solar eclipse, the sun from the west-side; hence the eastern part of the moon is first touched, but not that of the sun.

Stanzas 11-13 contain some rather general directions how to draw the projection of a lunar eclipse, on the ground of the latitude-based deflection previously calculated. Compare the <term>Sanskrit Commentary</term> <note>The traditional scholarly explanations written in Sanskrit that accompany the primary astronomical verses</note>.

# CHAPTER VII.

->Solar Eclipses, according to the Pauliśa Siddhânta.<-

---

1. As many <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; there are 60 in a day.</note> as there remain until midday (from the time of conjunction), or as many as have elapsed since midday, have to be multiplied by six. The thirtieth part of the corresponding sine is the "bending" (displacement) of the <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, or the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note> (i. e. the parallax in longitude).

A rule for calculating the parallax in longitude. We ascertain the hour angle (multiplying the given nâḍikâs by 6, six degrees going to each nâḍikâ), and establish the following proportion:

->Radius : greatest parallax = sine of the hour angle : desired parallax.<-

The greatest parallax being assumed equal to the mean motion during four nâḍikâs, we thus have:

->Desired parallax = (4 × sine of the hour angle) / 120 = (sine of the hour angle) / 30.<-

2—4. [Three stanzas of doubtful import.]

5. Deduct twenty-six minutes from the longitude of <term>Râhu</term> <note>In Indian astronomy, Râhu is the ascending node of the moon, personified as a demon who swallows the sun or moon during an eclipse.</note>, and take the degrees intervening between Râhu and the moon. If they are within thirteen, there takes place an eclipse of the moon; and an eclipse of the sun, if they are within eight.

A stanza agreeing, as far as lunar eclipses are concerned, in contents and enunciation with stanza 2 of chapter VI.

6. Deduct, in the case of the moon, the square of the degrees of the interval from 169, in the case of the sun from 64; the square roots of the remainders minus their fourth parts indicate the duration of the lunar and solar eclipses.

->( 47 )<-

If we calculate the moon's latitude at the moment when complete obscuration begins, in the manner taught in stanza 5 of the preceding chapter, with the one difference of making the greatest latitude equal to 270 (*not* 240) minutes, we obtain:

->latitude = 270 x 21/10 x degrees of interval / 120<-
->= 270 x 2 x degrees / 120 = 9 x degrees / 2 (approximately).<-

By means of the latitude so found, and assuming half the sum of the diameters of moon and shadow to be equal to 58 minutes, we find—in the customary manner:

->Measure of half duration of eclipse = √ 58² — latit.²<-
->= √ 58² — 81/4 (degrees of interval)² = 9/2 √ (58 x 2 / 9)² — degrees²<-
->= 9/2 √ 13² — degrees² (approximately).<-

In order to find from the latter expression the whole duration of the eclipse in terms of <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time, also known as a ghati, equivalent to 24 minutes.</note>, we multiply it by 2 x 60, and divide by the difference of the daily motions of sun and moon, when we obtain:

->duration of eclipse = 2 x 9 x 60 / 730 x 2 √ 169 — degrees² =<-
->9 x 6 / 73 √ 169 — degrees² = 3/4 √ 169 — degrees².<-

In the case of a solar eclipse we find by an analogous process, and assuming half the sum of the diameters of sun and moon to be equal to 35 minutes:

->Measure of half the eclipse = √ 35² — 81/4 x degrees²<-
->= 9/2 √ (35 x 2 / 9)² — degrees² = 9/2 √ 64 — degrees² (approximately).<-

And for the duration of the whole eclipse in <term>nâdikâs</term>:

->Duration = 2 x 9 x 60 / 730 x 2 √ 64 — degrees²<-
->= 3/4 √ 64 — degrees² (approximately).<-

# CHAPTER VIII.

->SOLAR ECLIPSES, ACCORDING TO THE ROMAKA SIDDHÂNTA.<-

---

1. Multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The count of elapsed days since the beginning of the epoch.</note> by 150, deduct 65, and divide by 54787; the result is the mean longitude of the sun in due succession (i. e. revolutions, signs, etc.), according to the <term>Romaka-Siddhânta</term> <note>A mathematical astronomical treatise influenced by Greek/Roman traditions.</note>.

This rule follows immediately from the nature of the <term>yuga</term> <note>A vast cycle of time used in Indian astronomy to calculate planetary positions.</note> acknowledged by the <term>Romaka Siddhânta</term>, as described in I. 15. Instead of the fraction 2850/1040953, the reduced fraction 150/54787 is employed. Sixty-five is the <term>kshepa</term>—a constant quantity enabling the calculations to start from the specific epoch chosen for this system.

2. The operation of finding the true places of the sun and the moon is performed by means of the quantities (about to be stated) measured for half signs of the anomaly of sun and moon, and arranged in direct as well as inverse order. Of the sun (the mean longitude) has to be deducted from half of Gemini, i. e., from two and a half signs.

The <term>Romaka Siddhānta</term> calculates the equation of centre <note>The correction needed to find the actual position of a body moving in an elliptical or eccentric orbit.</note> of the sun and moon for each half sign, i. e., progressing from 15 to 15 degrees. The six quantities thus obtained for the first quarter of the circle are employed for the second quarter in the inverse order and so on.—In order to obtain the <term>kendra</term> <note>The anomaly, or the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee).</note>, i. e., the anomaly of the sun, we have to take the difference of his mean longitude and of the longitude of his apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note>, which is estimated at 2½ signs = 75°.

3. Twenty increased in succession by fifteen, fourteen, ten and four, and diminished by six and fourteen are the minutes (which added up in succession give the amounts of the equation for 15° 30° 45° etc). Eighteen and five seconds have to be deducted (from the first and second quantities); (to the four others) two, ten, sixteen, eighteen seconds have to be added.

The six quantities indicated in the above stanza stand as follows:

| Interval | Minutes | Seconds | Total Equation |

| 30° | 35 | -5 | 34' 55" |
| 45° | 49 | +2 | 49' 2" |
| 60° | 59 | +10 | 59' 10" |
| 75° | 63 | +16 | 63' 16" |
| 90° | 49 | +18 | 49' 18" |

4. Multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The total number of elapsed days since a specific epoch.</note> by 38,900, deduct 1,984, and divide by 1,040,953; the quotient indicates the mean longitude of the moon.

This rule follows immediately from the constitution of the <term>yuga</term> <note>A vast cycle of time in Indian cosmology.</note> assumed in the <term>Romaka Siddhânta</term> <note>A 4th or 5th-century Indian astronomical treatise influenced by Greek (Roman) methods.</note> (excepting the <term>kshepa</term> <note>An additive constant or epochal value.</note> quantity).

5. The assumption here is that the <term>kendra</term> of the moon performs 110 revolutions in 3,031 <term>sāvana</term> <note>Civil or solar days measured from sunrise to sunrise.</note> days or, in other words, that the latter period contains 110 <term>anomalistic months</term> <note>The time it takes the moon to return to its perigee.</note>.

6. One degree plus 14, 11 and 2 (minutes); four times eighteen (i.e., seventy-two) lessened by eight times three (24); five times six (30); and sixty minus eight times six (12). The last two quantities are to be lessened by one.

7. The daily motion of the moon amounts to 790 minutes, that of the moon's anomaly to 784. By taking the difference of the true motions (on two consecutive days) we obtain the past true daily motion, as well as the one during the coming night (i.e. <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>A full period of 24 hours, including day and night.</note>).

8. Multiply the <term>ahargana</term> <note>The total number of elapsed days since the beginning of a specific epoch.</note> by 24, add 56266 and divide by 163111; the result is the successive position (in revolutions, signs, etc.) of the head of <term>Râhu</term> <note>The mythological demon associated with eclipses; here used as the technical term for the moon's ascending node.</note> (*i. e.*, the moon's ascending node), reckoning backwards from the end of Pisces (= first point of Aries).

Twenty-four revolutions of the node — whose movement is retrograde — are supposed to take place in 163111 <term>sâvana</term> <note>Civil or solar days measured from sunrise to sunrise.</note> days.

9. As many <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 nâḍikâs make one day.</note> as there remain until midday, or else as many <term>nâḍikâs</term> as have elapsed since midday, are to be multiplied by six. The thirtieth part of the corresponding sine is the displacement of the <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, or the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note>, (*i. e.*, the parallax in longitude).

A rule literally agreeing with the corresponding rule of the <term>Paulisá Siddhânta</term> <note>One of the five early systems of Indian astronomy, often associated with Greek influence.</note> (VII. 1).

10. And from the <term>nâḍikâs</term> which have elapsed since sunrise calculate the orient ecliptic point <note>The point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon; the ascendant.</note>; from the latter plus nine signs (*i. e.*, from the point called <term>vitribha</term> or <term>tribhona</term> <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant, representing the highest point of the ecliptic.</note>) ascertain the degrees of declination.

A rule for finding the highest point of the ecliptic, the so-called <term>tribhona</term> or <term>vitribha</term>, whose longitude is less by three — or more by nine — signs than that of the orient ecliptic point.—In order to find the zenith distance of that point we have at first to determine its declination.

11. Multiply the sine of the difference of the orient ecliptic point, of three and of the node by two, and divide by sixty. The result in degrees is to be deducted from the declination (calculated above) if the directions of the two are opposite; while the two are to be added, if the result (and the declination) have the same direction.

12. If northern, (the declination so corrected) deducted from the terrestrial latitude—and, if southern, added to it—is to be considered as the southern (zenith distance of the <term>tribhona</term>) ; while if northern and greater than the terrestrial latitude it is to be viewed as northern (zenith distance).

A process preliminary to the calculation of the parallax in latitude. What we require—and what generally is ascertained in Hindu Astronomy to that end—is the zenith distance of that point of the ecliptic which has the greatest altitude (which point is called <term>vitribha</term> or <term>tribhona</term>); the sine

14. Multiply the sine of the distance of the moon from the node—taken at the moment of conjunction when it shares the same longitude as the sun—by twenty-one and divide the result by nine. Take the sum of this result and the parallax in latitude if they are in the same direction; take the difference between the two if they are in opposite directions.

->Rules for finding the parallax in latitude and the moon’s true latitude.<-

The rule for finding the parallax is founded on the supposition that the greatest parallax is equal to the fifteenth part of the moon’s daily motion; we therefore have the proportion:

->Radius : $\frac{\text{daily motion}}{15}$ = sine of the zenith distance of the <term>tribhona</term> <note>The 'tribhona' refers to the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the meridian, often called the 'nonagesimal'.</note> : parallax<-

->$\therefore$ Parallax = $\frac{\text{daily motion} \times \text{sine of the zenith distance}}{15 \times 120}$<-

In order to find the latitude of the moon, we at first establish the proportion:

->Radius : sine of greatest latitude (equal to 270 minutes) = given sine of moon’s distance from node : desired latitude.<-

We therefore have:

->Latitude = $\frac{270 \times \text{sine of the distance}}{120} = \frac{27 \times \text{sine of the distance}}{3 \times 4} = \frac{21 \times \text{sine of the distance}}{\frac{3 \times 4 \times 21}{27}} = \frac{21 \times \text{sine of the distance}}{3 \times 3}$ (approximately).<-

By increasing or diminishing the latitude found in this way by the parallax calculated above, we obtain the true latitude.

15. Multiply the true motion of the sun and the moon by their mean diameters <note>The text uses 'measure' to refer to the angular diameter of the celestial bodies.</note>, and divide by the mean motion; the result is the true diameter, in minutes of arc, of the two bodies at the given time.

16. Subtract the square of the <term>avanati</term> <note>Avanati is the technical term for the moon's latitude after it has been corrected for parallax.</note> (that is, the latitude of the moon as corrected for parallax of latitude) from the square of half the sum of the diameters of the sun and moon. From the double square root of the remainder, determine the duration of the eclipse, following the same method used for calculating the elapsed portion of a <term>tithi</term> <note>A tithi is a lunar day in the Hindu calendar, representing the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note>.

A rule for determining the duration of the eclipse. We at first take the right-angled triangle of which half the sum of the diameters of the sun and moon forms the hypotenuse <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle</note>, and the moon’s corrected latitude the perpendicular; the base of this triangle represents half the time of the duration, expressed in minutes of arc. ->Minutes of difference of the sun's and moon's motion : 60 <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> = minutes<-
->of arc of duration of eclipse : <term>nâḍikâs</term> of duration.<-

17. As many minutes as there remain on the corrected latitude being deducted from half the sum of the measures of the sun and moon, so *many <term>angulis</term>* <note>A traditional unit of measurement, literally 'fingers'</note> of the sun know to be obscured by the moon.

18. Describe the circle of the sun with half his diameter and mark off from its centre the true latitude, in its appropriate direction. From the end of that latitude describe the circle of the moon with half her diameter, and thereby show the amount of obscuration.

Fig. 7.

The obscured amount D C is therefore equal to the Sun’s Radius minus A D; which latter quantity is itself equal to the true latitude minus the Radius of the moon. Hence the obscured amount is equal to the sum of the two Radii minus the latitude. — The rule for delineating the eclipse, given in stanza 18, presents no difficulties.

# CHAPTER IX.

---

## SOLAR ECLIPSES ACCORDING TO THE SURYA SIDDHANTA.

---

1. According to the Surya Siddhanta the (mean place of the) sun is found successively (*i. e.*, in revolutions, signs, etc.) by multiplying the <term>ahargana</term><note>The total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to the current date.</note> by 800, deducting 442, and dividing by 292207; (the place so found is) for midday at Avanti<note>Modern Ujjain, the prime meridian of ancient Indian astronomy.</note>.

According to I. 14 the Surya Siddhanta teaches that 180000 revolutions of the sun take place in 65746575 days. Hence the sun performs in a given <term>ahargana</term>

-> 180000^rev^ x ahargana / 65746575 , which fraction reduced by 225 is equal to 800 x ahargana / 292207 . <-

The <term>kshepa</term><note>An additive or subtractive constant used to adjust a calculation to a specific starting epoch.</note> quantity—442 is introduced in order to enable us to start in the calculation from the epoch of the *Panchasiddhantika*<note>Varahamihira's "Five Astronomical Treatises," a 6th-century compendium.</note>, *viz.*, 427 Saka<note>The Saka era began in 78 CE; 427 Saka corresponds to 505 CE.</note>. About its calculation see later on.

2. Multiply the <term>ahargana</term> by 900000, deduct 670217, and divide by 24589506; the result is the (mean place of the) moon.

From the elements of the <term>yuga</term><note>A vast cosmic cycle of time; in this context, the Maha-yuga of 4,320,000 years.</note> of the Surya Siddhanta as stated in the first chapter we deduce the number of the sidereal revolutions of the moon within that period, and thus obtain 2406389. In order to find the revolutions in a given <term>ahargana</term> we therefore should have to multiply the latter by 2406389 and divide—as in the case of the sun—by 65746575. These being however rather unwieldy numbers, 900000 is substituted for the former and 24589506 for the latter. The substitution involves an inaccuracy; for—as appears from an exact calculation the steps of which are exhibited in the Sanskrit Commentary on the above stanza—the motion of the moon within a given <term>ahargana</term> strictly amounts to

-> 900000 x aharg. / 24589506 — 746166 x aharg. / 24589506 x 65746575 <-

The former quantity only is introduced into the general rule for finding the moon's place; the latter one is provided for by a special correction stated further on. — About the *kshêpa*-quantity <note>original: "kshêpa"; an additive constant or "interpolation" used to adjust calculations to a specific epoch</note> see later on.

3. Multiply the *ahargaṇa* <note>original: "ahargaṇa"; the total count of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch</note> by 900, add 2260356, and divide by 2908789; the result is the place of the moon's *uchcha* <note>original: "uchcha"; the moon's apogee, or the point in its orbit furthest from the Earth</note>.

The above rule implies that 900 revolutions of the moon's *uchcha* take place in 2908789 *sâvana* <note>original: "sâvana"; terrestrial or civil days measured from sunrise to sunrise</note> days. Ascertaining therefrom the length of one revolution and the number of revolutions in one *mahâyuga* <note>original: "mahâyuga"; a "great age" in Hindu cosmology, consisting of 4,320,000 years</note>, we find for the latter 488219. The expression for calculating the motion of the *uchcha* in a given *ahargaṇa* would therefore be <sup>488219 x aharg.</sup>/<sub>1577917800</sub> (the denominator of the fraction being the *sâvana* days of a *mahâyuga*).

The fraction <sup>488219</sup>/<sub>1577917800</sub> is transformed (see *Sanskṛit Commentary*) into <sup>900</sup>/<sub>2908789</sub> + <sup>36791</sup>/<sub>1577917800 x 2908789</sub>, of which expression only the former term is employed for the general rule, while to make up for the neglect of the latter a correction is stated in the next stanza.

4. Multiply the revolutions of the moon by 51, and divide by 3120; deduct the result taken as seconds. — Also multiply the revolutions of the moon's *uchcha* by 10 and divide by 297; the resulting seconds are to be added to the moon's *uchcha*.

This stanza states the corrections referred to above, which have to be applied to the mean places of the moon and her apogee as calculated according to the general rules embodied in stanzas 2 and 3. — A calculation (about whose details see the *Sanskṛit Commentary*) shows that, in order to make up for the terms neglected in the general rule, <sup>51</sup>/<sub>3120</sub> seconds for each completed revolution have to be deducted from the moon's mean place; and that on the other hand <sup>10</sup>/<sub>297</sub> seconds for each revolution have to be added to the place of the moon's apogee.

5. Multiply the *ahargaṇa* by 270, add to it ————, and divide by 1834582; the result is the place of *Râhu* <note>original: "Râhu"; in Indian astronomy, the personification of the moon's ascending node</note> in revolutions, etc.

6. Deducting this from 12 signs we have the head of *Râhu* (*i. e.*, the moon's ascending node): while by adding six signs we have the tail of *Râhu* (*i. e.*, the descending node). The minutes of arc intervening between *Râhu* and the moon (serve to calculate) the moon's latitude; 270 minutes (are the greatest latitude).

# Page 56

The rule mentioned above for calculating the position of the moon's node <note>The points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic; in Indian astronomy, the ascending node is personified as the shadow-planet Rahu</note> requires the assumption of 232,226 revolutions of the node in a *mahâyuga* <term>mahâyuga: a "great age" consisting of 4,320,000 years</term>; for in that case we have the proportion 232,226 / 15,779,178,000, which may be reduced to 270 / 18,345,820.

The line stating the *kshepa* <term>kshepa: an additive constant or "epochal value" used to determine a planet's position at a specific starting date</term> quantity of Rahu is too corrupt to lend itself to emendation; we may however in this place state the principles on which all the *kshepa* quantities given in the preceding stanzas of this chapter are calculated. They of course all have the purpose of throwing the rules for finding the mean places into a shape enabling us to begin our calculations not from a very remote period—which would oblige us to use inconveniently large multipliers and divisors—but from the epoch of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* <note>Varahamihira's "Five Treatises," a seminal 6th-century astronomical work</note>, namely, 427 of the Saka era <note>Equivalent to 505 CE</note>. 

From tentative calculations it appears that the *kshepas* exhibited by Varahamihira are calculated, not from the beginning of the *Kaliyuga* <note>The current "dark age" in the Hindu cycle of time</note> or the *mahâyuga*, but from the beginning of the *Kalpa* <note>An immense cosmic period of 4.32 billion years</note>. We therefore have to form the *ahargana* <term>ahargana: the "heap of days," or the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch to the current date</term> from the beginning of the *Kalpa* down to 427 Saka (compare the Sanskrit Commentary and also *Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal* vol. LIII. 1884 p. 268 ff), and to treat that *ahargana* according to the general rules for calculating the mean places. 

We thus find that the place of the sun at the epoch of the *Pañchasiddhântikâ* was 42 / 292,207 revolutions. But as the *Sûrya Siddhânta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most influential Indian astronomical texts</note> makes all its calculations for midnight, while Varahamihira declares that the rules given by him are adapted to midday, we have to deduct a further amount equal to the sun's motion during half a day (= 800 / (2 x 292,207) = 400 / 292,207) and thus finally obtain 442 / 292,207, which agrees with the *kshepa* stated in the text. 

Calculating the moon's position at the epoch in an analogous manner, and again making an allowance for the moon's motion between midday and midnight, we obtain for the *kshepa* 670,197, which differs by an inconsiderable amount only from the *kshepa* stated in the text, namely 670,217. And finally applying the same process to the moon's *uchcha* <term>uchcha: the apogee, or the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> we find for its *kshepa* 2,260,355, which differs by one only from the quantity stated in stanza 3.

---

### 7—8. 
By deducting eighty degrees from the sun's longitude the anomaly <note>The angular distance of a planet from its perihelion or aphelion</note> is found, and the moon's anomaly by diminishing her longitude by that of her apogee. Multiply the sine of the anomaly by fourteen in the sun's case, and by thirty-one in the moon's case, and divide by 360; take the arcs corresponding to the results. Put the arcs down in two places. The result which follows from the calculation for the moon is subtractive in the first half of the circle and additive in the second.

The longitude of the sun's apogee <note>The point in the sun's orbit most distant from the Earth.</note> is assumed to amount to 80°, and the circumferences of the epicycles <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles, used to explain planetary orbits.</note> of sun and moon to 14° and 31° respectively. — The direction to put down the result in two places seems due to the circumstance that it is employed also in the calculation taught in the next stanza. — What, in the latter half of the second stanza, is said about the moon's equation <note>The correction applied to the mean motion to find the true position.</note>, is valid for the sun's equation as well.

9. Multiply the sun's equation, which had been put down separately, by the sun's daily motion, divide by 21600, and treat the result in the case of the sun as in the previous process (*i. e.*, add it if the equation of the centre was found to be positive, and subtract it in the opposite case). Proceed in the case of the moon analogously to the operation in the case of the sun.

A rule for calculating the so-called <term>bhujântara</term> <note>A correction for the equation of time due to the difference between the mean and true sun.</note> equation, by means of which the places of sun and moon are found for true noon.

10. From 53⅓ <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles.</note> to the east or west (of the prime meridian) there results one <term>nâdikâ</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> which has to be deducted or added respectively.

The above rule for allowing for difference of terrestrial longitude bases on the assumption of the earth's equatorial circumference being equal to 3200 <term>yojanas</term>. We then have the proportion

->3200 yoj. : 60 <term>nâdikâs</term> = 53⅓ yoj. : one <term>nâdikâ</term>.<-

11. The mean daily motion of the moon amounts to 790' 34", that of the sun to 59' 8".

12. Seven minutes minus one-third (= 6' 40") is the daily motion of the moon's apogee. The mean motion of the moon lessened by that of the apogee is the motion of the anomaly <note>The angular distance of a planet from its apogee.</note>. From the latter the true motion is to be calculated.

13. Multiply (the motion of the anomaly) by the difference of the sines of anomaly, and divide by 225 ; reduce the result (to terms of the epicycle). The arc of the result is to be deducted from the mean motion in the six signs beginning with Capricorn, and to be added to it in the six signs beginning with Cancer.

14. The result is to be known as the true daily motion at the time (which is thus ascertained) from the difference (of the places on two consecutive days) of the moon. — Multiply the mean motion by the Radius and divide by the true motion ; you thus obtain the true hypothenuse.

The process here described for finding the true motion of the moon is the same as the one taught in the modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, likely dating in its current form to the 4th or 5th century CE.</note> II. 47—49 and therefore requires no detailed elucidation. The “reduction” of stanza 13 means that we have to multiply the result by the degrees of the epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used to explain the perceived irregularities in planetary orbits.</note> and to divide by 360.—The rule for finding the variable <term>hypothenuse</term> <note>In this context, the distance from the Earth to the planet.</note> is founded on the consideration that the more the motion decreases the more the distance (variable <term>hypothenuse</term>) increases.

15. The true <term>hypothenuse</term> multiplied by 5347 and divided by 120 gives the <term>kakshâ</term> of the sun; the true <term>hypothenuse</term> of the moon multiplied by 3 gives the <term>kakshâ</term> of the moon.

By the term ‘<term>kakshâ</term>,’ <note>original: "kakshâ" - literally "orbit" or "circle."</note> which in later terminology (also in that of the modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term>) denotes the orbit of a planet, we have in the above rule clearly to understand the distance of the planet from the earth in <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly equivalent to 5 to 9 miles.</note>. The rule thus teaches how to calculate from the true distance of the planet expressed in terms of the Radius—which was found in stanza 14—the true distance in <term>yojanas</term> (the later so-called <term>sphuṭa-yojanakarna</term> <note>The "corrected distance in yojanas."</note>). The mean distance of the sun in <term>yojanas</term> is put equal to 5347, that of the moon to 360

-> $(\frac{360}{Rad = 120} = 3)$. <-

16. Take 5147080 for the sun and 333640 for the moon and, in order to find their (apparent) dimensions for a given time, divide those two quantities separately by the true distances in <term>yojanas</term>.

A rule for finding the apparent diameters of sun and moon at a given time.—If we divide 5147080 by the mean distance of the sun in <term>yojanas</term> as given in stanza 15, we get 962.6 which according to the tenour of the rule ought to be the mean diameter of the sun. But 962.6 can represent that quantity only if it be divided by 30, when we obtain 32' 5."2 for the mean diameter. The rule for finding the true diameter then stands as follows:

Multiply the mean diameter by the mean distance and divide by the true distance

-> $i. e. \frac{962.6 \times 5347}{30 \times \text{true dist.}} = \frac{5147080}{30 \text{ true dist.}}$ <-

(the true diameter decreasing in the same proportion as the true distance increases). But for some reason or other the text—provided it be correct—does not mention the divisor 30.—The rule for finding the true diameter of the moon is analogous, and we there also miss the mention of the divisor 30.

The mean measure of the diameter is supposed to be <sup>926.8</sup>/<sub>30</sub>; hence the true

->measure = <sup>926.8 x 360</sup>/<sub>30 x true distance</sub> = <sup>333640</sup>/<sub>30 x true distance</sub>.<-

17. The degrees, which correspond to the time by which the end of the <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day in the Hindu calendar, representing the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and the sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note> is separated from noon, and which are calculated by the (times of) the rising of the signs in the right sphere—the signs being taken in reverse order—are, in the eastern hemisphere, to be deducted from the sun's longitude, and to be added, in due succession, in the western hemisphere.

18. That (which is thus found) is what is called the <term>madhyalagna</term> <note>original: "madhyalagna"</note> (*i. e.* the point of the ecliptic on the meridian). Find the degrees of the arc of declination of that point, and either deduct them from—or add them to—the latitude; the sine of that sum—or difference—is called the middle sine (<term>madhyâ</term>).

A rule for finding the so-called <term>madhya-jyâ</term> <note>The sine of the zenith distance of the meridian ecliptic point.</note> *i. e.*, the sine of the zenith-distance of the <term>madhya lagna</term>, *i. e.*, that point of the ecliptic which at the time is on the meridian.—First the longitude of the <term>madhya-lagna</term> is found from the <term>natakâla</term>, *i. e.*, the time intervening between the moment of conjunction and noon. We calculate from that time the corresponding degrees of the ecliptic, and deduct them from—or add them to—the sun's place, according as the sun is in the eastern or western hemisphere.—The sine of the <term>madhya-lagna</term>'s zenith distance is thereupon found without difficulty.

19. Multiply the sine of the longitude of the lagna of the end of the <term>tithi</term> by the sine of greatest declination, and divide by the sine of colatitude. Multiply the result by the sine of the zenith-distance of the point of the ecliptic on the meridian (<term>madhya-jyâ</term>) and divide by Radius. Square the result.

20. Deduct it from the square of the <term>madhya-jyâ</term>, and put the difference down in two places. Take its square root; thus you obtain what is called the sun's <term>drikkshepa</term> (*i. e.* the sine of the zenith distance of the <term>tribhona lagna</term> <note>The "highest point" or nonagesimal; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point.</note>). For better remembrance sake put it down separately.

21. Deduct the square of the <term>drikkshepa</term> from the square of the Radius; multiply the square root of the remainder by the sine of the distance of the sun from the orient ecliptic point, and divide by the Radius; the result is the sine of the altitude (<term>Śanku</term>) of the sun.

22. From the square, which above had been put down in two places, deduct the difference of the squares of the so-called <term>ańgulis</term> <note>A unit of measurement, literally "fingers," used here to denote specific trigonometric values in the calculation</note> of altitude and the Radius; take the square root of the remainder, multiply it by eighteen, and divide separately by the distances of the sun and the moon.

23. From the difference of the degrees (of the arcs corresponding to the two last results) (ascertain the true end of the <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, representing 1/30th of a lunar month</note>), in the same way as in the case of the tithi (*i. e.*, in the same way as the past and the remaining part of a tithi is ascertained); with the end of the tithi (so found) perform again the same operation. The time ascertained is thus to be inquired into (*i. e.*, tested and corrected), until no difference remains.

The above five stanzas teach the method of calculating the <term>parallax in longitude</term> <note>original: "lambana"</note>. We first ascertain the sine of amplitude of the orient ecliptic point (B C in figure 6) by the formula

->Sine of amplitude = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{sine of greatest declination} \times \text{sine of longitude of the rising point}}{\text{Radius} \times \text{sine of colatitude}}$ = $\frac{\text{sine of greatest declination} \times \text{sine of longitude of the rising point}}{\text{sine of colatitude}}$<-
<note>The "rising point" refers to the Lagna, the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon.</note>

By multiplying the sine of amplitude thus found by the <term>madhyajyâ</term> <note>The meridian sine, specifically the sine of the zenith distance of the meridian ecliptic point</note> (Z L) and dividing by Radius we obtain the sine of that arc of the ecliptic (T L) which is intercepted by the meridian and the vertical circle passing through the <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon; the highest point of the ecliptic</note> (T). From this and the madhyajyâ—and treating the small spherical right angled triangle T L Z like a plane triangle—we find the <term>dṛikkishepa</term> <note>The sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal</note> (T Z) *i. e.*, the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal. By deducting the square of the dṛikkishepa from the square of the Radius and taking the square root of the remainder we obtain the cosine of the dṛikkishepa (T D) *i. e.*, the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal. From this we find the <term>śańku</term> <note>Literally "gnomon," here referring to the sine of the altitude</note>, *i. e.*, the sine of the sun's altitude (mG; m being the place of the sun) by means of the proportion

->Radius : sine of altitude of nonagesimal = distance of sun from rising point : sine of altitude of sun.<-

Deducting the square of the latter from the square of the Radius we obtain the square of the sine of the sun's zenith distance (m Z). We deduct from this latter square the square of the dṛikkishepa (Z T) and take the square root of the remainder; the result is (according to spherical trigonometry) equal to the product of the sine of T m (*i. e.*, the arc of the ecliptic intercepted by the latitude—circles of the nonagesimal and the sun) and the cosine of T Z (Radius being put equal to unity); which product itself is equal to the sine of Z F *i. e.*, the arc drawn from the zenith at right angles to P'm, P' being the pole of the ecliptic). We then establish the proportion

Sine *Z m* : sine of the opposite angle (where the sine equals the Radius) = sine *Z F* : sine of the opposite angle; thus, find the sine of angle *Z m F*, which is equal to the cosine of angle *T m Z*. We then finally have the proportion:

Now, in the above proportion, the sine of *m M* may be found from the greatest vertical parallax by means of the proportion:

In this manner, the sines of the parallaxes in longitude are found separately for the sun and the moon. This is done by multiplying the difference by sixty and dividing by the difference of the motions of the sun and moon.

24. Multiply the <term>dṛikkshepa</term> <note>The sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic.</note>—derived from the same time—by 18, and divide by the true distance of the sun and the moon; the degrees of the arc of the difference of the two results represent the parallax in latitude <note>The apparent shifting of the moon's position north or south due to the observer's perspective.</note>, whose direction is determined by that of the <term>madhyajyâ</term> <note>The sine of the meridian ecliptic point.</note>.

Then you may declare the duration of obscuration <note>The total time the sun remains covered.</note> according to the dimensions.

A rule for calculating the parallax in latitude. The proportion is:

Radius : sine of greatest parallax = <term>dṛikkshepa</term> : sine of desired parallax in latitude.

Therefore: Sine of desired parallax = (18 × Radius × <term>dṛikkshepa</term>) / (Radius × true distance) = (18 × <term>dṛikkshepa</term>) / true distance. The remainder requires no comment.

26. Deduct the square of the <term>avanati</term> <note>The moon's apparent latitude after being corrected for parallax.</note> from the square of half the sum of the measure of sun and moon. From the double square root of the remainder determine the time of the eclipse, as in the case of the calculation of the elapsed portion of a <term>tithi</term> <note>A lunar day, or 1/30th of a lunar month.</note>.

->Compare chapter VIII, stanza 16.<-

27. The difference of the displacement of the <term>tithi</term> (that is, the parallax in longitude <note>The apparent shifting of the moon's position along the path of the sun.</note>) as calculated for the beginning of the eclipse and of the half duration gives the true half duration of the eclipse; if the eclipse takes place in the western hemisphere, the parallax has to be added. We proceed in an analogous manner with regard to that half of the duration which precedes the separation <note>The moment the two celestial bodies appear to move apart.</note>.

## LUNAR ECLIPSES, ACCORDING TO THE SÛRYA SIDDHÂNTA.

---

1. Multiply the true distance of the sun by 90, and divide by 276; the result is to be employed as the divisor of the true distance of the moon multiplied by 36. Deduct the result from 36.

2 *a*. Multiply the remainder by 120, and divide by the true distance of the moon; the corresponding arc is the diameter of the shadow.

A rule for calculating the diameter of the true shadow. Let S (fig. 8) be the centre of the sun, E the centre of the earth, *o p* a part of the path of the shadow, *m n* half the diameter of the true shadow which—D *m* being drawn parallel to F *n*—is equal to F D. E *u* being drawn parallel to F *t*, we have the two similar triangles *u* S E and E D *m*, in which S *u* is equal to the Radius of the sun minus the Radius of the earth, *i. e.* (the abridged diameters of the sun and the earth being put equal to 146 and 36 <note>These values are expressed in <term>yojanas</term>, a traditional Indian unit of distance roughly equal to 8 or 9 miles.</note>) to 73 — 18 = 55; hence E D = $\frac{55 \times \text{true dist. of moon}}{\text{true dist. of sun}} = \frac{55 \times \text{true dist. moon} \times 90}{\text{true dist. sun} \times 90}$

-> $= \frac{\frac{55 \times 90}{276} \times \text{true dist. moon}}{\frac{90 \times \text{true dist. sun}}{276}} = \frac{18 \times \text{true dist. moon}}{\frac{90 \times \text{true dist. sun}}{276}}$ <-

The quantity so found being deducted from eighteen, *i. e.*, the Radius of the earth, we obtain the value of D F.—The process prescribed in stanza 2 has the purpose of expressing the half diameter—so far found in <term>yojanas</term>—in minutes of arc.—In order to double the result (so as to find the whole diameter), 36 is substituted for 18 in the above expressions.

<note>The Sûrya Siddhânta uses these geometric ratios to determine the size of the Earth's shadow cone at the specific distance where the Moon passes through it.</note>

->( 64 )<-

2 *b*. Divide the sum of the diameters of the moon and the shadow by 2, and take the square of the quotient;

3. Subtract from that the square of the latitude, and take the approximate square root. Multiply this root by 120, and divide by the difference between the motions of the sun and the moon; the result provides the <term>nadikas</term> <note>A unit of time used in ancient Indian astronomy, equal to 24 minutes</note> of the total duration of the eclipse.

4. Using that result, calculate the latitude of the moon at the specific moment of first contact. With that new value, repeat the calculation described above to find the duration of the eclipse again. Repeat this operation multiple times until the result for the duration no longer changes.

This is a rule for calculating the duration of a lunar eclipse. First, we calculate the so-called <term>bhuja</term> <note>Literally "arm" or "side"; here referring to the base of a right-angled triangle</note>, which represents one side of a right-angled triangle. In this triangle, the hypotenuse is formed by the combined radii of the moon and the earth's shadow, and the other side is the latitude of the moon at the moment of contact. However, because that specific latitude is not yet known, we initially substitute the moon's latitude at the moment of conjunction <note>The exact moment the sun and moon are aligned</note>. From this, a proportion is established:

->Minutes of difference between the motion of the sun and moon : 60 <term>nadikas</term> = minutes of the <term>bhuja</term> : half-duration of the eclipse<-

->Therefore, Half-duration = (60 × <term>bhuja</term>) / minutes of difference and<-

->Total Duration = (120 × <term>bhuja</term>) / minutes of difference<-

Since we now have an estimate for the longitude of the moon at the time of first contact, we can calculate the latitude for that same moment. We then use that to determine the <term>bhuja</term> and the duration once more. This iterative process is repeated until the results are consistent.

5. Multiply the difference of the motions of the sun and moon by the given <term>nadikas</term>, and divide by sixty. Take the difference between those minutes and the minutes of duration calculated previously; then, determine the latitude of the moon at the given time;

<summary>This page outlines the iterative mathematical process for determining the precise duration of a lunar eclipse using right-angled trigonometry and the relative motions of the sun and moon. It explains how to refine the calculation by repeatedly adjusting for the moon's changing latitude at the moment of contact.</summary>

6. Subtract the square root of the sum of the squares of those two quantities from half the sum of the diameters <note>The original uses "measure," referring to the angular diameters</note> of the moon and the earth's shadow, expressed in minutes of arc. The remaining value indicates the portion of the moon or the sun that is hidden from view at that specific time.

->**A rule for finding how large a part of the moon (or sun) is obscured at a given moment.**<-

We calculate the *bhuja* <term>the horizontal distance or "arm" of a right triangle</term> and the latitude of the moon for the chosen moment; the square root of the sum of the squares of these two quantities represents the distance between the centers of the shadow and the moon at that time. The difference between this distance and the combined radii of the two celestial bodies indicates the total amount obscured. **With the necessary changes being made** <note>original: "Mutatis mutandis"</note>, the same rule may be applied to calculate the obscured portion of the sun during a solar eclipse.

7. Take (1) half the difference between the diameters of the body being eclipsed and the body causing the eclipse, and (2) the latitude. Multiply the square root of the difference of the squares of those two quantities by two, and process the result in the same manner as a *tithi* <term>a lunar day, or 1/30th of a lunar month</term>. The final result is the duration of the total obscuration for the sun or the moon.

The rule provided above for calculating the duration of total obscuration is entirely similar to the previous rule for finding the overall duration of the eclipse; therefore, it requires no further explanation.

# CHAPTER XI.

---

## (ON THE PROJECTION OF ECLIPSES ACCORDING TO THE SUN-TREATISE).
<note>original: "Sûrya Siddhânta." This is one of the most foundational texts of Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th or 5th century CE.</note>

1. By means of a staff, on which the <term>finger-breadths</term> <note>original: "angulis." A traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger.</note> are marked, describe a first circle with a Radius equal to the sum of half (the diameters of) the obscuring and obscured bodies, and mark on it the different directions. Describe a second circle with half the diameter of the obscured body.

2. Multiply the sine of terrestrial latitude by the versed sine of the degrees intervening between the moon and the zenith; add the degrees corresponding to the 120th part (of that product) to the north or south respectively in the eastern and western hemispheres.

3. Add three signs <note>In ancient astronomy, a "sign" refers to a 30-degree arc of the zodiac.</note> to the longitude of the moon, and treat the corresponding degrees of declination according to their direction. Thus the east-west direction is ascertained; the north and south points are to be determined therefrom by means of a fish-figure. <note>A "fish-figure" or *matsya* is a geometric construction using intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular line, resembling the shape of a fish.</note>

4—5. Draw a line, representing the moon’s latitude, in the direction opposite (to that latitude), which extends up to the east-west line and cuts the second circle. The first contact takes place at the point where a line drawn from the centre cuts the other circle (*viz.* the circle representing the eclipsed body). The point of separation also is to be determined analogously, in the opposite way; in ascertaining the direction one has to start, in one’s considerations, from the moon at the moment of separation.

Rules for calculating the <term>deflection</term> <note>original: "valana." The angle between the ecliptic and the local horizon or equator.</note>, the <term>latitude-based deflection</term> <note>original: "âksha."</note> as well as the <term>solstitial deflection</term> <note>original: "âyana."</note>, and for drawing a projection of the eclipse. The rules altogether agree with those of the modern Sun-Treatise. For the details see the Sanskrit Commentary.

6. On the horizon two minutes (of the diameter of some heavenly body) go to one <term>finger-breadth</term>; while three go to it (when the heavenly body is) in the zenith. If the body is placed between (the horizon and the zenith), a proportionate calculation is to be made, to the end of bringing about agreement between observation and theory.

It details how to determine the points of first contact and separation by calculating the deflection of the moon's path relative to the observer's horizon.</summary>

## CHAPTER XII.

---

### THE SYSTEM OF PITÂMAHA.
<note>original: "PAITÂMAHA SIDDHÂNTA." This refers to the "Grandfather's Tradition," an early school of Indian astronomy attributed to the god Brahma.</note>

---

1. According to the teaching of Pitâmaha, five years constitute a <term>yuga</term> <note>a cosmic cycle or age</note> of the sun and moon. The <term>adhimâsas</term> <note>intercalary or "extra" months added to align the lunar and solar years</note> are brought about by thirty months, and an omitted lunar day (<term>avama</term>) by sixty-two days.

2. Lessen the time of the <term>S'aka king</term> <note>The Shaka era, beginning in 78 CE, commonly used in Indian astronomical dating</note> by two, and divide by five; with the remaining years form the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>the "heap of days," or the total number of elapsed days since a specific epoch</note>, which begins with the light half of the month of Mâgha. The <term>ahargaṇa</term> begins with the day, *viz.*, from sunrise.

In the five-year <note>original: "quinquennial"</note> lunisolar cycle of the Paitâmaha system, one extra month is comprised within each period of thirty solar months, and one <term>avama</term>, *i. e.*, omitted lunar day, within each period of sixty-two days.

According to Stanza 2, which directs us to deduct two from the number of elapsed Shaka years, a new cycle began with 2 Shaka elapsed <note>corresponding to 80 CE</note>.

3. If the total days (<term>ahargaṇa</term>) is increased by its own sixty-first part, the result is the <term>tithis</term> <note>lunar days, which are slightly shorter than solar days</note>. If it is multiplied by nine and divided by 122, the result is the <term>nakshatra</term> <note>lunar mansion or star constellation</note> of the sun. Multiply the total days by 7, divide by 610, and deduct (the result from the total days); the result is the lunar <term>nakshatra</term>, counting from the star Dhanishthâ.

Rules for calculating the lunar days contained within a given total of days, and the star mansions in which the sun and the moon are at a given time.—The cycle comprising 1830 <term>sâvana</term> <note>civil or terrestrial</note> days, and at the same time 1860 lunar days, the number of lunar days of a given total = (1860 x total days) / 1830 = (62 x total days) / 61 = total days + total days / 61.

As the sun revolves in one cycle five times through the twenty-seven star mansions, the mansions through which he passes during a given total of days = (27 x 5 x total days) / 1830 = (9 x total days) / 122.

As the moon passes in one cycle through 27 x 67 star mansions (the cycle comprising 67 <term>sidereal</term> <note>relative to the stars</note> revolutions of the moon), she passes within a given total of days through = (27 x 67 x total days) / 1830 = (603 x total days) / 610 = total days - (7 x total days) / 610.

# Page 68

The <term>nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in Indian astronomy to track the moon's path.</note> are to be counted from <term>Dhanishṭhâ</term> <note>The 23rd nakshatra, associated with the star Delphini.</note>, in which sun and moon are in conjunction at the beginning of the <term>yuga</term> <note>A cosmic or astronomical age; here referring to the five-year cycle.</note>.

4*a*. [See the Sanskrit Commentary].

4*b*. Multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note> by 12, and divide by 305; the result are the <term>vyatipâtas</term> <note>A specific astronomical alignment or "yoga" considered significant in Vedic astrology.</note>.

A rule for finding how many of the <term>yogas</term> <note>Astronomical "unions" or longitudinal sums of the sun and moon.</note> called <term>vyatipâtas</term> have occurred within a given <term>ahargaṇa</term>. There are 27 <term>yogas</term> which are calculated by dividing the sum of the longitudes of sun and moon by 27. At the beginning of the quinquennial <term>yuga</term> sun and moon are in conjunction at the beginning of <term>Dhanishṭhâ</term> or—which is the same—at the end of <term>Śravaṇa</term>. The longitude of each therefore amounts to 22 <term>nakshatras</term>—if we count in the ordinary way from <term>Aśvinî</term>—, and the sum of their longitudes to 44 <term>nakshatras</term>. Forty-four being divided by 27, the remainder (= 17) indicates that the <term>yoga</term> at the beginning of the <term>yuga</term> is the 17th of the series, *i. e.*, <term>Vyatipâta</term>. Now in one entire <term>yuga</term> the accumulated longitude of the sun amounts to 5 x 27 <term>nakshatras</term>, and that of the moon to 67 x 27 <term>nakshatras</term>; hence the sum of the two to 72 x 27. Dividing this sum by 27, the quotient 72 indicates how many <term>vyatipâtas</term> take place in one <term>yuga</term>. Hence the proportion

->1830 (= days of <term>yuga</term>) : 72 = given <term>aharg.</term> : *x* —<-
->$\therefore$ *x* = (72 x aharg.) / 1830 = (12 x aharg.) / 305.<-

5. Add to 732 those days of the northern progress of the sun <note>The <term>uttarâyaṇa</term>, or the period between the winter and summer solstices.</note> which are passed, and in the case of the southern progress <note>The <term>dakshiṇâyana</term>, or the period between the summer and winter solstices.</note> those days which are yet to come; multiply by 2 and divide by 61; the result is the measure of the day minus twelve.

A rule for finding the length of any given day of the year. The supposition being that the length of the shortest day is twelve <term>muhûrtas</term> <note>A traditional unit of time; 1/30th of a day, or 48 minutes.</note>, and that of the longest day eighteen <term>muhûrtas</term>, and each <term>ayana</term> <note>A half-year period or solar journey.</note> comprising 183 days, the length of any day of the year is found by adding to twelve the product of six and the number of the day, divided by 183. In the case of the <term>uttarâyaṇa</term> the number of the day is counted forward from the winter solstice, while in the case of a day in the <term>dakshiṇâyana</term> it is counted backward from the same point of time. We then transform the expression for the length of the day in the following manner

->12 + (6 x given day) / 183 = 12 + (2 x day) / 61 = 24 + (2 x day) / 61 - 12 = (24 x 61 + 2 x day) / 61 - 12<-
->= 2/61 (12 x 61 + day) - 12 = 2/61 (732 + day) - 12.<-

# CHAPTER XIII.

---

### ON THE CONSTITUTION OF THE UNIVERSE.

---

1. The round ball of the earth, composed of the five elements <note>The five elements in Indian philosophy are earth, water, fire, air, and ether (Akasha).</note>, abides in space in midst of the starry sphere, like a piece of iron suspended between magnets;

2. Covered on all sides with trees, mountains, towns, groves, rivers, oceans and other things.—In its middle there is <term>Sumeru</term> <note>Also known as Mount Meru, the sacred five-peaked mountain considered to be the center of all the physical, metaphysical and spiritual universes.</note>, the abode of the gods. Below (*i. e.* at the pole opposite to <term>Meru</term>) there are placed the <term>Asuras</term> <note>A class of beings in Indic religions, often translated as demigods or titans, who live in opposition to the gods.</note>.

3. As the reflections of men standing on the brink of water are seen with the faces downwards, so the gods consider the condition of the Asuras to be; and those on their part deem the gods to be below.

4. Just as here in the region of men the flame of the fire rises upwards into the air, and as a heavy object when being thrown falls to the earth; so it also happens below there in the region of the Asuras.

5. Straight above Meru in space one pole is seen; the other pole is seen below, placed in space. Fastened to the poles the sphere of the stars is driven round by the <term>pravaha wind</term> <note>In ancient Indian astronomy, this is the "provector" wind believed to be responsible for the diurnal motion of the planets and stars.</note>.

6. Others maintain that the earth revolves as if it were placed in a revolving engine, and not the s<unclear>ph</unclear>ere; if that were the case, falcons and other (winged creatures) could not return from the ether to their nests.

7. And, to mention another argument, if the earth revolved in one day, flags and similar things would, owing to the quickness of the revolution, stream constantly towards the west. If the earth, on the other hand, moves slowly, how does it revolve (once within 24 hours)?

8. If, in agreement with the doctrine of the <term>Arhat</term> <note>A reference to Jain cosmology, which historically proposed a system involving multiple suns and moons to explain celestial cycles.</note>, there were two suns and moons rising by turns, how then is it that a mark made in the polar constellation by means of a line drawn from the sun revolves within one day?

<summary>This chapter describes the Earth as a stationary sphere suspended in space by magnetic-like forces, centered on Mount Meru. The author presents classical arguments against the Earth's rotation, suggesting that if the Earth moved, birds could not find their nests and flags would always blow westward.</summary>

<keywords>Sumeru, Mount Meru, Asuras, pravaha wind, Arhat, Jain cosmology, geocentrism, five elements, starry sphere, earth's rotation, Indian astronomy</keywords>

->( 70 )<-

The Jaina doctrine <note>A reference to the cosmology of Jainism, which posits a complex system of multiple celestial bodies</note> is that there are two suns, two moons, etc., rising on alternate days. But if we at sunset draw a line from the sun to the constellation of the polar fish <note>likely referring to the constellation Ursa Minor or a specific Vedic asterism used for orientation</note>, we observe that that point of the constellation which the line reaches, *i. e.*, a point on its western side is on the next morning reached by a line drawn from the rising sun; hence we conclude that the constellation as well as the sun performs one complete revolution within 24 hours.

9. For the gods the rising sun, when at the first point of <term>Aries</term> <note>The first sign of the Zodiac, marking the vernal equinox</note>, revolves to the right, moving in the horizon; at <term>Laṅkâ</term> <note>A theoretical point on the equator used as a prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note> he then revolves right overhead; and in an opposite direction (*viz.* to the left in the horizon) for the <term>Asuras</term> <note>In this context, beings inhabiting the southern polar regions, opposite the gods at the north pole</note>.

10. At the end of <term>Gemini</term> the sun revolves for the gods at the height of 24 degrees above the horizon, while at <term>Avanti</term> <note>The city of Ujjain, a major center for Indian astronomy</note> he then moves right overhead.

11. In the same place there is then no shadow at noon, while the shadow falls towards the north for all who dwell to the north of <term>Avanti</term>, and to the south for the inhabitants of the countries south of <term>Avanti</term>.

12. Those who have maintained that for the gods dwelling on <term>Meru</term> <note>The sacred mountain at the center of the world, representing the North Pole</note> it is day as long as the sun stays in <term>Aries</term>, <term>Taurus</term> and <term>Gemini</term>, but night when he is in <term>Cancer</term>, <term>Leo</term> and <term>Virgo</term>, to them reverence is due indeed! <note>This is a sarcastic remark by the author, mocking the ignorance of those who do not understand that the sun remains visible at the pole throughout all six northern signs</note>

13. In the very same places, in which the sun goes to the north from <term>Aries</term>, he moves when returning from the north; how then should he be visible at one time and invisible at another, while all along he is in the same region?

A criticism on those—unknown—authors who were ignorant of the fact that the sun while in <term>Cancer</term>, <term>Leo</term> and <term>Virgo</term> describes the same day circles, in reverse order, which he had described while in <term>Aries</term>, <term>Taurus</term> and <term>Gemini</term>.

14. In the visible half of the sphere there are three signs, extending from the middle of the sky (down to the western horizon); they contain ninety degrees. The same divisions are to be assumed from the rising (*i. e.* the eastern horizon, up to the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>).

15. One degree answers to nine <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles</note> minus one ninth of a <term>yojana</term> (on the earth); this fact is manifest to those, who dwell on the same meridian, from the deflection (of the heavenly bodies) from the zenith.

16. Thus, a difference of ninety degrees results in a distance of eight hundred <term>yojanas</term><note>A yojana is an ancient Indian unit of distance, roughly equal to 8 or 9 miles.</note>. What is sunrise for one observer is noon for another observer in a place distant by that amount.

The circumference of the earth being equal to 3,200 yojanas, 8 and 8/9 yojanas correspond to one degree, and 800 yojanas correspond to 90 degrees.

17. <term>Ujjayinî</term><note>Modern Ujjain, a city in India traditionally used as the prime meridian by Indian astronomers.</note> is near to <term>Laṅkâ</term><note>In this context, a mythical place on the equator, not necessarily the modern island of Sri Lanka.</note>, being situated to the north on the same <term>meridian</term><note>An imaginary line from north to south used to measure time and longitude.</note>; hence the noon of the two places occurs at the same time; but their days are unequal in length, with the exception of the <term>equinoctial days</term><note>The two days a year when day and night are of equal length everywhere.</note>.

18. Three thousand two hundred yojanas are the measure of the circumference of the earth. The sun, when at the equinoctial point, revolves around that much of the earth, with <term>Meru</term><note>Mount Meru, considered the sacred center of the world and the North Pole in this cosmological system.</note> as the center.

The sun, when moving in the celestial equator, revolves around the terrestrial equator, of which Meru is the pole.

19. Going 586 and 2/3 yojanas north from <term>Avanti</term><note>Another name for the region around Ujjayinî.</note>, we reach the middle of the earth (Meru); so also by going 800 yojanas to the north from Laṅkâ.

Ujjayinî has 24° northern latitude, and is therefore 66° from Meru. The distance in yojanas is then found by a simple proportion.

20. In any country, by as many degrees as the pole is raised above the horizon, by so many degrees the sun is depressed from the <term>zenith</term><note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note> to the south on the day of the equinox.

21. If we go 373 and 1/3 yojanas north from Ujjayinî, this whole sphere (as described above) comes to an end.

22. There, the sun is once seen for 60 <term>nâḍikâs</term><note>An ancient Indian unit of time; 60 nâḍikâs equal 24 hours.</note> after his rising. The farther we proceed towards the north, the longer the day becomes, until at <term>Sumeru</term><note>The "Great Meru," or the North Pole.</note> we have a day six months long.

We find by an easy calculation that going 373 and 1/3 yojanas north from Ujjayinî we reach 66° northern latitude. In that latitude, the last point of <term>Gemini</term><note>The third sign of the zodiac.</note>—whose northern <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> amounts to 24°—revolves in a day circle which is raised in its whole extent above the horizon; and the sun, when he

23. If we go 403 5/9 *yojanas* <note>A yojana is a measure of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles.</note> to the north of Avanti <note>Modern-day Ujjain, used as the prime meridian in ancient Indian astronomy.</note>, the two signs Sagittarius and Caper <note>Capricorn</note> never become visible.

The above statements base on the assumption that Sagittarius and Caper do not rise above the horizon in 69° 24′ northern latitude; Scorpio and Aquarius in 78° 15′ northern latitude; and the whole latter half of the ecliptic <note>The path of the sun across the sky.</note> in 90° northern latitude.

The corresponding *yojanas* of distance from Avanti are easily found by proportion.

26. The people at Laṅkâ <note>A city on the equator, not necessarily modern Sri Lanka in this context.</note> see the polar star in the horizon; those on Meru in the zenith; those dwelling between see it between (the horizon and the zenith).

27. For those who dwell on the back of Meru the sun once risen remains visible for six months, while he moves in the six signs beginning with Aries; for the Asuras <note>In this astronomical context, the Asuras are the inhabitants of the South Pole, the opposites of the gods on Meru.</note> he is visible as long as he is in the latter (half of the ecliptic).

28. Mars being, in astrological parlance, the Lord of Aries, all the sub-divisions of Aries also belong to him, *i. e.*, are ruled by him.

Those who live on the far side of the moon see the sun during one half of each lunar fortnight <note>A period of two weeks, or half a lunar month</note>, since there is no shadow obscuring the sun from their perspective to the extent of three signs <note>A "sign" refers to a zodiacal sign, representing 30 degrees of the celestial circle</note> on each side of the conjunction.
