# CHAPTER XIV.

---

## ON ASTRONOMICAL INSTRUMENTS, OBSERVATIONS AND THE LIKE.

---

1. Draw upon the ground a level circle with a diameter one hundred and eighty <term>finger-breadths</term> <note>original: "angulis"; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a finger</note> long, and mark upon its circumference the signs (degrees, etc.) at equal distances, and also the degrees of declination <note>the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the signs.

2. Further describe from the centre of the first circle three other circles, taking for their Radii the strings running at right angles from the string, which marks the north-south line, to those points on the circumference of the first circle where the degrees of declination of the signs of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note> are marked; and mark those circles with the degrees, as you did with the first one.

3. Thereupon draw a line from the centre towards the latitude <note>the specific point on the circle corresponding to the observer's geographic latitude</note>, and lengthen it up to the sphere. Take that piece which is due to the declination of a given sign of the ecliptic and is intercepted by the line of latitude and the north-south line;

4. Double it and mark it off on the circle belonging to that sign; multiply half the degrees of the corresponding arc by ten. The result represents the <term>units of time</term> <note>original: "vinâḍikâs"; a traditional Indian unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note> of ascensional difference <note>the difference between the time it takes for a celestial body to rise and the time it would take if it were on the equator</note> in the case of the first sign; in the case of the two other signs the <term>units of time</term> come out mixed.

The above stanzas teach how to find the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>The difference between the time of sunrise at a specific location and the time of sunrise at the equator.</note> for any given <term>latitude</term> without calculation, by the mere inspection of a kind of diagram.

->Fig. 9.<-

—In diagram 9 N E S W represents the first circle whose circumference is supposed to be divided into 360 degrees. We further mark off on the circumference the degrees of <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the first three signs of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky.</note>, the <term>declination</term> of Aries = Wa' that of Taurus = Wt', that of Gemini = Wg' and then draw the perpendiculars a' a, t' t, g' g on NS. Taking these perpendiculars as <term>Radii</term>, we describe from the centre C three circles (of which the diagram however represents only one, viz., that one whose Radius = a a'). We then lay off from N the degrees of the <term>latitude</term> of the given place = N P, draw the perpendicular P l and join P C. Comparing the similar triangles P C l and d C a we establish the proportion

->C l (= <term>sine of colatitude</term> <note>The sine of the complement of the latitude (90° minus latitude).</note> given place) : P l (= <term>sine of latitude</term>) = C a<-
->(= <term>sine of declination</term> of Aries) : a d (= <term>ascensional difference</term> for Aries).<-

Doubling a d and applying it as a <term>chord</term> (d' d'') to the day circle of Aries, we take—from an inspection of the degrees marked on the circumference—the degrees of arc corresponding to half that <term>chord</term> and, in order to turn them into <term>vinâḍikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time; 60 vinâḍikâs make one nâḍikâ.</note>, multiply them by ten (one degree = 1/6 <term>nâḍikâ</term> = 10 <term>vinâḍikâs</term>).—In the case of Taurus and Gemini the <term>vinâḍikâs</term> come out mixed *i. e.*, the result gives us the sum of the <term>vinâḍikâs</term> for Aries + Taurus, and for Aries + Taurus + Gemini. An appropriate subtraction then furnishes the desired result.

5. Multiply the given <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> by six ; they are thus turned into degrees. Take the <term>versed sine</term> <note>A trigonometric function defined as 1 minus the cosine of an angle.</note> of those degrees and deduct it from the <term>Radius</term> ; there remains the shadow. Thus there is found the shadow up to noon. In order to find the <term>nâḍikâs</term>, lessen the <term>Radius</term> by the shadow.

6. Take the sixth part of the degrees of arc corresponding to the sine of the interval between the end of the shadow and the horizon; that sixth part represents the elapsed <term>nâḍikâs</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 nâḍikâs make one full day.</note> in the eastern hemisphere, those to come in the western hemisphere.

The above stanzas teach a rough process for ascertaining, from the sun's altitude, the length of the shadow, and *vice versâ*. In the first place the sine of the sun's altitude at a given moment is roughly identified with the sine of that arc of the day-circle, which the sun has described up to that moment; hence the direction to turn the elapsed <term>nâḍikâs</term> into degrees. If we then construct an artificial sphere, as in figure 10, in which c e is the height of the <term>gnomon</term><note>The vertical part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, we know in the triangle b c f the side f b = sine of sun's altitude; and by deducting a b—which is the versed sine* corresponding to b f—from the Radius we have b c. To this b c the line c d i. e. the length of the desired shadow is now assumed to be equal, the two hypothenuses c f and d e—which in reality meet in the sun—being looked upon as parallel.

->Fig. 10.<-

7. Take that line which constitutes the east-west line corresponding to the oblique line, and the north-south line representing the degrees of declination; the degrees of the corresponding arc, multiplied by ten, give the <term>vinâḍikâs</term><note>A smaller unit of time; 1/60th of a nâḍikâ, equal to 24 seconds.</note> of the rising of the signs in succession.

A rule for finding, by the inspection of a diagram or globe, the time of the rising of the individual signs of the ecliptic on the equator. The rule is rather obscurely worded; it however appears that by the oblique line we have to understand the sine of one, two, etc. signs of the ecliptic, while the north-south line is the sine of the declination of the end point of the respective sign. The east-line then is the other side, at right angles to the north-south line, and represents the so-called <term>udayajyâ</term><note>The 'rising-sine' or the sine of the amplitude of the rising point on the horizon.</note> which is a segment of the day circle described by the end point of the sign of the ecliptic.

Each degree of the corresponding arc represents 1/6 <term>nâḍikâ</term> = 10 <term>vinâḍikâs</term>; the degrees multiplied by 10 therefore give the <term>vinâḍikâs</term> of rising.

10*b*. 11. Having ascertained, for the given day, the <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the sun—which is either greater than the terrestrial <term>latitude</term> or less than it—place its <term>sine</term> <note>A mathematical function of an angle used in trigonometry</note> between the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path among the stars</note> and the <term>equator</term>; in which degree that <term>sine</term> intersects the <term>ecliptic</term>, to that degree know the sun to be equal in <term>longitude</term> <note>The position of a celestial body along the ecliptic</note>, according to that part of the sphere (in which he is at the time).

->A rule for finding the <term>longitude</term> of the sun from observation.<-

The <term>declination</term> of the sun is ascertained from the observation of the sun's <term>zenith</term> distance at noon, to which the terrestrial <term>latitude</term> is added if the <term>zenith</term> distance is north, while it is deducted from it, if the <term>zenith</term>-distance is south. The <term>longitude</term> of the sun is thereupon calculated as the <term>hypothenuse</term> of a right angled triangle, in which there are given one side, *viz.*, the <term>sine</term> of the sun's <term>declination</term> and the opposite angle, *viz.*, the inclination of the <term>ecliptic</term> = 24°. The resulting degrees are to be taken as they are in the first quarter, in the second quarter they have to be deducted from 180° and so on.

12. By means of an observation, made by means of two staffs equal to Radius and placed in the centre, ascertain the degrees intervening between sun and moon. The twelfth part of those degrees represents the elapsed true <term>tithis</term> <note>A lunar day in the Hindu calendar, defined as the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the moon and the sun to increase by 12 degrees</note>. From this (observed interval) again the next <term>tithi</term> is to be ascertained.

13. Adding to the degrees (intervening between sun and moon) the <term>longitude</term> of the sun as ascertained by observation (stanza 10), we obtain the <term>longitude</term> of the moon at the given time by mere observation.

->A rule for finding the number of elapsed true <term>tithis</term> and the longitude<-
->of the moon by observation.<-
—When the distance of the moon from the sun amounts to 12°, one <term>tithi</term> has elapsed, and so on.

14. 15. Mark three times, from the center, the end of the gnomon's shadow, and then describe two <term>fish-figures</term> <note>A "fish-figure" or *vesica piscis* is a geometric shape formed by the intersection of two circles with the same radius, used here to find perpendicular bisectors.</note>. Thereupon describe a circle, taking for Radius a string, that is fastened to the point in which the two strings issuing from the heads of the fish-figures intersect, and that is so long as to reach the three points marked. On the given day the shadow of the gnomon moves in that circle, without departing from it.

16. The line joining the center of that circle and the base of the gnomon is the south-north line; and the interval in the north direction (between that circle and the gnomon) is the midday shadow.

A rule for finding the path described by the extremity of the shadow, based on the (erroneous) assumption that that path is the arc of a circle <note>In reality, the path of a shadow's tip over a day is typically a hyperbola, not a circle.</note>. We mark the extremity of the shadow at three different moments of the day, and thus obtain the points a, b, c (fig. 11).

<margin>Fig. 11.</margin>
In order to lay a circle through these three points, we describe from a and b the fish-figure d e, and from b and c the fish-figure f g; the point h in which the cords d e and f g meet is the center of the desired circle.—It is then easy to show that the line joining h and g (*i. e.* the foot of the gnomon) is the meridian line, and g l the midday shadow.

17. 'Horizon' we call that (circle) in which the sky is joined as it were to the earth; we draw in it even east-west and north-south lines.

18. The interval between the pole and the horizon is the terrestrial latitude; and the difference of the latitude and ninety (degrees) is called colatitude, which declines from the zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note> towards the pole. The day-circle is what intervenes between (the sun's etc.) rising and setting.

19. Make, for the purposes of observation, a circle with marks (indicating the <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time; one nâdikâ is 24 minutes.</note> of rising of the signs of the ecliptic) in reverse order, and indications of the directions. Mark the center and place the circle on even ground in such a way as to raise its axis to the amount of the given latitude.

20. Mark the spot touched by the shadow where the two strings cross—that is, the center of the circle. Add to the sun's current position the degrees it has traveled through at a specific hour of the day; this calculation reveals which zodiac sign is rising in the east at that moment. From these same degrees, one can also calculate the elapsed <term>nadikas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time, where 1 nadika equals 24 minutes</note> of the day.

->The circle is to be placed in the plane of the celestial equator. By observing where the shadow of the center pin touches the circle's edge at different hours, we learn how many degrees the sun has moved. From this, we calculate the specific point of the ecliptic on the eastern horizon and the current time of day.<-

21. 22. Take a circular hoop with 360 degrees marked evenly around its edge. It should have a diameter of one <term>hasta</term> <note>A "cubit," roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</note> and a width of half an <term>anguli</term> <note>A "finger's breadth," approximately 0.75 inches</note>. In the middle of the hoop's width, drill a hole. At noon, allow a ray of sunlight to pass through this small hole at an angle. Measure the degrees on the lower half of the circle between the spot of light and a plumb line hanging straight down from the center. These degrees represent the <term>zenith-distance</term> <note>The angular distance between the sun and the point directly overhead</note> of the midday sun.

->An easily understood rule for finding the sun’s zenith-distance at noon through direct observation.<-

23. Construct a delicate, perfectly rounded sphere from a suitable material. On its surface, mark the endpoints of two lines known as the lines of the portions of time (<term>kalabhoga</term>). These lines correspond to the points where the sun appears to stop its north-south movement—the solstices.

24. Between those two lines, based on observation, mark the degrees of <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> for the various zodiac signs on both sides of the first point of Aries. These marks are used for making oblique observations.

25. Tilt this globe toward the north according to the degrees of latitude of your specific location. Measure the <term>nadikas</term> between the point of your observation and the horizon. These represent the elapsed <term>nadikas</term> of the day; when multiplied by six, they provide the measurement in degrees.

->Fig. 12.<-

meaning of the text, the construction and phraseology of which are, at the best, particularly involved and vague. The accompanying diagram shows a projection of the sphere on the plane of the meridian (H P Z H' P'), H H' being the horizon and P P' the poles of the sphere. We ascertain on the circumference of the sphere the points B and B', in which the sun rises and sets on the days of the two solstices <note>The longest and shortest days of the year</note>, and draw the day-circles in which the sun moves on those days. Between those two day-circles we then draw the day-circles in which the sun moves when entering each sign of the ecliptic <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky</note> (and, possibly, as many more intervening day-circles as there is room for). We then, at any given moment, ascertain, by observation from the centre, the place of the sun in his day-circle, *for instance* S and take the <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> or degrees—which are to be considered as marked on each day-circle—intervening between the place of the sun, and the intersection of the day-circle and the horizon (*for instance* between S and T). A mere inspection of the globe thus will furnish the time of day.

26. As long as, in the rising sphere, there rises that part which begins with the east point (*i. e.* the first point of <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram; the starting point of the zodiac</note>), there takes place an increase of the day; while in the opposite case a decrease takes place.—From what has been explained, the remaining points (not expressly referred to) may be understood.

27. The fundamental arrangements of all instruments depend on strings, water and bits of earth. By means of them one may make on a level surface instruments shaped like a tortoise, a man and so on.

28. The teacher is to communicate those things (only) to a pupil of steadfast mind; and the pupil after having learned them is to make his mechanical contrivances in such a way as to keep them secret from his own son even. <note>This reflects the historical tradition of keeping scientific and mechanical "wonders" as guarded, esoteric knowledge.</note>

> 29. 30. Let the astronomer observe the position of the moon in a given locality, at that time when, according to calculation, full moon takes place on the prime meridian on the equator <note>The "prime meridian" here refers to the line passing through Ujjain and Lanka, the zero-point for Indian longitude</note>. Let him divide the observed difference of degrees in the manner of the <term>tithi</term> <note>tithi: a lunar day, or 1/30th of a lunar month, calculated by the angular distance between the sun and moon</note>. The resulting time is to be deducted from the time of full moon at <term>Laṅkâ</term> <note>Laṅkâ: the mythical city on the equator used as the reference point for the prime meridian</note> in the case of the degrees being more, and to be added in the case of their being less. Let him increase the result by the time of <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>ascensional difference: the difference between the right ascension of a celestial body and its oblique ascension; essentially a correction for the observer's latitude</note>, when the sun is in the six signs beginning with Aries, and diminish it by the same, when the sun is in the six signs beginning with Libra. In this way he ascertains the difference in longitude.

While there can be hardly any doubt about the purport of the above stanzas, their wording and construction are obscure, and the translation therefore merely aims at rendering the general sense.—The rule teaches how to ascertain the longitude of a given place by an observation of the moon at the hour when—according to astronomical calculation—full moon takes place at <term>Laṅkâ</term>. We are directed to find at that time the degrees of interval between the moon and the sun, according to the method taught above in stanza 12; if those degrees are more than 180, the given locality is to the west of the prime meridian; if less, it is to the east. From the degrees of interval the difference of longitude in time is calculated proportionally; and finally an allowance made for the <term>ascensional difference</term>.

> 31. The sixtieth part of so much water as within a <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>nychthemeron: a full period of 24 hours, including one day and one night</note> escapes from a vessel through a given aperture fixes the duration of one <term>nâḍikâ</term> <note>nâḍikâ: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes, or 1/60th of a day</note>; or else one hundred and eighty respirations of a man.

> 32. Make a copper vessel shaped like the half of a jar, and pierce a hole in its bottom. Place it in a basin filled with pure water; when it has become full of water, a <term>nâḍikâ</term> has elapsed. On account of the smallness of the bottom <note>The translator notes this phrase is unclear in the original</note>, the hole has to be made in such a way that sixty immersions take place in one <term>nychthemeron</term>.—Or else a <term>nâḍikâ</term> may be measured by the time in which sixty <term>Ślokas</term> <note>Ślokas: a specific meter of Sanskrit verse</note>, each consisting of sixty long syllables, can be read out.

The above three stanzas are clear, with the exception of one line in 32 which is not very perspicuously expressed.—It will be observed that stanza 32 consists of 60 long syllables, and thus constitutes a <term>Śloka</term> such as—according to <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>Varâha Mihira: a 6th-century Indian astronomer and mathematician</note>—may be recited in the sixtieth part of a <term>nâḍikâ</term>.

> 33. Having ascertained the latitude of the moon and observed the distance of the moon from the fixed star, and having made the requisite calculations one may then declare the conjunction of the moon with the star.

**34.** The junction-star <note>original: "yogatârâ"; the principal star of a lunar mansion used for calculating conjunctions</note> of the Pleiades <note>original: "krittikâ"</note> is located at the end of the sixth degree of its lunar mansion, and three and a half cubits <note>original: "hastas"; a unit of measure approximately 18-24 inches, here used as an angular measurement</note> to the north of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>; that of Aldebaran <note>original: "Rohinî"</note> is at the end of the eighth degree, and five and a half cubits to the south of the ecliptic.

**35.** The two stars of Castor and Pollux <note>original: "Punarvasu"</note> are at the eighth degree, and to the north and south of the ecliptic at an interval of eight cubits; the star of the Beehive Cluster <note>original: "Pushya"</note> is at the fourth degree, three and a half cubits to the north.

**36.** Of the Hydra <note>original: "Aśleshâ"</note> the southern star is at the first degree, one cubit south of the ecliptic; the northern star is positioned likewise. Of Regulus <note>original: "Maghâ"</note> the conjunction with the moon takes place in its own field <insert>that is, in the ecliptic</insert>, at the sixth degree of the lunar mansion.

**37.** Of Spica <note>original: "Chitrâ"</note> the junction-star is at seven and a half degrees, three cubits to the south.—The finger-breadths <note>original: "aṅgulis"; a smaller unit of measure</note> are to be calculated from the centre of the moon.

**38.** Deduct seventeen from the latitude of the star, multiply the remainder by fifteen, and take its thirty-fourth part; the result is to be taken as the measure in finger-breadths. The time of conjunction is to be calculated from the difference of the moon's daily motion.

The above stanzas contain the statement of the longitudes and latitudes of the so-called junction-stars of some lunar mansions <note>original: "nakshatras"</note>. The longitude has to be reckoned from the beginning of each lunar mansion, <italic>i. e.</italic>, the twenty-seventh part of the ecliptic. The latitudes are expressed in finger-breadths of which twenty-four go to one cubit, while the diameter of the moon—whose mean value is thirty-four minutes—is divided into fifteen finger-breadths. In order to express the distance of the star from the edge of the moon in finger-breadths, seventeen <insert>the moon's radius</insert> is deducted from the distance in minutes (taken from the moon's centre), and the remainder turned into finger-breadths by means of the proportion supplied by the dimensions of the moon.

**39.** Multiply twenty-five by half the equinoctial shadow <note>the shadow cast by a vertical rod at noon on the day of the equinox</note>; take the corresponding arc to which fifteen is to be added, multiply by ten, and add twenty-one times the equinoctial shadow; the result is the time in small units <note>original: "vinâḍikâs"; a unit of time equal to 24 seconds</note>.

## A rule for calculating the time of the heliacal rising <note>The first time a star becomes visible in the dawn sky after a period of being hidden by the sun's light.</note> of Agastya

->Fig. 13.<-

( <term>Canopus</term> ) in a given latitude. In order to explain its rationale, we at first apply the longitude and latitude of <term>Agastya</term> given in the modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to roughly the 4th-5th century CE.</note>, <term>namely</term> <note>original: "viz."</note> 90° longitude and 80° southern latitude. Let H H' be the horizon, P the pole of the equator, E E' an arc of the equator, A L an arc of the Ecliptic, C the place of <term>Canopus</term> on the horizon, G the last point of <term>Gemini</term> (on first point of <term>Cancer</term>) which has the same longitude as <term>Canopus</term>, <term>namely</term> 90°; P G C' C a circle of declination (on which according to Hindu practice the latitude is measured). The segment C' S' of the equator represents the time which <term>Canopus</term> must rise before the sun in order to be visible in the morning. It divides itself into three parts, <term>namely</term>, C' B representing the ascensional difference <note>The difference between the time of rising of a celestial body and the time it would rise if it were on the celestial equator.</note> of <term>Agastya</term>, B G'' representing the ascensional difference of the last point of <term>Gemini</term>, and G'' S' representing the amount to which the sun must be below the horizon in order that a star may be visible at its rising. This latter amount the Hindus

<summary>This page describes the mathematical and geometric principles used in Indian astronomy to calculate the heliacal rising of the star Agastya (Canopus). always measure on the ecliptic (instead of measuring it, as would be proper, on a vertical circle). The modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to roughly the 4th-6th century CE.</note> assumes it to be equal to 12°; but <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian polymath and astronomer who authored the Pañca-siddhāntikā.</note>—as we understand him—to 15°. In order to find BG'' we make use of the statement made above in III. 11 *viz.*, that at the end of Gemini the ascensional difference amounts to 21 <term>palas</term> <note>A unit of time; 1 pala equals 24 seconds.</note> in those places where the equinoctial shadow <note>The length of a shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox.</note> is equal to one. We thus obtain the following expression

->Required ascensional difference = 21 x equinoctial shadow<-

Dividing this result by ten we obtain the degrees corresponding to the <term>palas</term> (60 <term>palas</term> going to one <term>nâdikâ</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> which answers to 6 degrees).

In order, finally, to determine C' B, at first ascertain the value of D C, the so-called earth-sine (<term>kujyâ</term>) <note>A technical term in Indian astronomy representing the distance between the rising-setting line and the diurnal circle's center.</note> of Canopus, by means of the proportion

->12 : equinoctial shadow = sine of declination of Canopus : earth-sine<-

If, as said above, CG (=latitude of Canopus) is supposed equal to 80°, the declination of Canopus amounts to 56° (for C' G = declination of last point of Gemini = inclination of Ecliptic = 24°); and we thus have

->Earth-sine = (equinoctial shadow x sine 56°) / 12 = (equinoctial shadow x 99) / 12<-

To turn the earth-sine so found into the sine of ascensional difference, we employ the proportion

->Cosine of declination : earth-sine = Radius : sine of ascensional difference<-

->$\therefore$ Sine of ascensional difference = (equinoctial shadow x 99 x 120) / (12 x cosine of declination)<-

->= (equinoctial shadow x 99 x 120) / (12 x 67) (67 = sine 34° = cosine 56°)<-

->= (equinoctial shadow x 990) / 67 = (1980 x equinoctial shadow) / (67 x 2) =<-

->((1980 / 67) x equinoctial shadow) / 2 = (30 x equinoctial shadow) / 2<-

Instead of this value of C' B the text however has (25 x equinoctial shadow) / 2, where-from it appears that <term>Varâha Mihira</term> estimated the latitude of Canopus at less than the modern <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> does. By an easy inverse calculation we find that a latitude of 75° 30' satisfies the expression given in the text.

# CHAPTER XV.

---

## THE SECRETS OF ASTRONOMY.

---

1. Following those who possess the knowledge of the relative positions of the sun, moon, stars, and earth, I give the following explanations:—An eclipse of the sun takes place constantly; however, in consequence of the difference of position, it only becomes visible in certain localities.

2. In the minds of those who are ignorant of these relative positions, knowledge may be engendered, just as—<note>The translator refers the reader to the original Sanskrit Commentary for the completion of this analogy.</note>

3. In those places where the sun is covered by the moon because of a straight line drawn from the eye to the sun <gloss>that is, for those locations where the moon sits directly in the line of sight</gloss> an eclipse of the sun takes place; and such an event occurs every day somewhere in space.

4. The Fathers <note>The "Fathers" or *Pitris* are ancestral spirits who, in Vedic cosmology, are believed to reside on the moon.</note> dwelling on the moon see the sun, if once obscured, for a half-month in that condition; and they also see him non-obscured for a half-month. The middle of the eclipse is at the full moon.

The text of this stanza appears to be correct, but its meaning is obscure to us. Might we, perhaps, have to understand by the "eclipse" of the sun referred to merely his being invisible for a lunar half-month to those beings which live on the side of the moon turned away from the earth? But a statement of this nature would have its proper place, not in the present chapter, but in the <term>trailokya-samsthâna</term> <gloss>The Structure of the Triple World</gloss>; and such a statement is in fact actually made there (xiv. 38). Moreover, the terms <term>grasta</term> <gloss>seized or swallowed</gloss> and <term>graha</term> <gloss>the seizer, referring to an eclipse</gloss> would appear to be rather misapplied in such a connection.

5. The beings that live on <term>Meru</term> <gloss>The sacred five-peaked mountain considered to be the center of all the physical, metaphysical, and spiritual universes</gloss> or near Meru never see an eclipse of the sun, owing to the fact of the sun and moon being, for them, not high above the horizon.

<summary>This chapter explains the mechanics of solar eclipses, noting that they occur continuously in space but are only visible from specific vantage points, including the perspective of ancestral spirits on the moon.</summary>

6. Those living on <term>Meru</term> <note>In Hindu cosmology, the sacred mountain at the center of the world, representing the North Pole.</note> or close to it never see the sun and moon in a straight line; therefore, they always see the two bodies separated by an interval.

Of these two stanzas also the text seems to be correct. But in that case, their contents are incomprehensible.

7. When an eclipse takes place at sunrise or sunset, then the sun stands low for us <note>The author is likely referring to the visual altitude above the horizon.</note> and the moon high; the latter, therefore, becomes the cause of the obscuration of the sun.

8. If, for us, an eclipse of the sun takes place at sunrise, it does not take place at the same moment for those for whom the sun is about to set, nor for those for whom it is midday.

9. For, on one and the same day, the eclipse may be past for those for whom it is sunrise, future—to the extent of two <term>kshaṇas</term> <note>A traditional unit of time; in this context, roughly equivalent to 48 minutes or a "moment."</note>—for those for whom it is sunset, and actually occurring for those for whom it is midday.

10. In the <term>Samhitâ</term> <note>A compendium or collection of knowledge, likely referring to the Brihat Samhita.</note>, in the beginning of the chapter on <term>Râhu's</term> <note>The shadow demon or lunar node responsible for eclipses in Vedic mythology.</note> course, I have fully explained to what causes, apart from <term>Râhu</term>, solar and lunar eclipses are due.

Stanza 7 is not fully intelligible. Stanzas 8 and 9 refer to the effect of <term>parallax</term> <note>The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> in accelerating or retarding the moment of an eclipse of the sun.

11. For <term>Meru</term> there exists no distinction of directions, because there the eastern direction is not indicated by the sun; for as long as the sun is risen there, he revolves round the earth along the horizon.

12. Should it be said that the distinction of the eastern direction may be based on the observation of the first small part of the sun when he rises; we reply that after he has moved for half a year above the horizon, he again sets at the same point; does that point then indicate the eastern or the western direction?

13. For those who live on <term>Meru</term>, the state of it being day depends on the sun's <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note>, not, as for us, on his daily revolution. For us, sixty <term>nâḍikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 nâḍikâs make a full 24-hour day.</note> constitute a *day-and-night* <note>original: "nychthemeron," a Greek term for a 24-hour period.</note>, while a year is a *day-and-night* of the gods.

14. Each year comprises a day and a night of the gods and the Asuras <note>In Hindu cosmology, Asuras are often described as the rivals or "demons" to the Devas (gods)</note>, it being day for the former while it is night for the latter, and vice versa. A full day and night <note>original: "nychthemeron"</note> of the fathers <note>The Pitris, or ancestral spirits</note> (whose abode is the moon) lasts one month, while one of men comprises sixty <term>nâdikâs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>.

15. The gods see the sun moving at a distance (from the horizon), equal to so much as he rises above the horizon in two <term>muhûrtas</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 48 minutes</note>; they never see him higher up.

The gods on Meru <note>The sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Hindu cosmology</note> never see the sun higher above the horizon than 24 degrees (to which height he rises when at the end of Gemini). The sun performing 360 degrees in thirty <term>muhûrtas</term> passes through 24 degrees in two <term>muhûrtas</term>.

16. The succession of the Lords of hours and days is not the same on Meru as with us; because the full day and night there does not consist of sixty <term>nâdikâs</term>.

17. The rule about the days of the week is not everywhere the same. As no (decisive) reason can be assigned for it, the astronomers disagree concerning this point.

18. 19. The day of the week is to be determined from the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</note>; the <term>ahargaṇa</term> itself depends on connection with place and time. According to the teaching of Lâṭâchârya the <term>ahargaṇa</term> is to be reckoned from sunset at Yavanapura <note>Literally "City of the Greeks," likely Alexandria or a similar western city</note>; according to Simhâchârya from sunrise at Laṅkâ <note>The mythical city on the equator used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note>; while it is to be reckoned from the moment when ten <term>muhûrtas</term> of the night of the Yavanas <note>The Greeks or Westerners</note> have passed, according to their teacher <note>original: "guru"</note> (*i. e.* the teacher—or master—of the Yavanas).

20. Âryabhaṭa <note>A famous 5th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> maintains that the beginning of the day is to be reckoned from midnight at Laṅkâ; and the same teacher again says that the day begins from sunrise at Laṅkâ.

21. If, there having been applied the correction for difference of meridian, the result does not agree with the actual circumstances of a given place; the following statement (at any rate) as to the correspondence of time has been made by the same teachers (mentioned above), in agreement with traditional science.

22. The sun, when rising in the <term>Bhâratavarsha</term><note>The Indian subcontinent in ancient cosmology</note>, at the same time makes midday in the region of the <term>Bhadrâśvas</term><note>The eastern continent</note>, sunset in that of the <term>Kurus</term><note>The northern continent</note>, and midnight in <term>Ketumâla</term><note>The western continent</note>.

24. The intercalary months, the omitted lunar days, the days of the planets, the lunar days, the days, Aries, the sun, the moon, the half-years, the seasons, the motions of the stars, and the nights; all of them begin together at the beginning of the <term>yuga</term><note>A vast cosmic cycle of time</note>.

25. The difference in longitude when taken from the Romaka-country is not the same as when taken from <term>Yavanapura</term><note>The "City of the Greeks," likely Alexandria or a similar western astronomical center</note>; and there is a difference between reckoning the beginning of the day from midnight or from sunrise at Lankâ.

26. And if we determine the Lord of each day by counting the <term>ahargana</term><note>The total number of elapsed days since the start of a cosmic epoch</note> from the moment when the sun has half set, we have in our favour neither any traditional authority nor reasoning of any kind.

27. Owing to the various positions of the sun, it is twilight in one place, day in another place, and night in another place. A small difference of place thus suffices to entangle the question as to who is the Lord of the day.

28. The question as to the <term>horâs</term><note>Planetary hours; the origin of the word "hour"</note> is in the same predicament; for the first hour belongs to the Lord of the day. If, then, the latter is not fully determined, how can the Lord of the hour be so?

29. Ordinary people, as a rule, proceed in their business according to the days of the week as known from tradition, without reflecting on such questions. The learned, on the other hand, declare such assumptions to be right as result in the proper determination of the true lunar day.

# CHAPTER XVI.

---

## THE MEAN MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS, ACCORDING TO THE SÛRYA SIDDHÂNTA.

---

1. The determination of the (mean places of the) smaller planets for midnight at <term>Avanti</term> <note>Modern Ujjain, the prime meridian of ancient Indian astronomy</note> is, according to the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, as follows.--- Mercury and Venus have the same motion as the mean sun.

2. For Jupiter multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The number of elapsed days since the beginning of a specific epoch</note> by 100, and divide by 433232. For Mars multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> by one, and divide by 687.

3. For Saturn multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> by 1000, and divide by 10766066. The quotients are the entire revolutions; from the remainders the mean places of the planets are ascertained in signs, degrees and so on.

4. For each revolution of Jupiter ten <term>tatparas</term> (<gloss>i. e., sixtieth parts of seconds</gloss>) have to be deducted. Fourteen <term>tatparas</term> have to be added for each revolution of Mars; five have to be deducted for each revolution of Saturn.

5. Four signs, two degrees, twenty-eight minutes and forty-nine seconds have to be added to the mean place of Saturn.

6. Eight degrees, six minutes and twenty seconds constitute the additive quantity for Jupiter. For Mars that quantity amounts to two signs, fifteen degrees and thirty-five minutes.

7. For the <term>Sîghra</term> <note>The "fast" motion or conjunction; used to calculate the anomaly of the inner planets</note> of Mercury multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> by 100, and divide by 8797. Add the product of the (accomplished) revolutions and four and a half <term>tatparas</term>.

8. For the <term>Sîghra</term> of Venus multiply the <term>ahargaṇa</term> by 10, and divide by 2247. Add ten and a half seconds, multiplied by the revolutions.

<summary>This chapter details the mathematical formulas and constants used in the Sûrya Siddhânta to calculate the mean positions of the five visible planets. It provides specific divisors for orbital periods and corrective factors (tatparas) to ensure precision over long time scales.</summary>
<keywords>Sûrya Siddhânta, Avanti, ahargaṇa, tatparas, Sîghra, mean motions, planetary calculation, Hindu astronomy, Indian mathematics, orbital periods</keywords>

--- Page 316 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of planetary mean motions, specifically focusing on the corrections and epochal constants (kshepa) for Mercury and Venus, and summarizing the methodology for all planets.</meta>

9. Twenty-eight degrees of Leo <note>that is, four signs plus twenty-eight degrees</note> and seventeen minutes are the additive quantity for the <term>Śîghra</term> <note>the "fast" anomaly or the conjunction of a planet</note> of Budha <note>Mercury</note>. From the <term>Śîghra</term> of Venus, 332,961 seconds are to be deducted.

The above nine stanzas contain rules for calculating the mean places of the planets. The complete calculation for each planet is subdivided into three distinct operations. We are at first taught how to find the mean place by means of a rough calculation resting on the assumption that the planet performs an integral number of revolutions within an integral number of <term>sâvana</term> <note>civil days, measured from sunrise to sunrise</note> days. Next, we are informed how to make up for the mistake involved in the above assumption. And finally, we are told what quantity has to be added to—or deducted from—the result found by means of the previous two processes, in order to enable us to start in our calculation, not from the beginning of the <term>kalpa</term> <note>a vast cosmic period of 4.32 billion years</note> or <term>yuga</term> <note>an age or epoch</note>, but from the epoch of the <term>karaṇa</term> <note>the specific date for which the astronomical handbook is calculated</note>.

The process by means of which we evolve from the rules of the text that duration of the sidereal revolutions of the planets which was assumed by Varâha Mihira’s <note>a 6th-century Indian astronomer</note> Sûrya Siddhânta <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note> is simple, and the same for all planets. We at first calculate the revolutions according to the approximative rules given in stanzas 1–3, and the first halves of stanzas 7 and 8. We thereupon deduce—from the corrections stated in stanza 4 and the second halves of 7 and 8—the amount of the modifications to be applied to the rough results found previously. We thus obtain the following numbers of revolutions within one <term>mahâyuga</term> <note>a "great age" of 4,320,000 years</note> of 1,577,917,800 days.

| Planet | Revolutions |
| :--- | :--- |
| Saturn | 146,564 |
| Jupiter | 364,220 |
| Mars | 2,296,824 |
| Venus | 7,022,388 |
| Mercury | 17,937,000 |

The correctness of these figures we are finally enabled to test by means of the <term>kshepa-quantities</term> <note>additive constants used to adjust a calculation to a specific starting epoch</note> stated in the fifth, sixth and ninth stanzas. For if—as we had done before in the case of the sun and the moon—we calculate, on the ground of the number of revolutions stated above, the mean positions of the planets at the epoch of the <term>karaṇa</term>, we find that they agree down to seconds with the mentioned <term>kshepa-quantities</term>. As in the case of sun and moon, the calculation has to be made from the beginning, not of the <term>mahâyuga</term>, but of the <term>kalpa</term>.

It explains the three-step process used to calculate mean planetary positions starting from a specific historical epoch rather than the beginning of time.</summary>

10. Seventeen seconds are to be added for each year to the mean place <note>The "mean place" refers to the calculated average position of a planet in its orbit, assuming a constant speed.</note> of Mars; ten to be deducted from that of Jupiter; seven and a half to be added to that of Saturn.

11. Forty-five are to be deducted from that of Venus; one hundred and twenty to be added to that of Mercury. Fourteen hundred seconds are to be deducted from the mean place of Jupiter.

These two stanzas state certain corrections to be applied to the mean places of the planets as found by means of the preceding rules. No other reason for those corrections appears to be assignable, but that they tended to effect an agreement between the rules of the <term>Sûrya Siddhânta</term> <note>The "Sun Treatise," one of the most significant early Sanskrit texts on Indian astronomy.</note> and the observations made by <term>Varâha Mihira</term> <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath who preserved much of the ancient astronomical knowledge.</note> or the astronomers of his time.

# CHAPTER XVII.

---

### THE TRUE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS.

---

1. For the other planets, starting with Mars, the Sun is considered the so-called <term>Śîghra</term> <note>The "Fast-moving" point or apex of conjunction, which in Indian astronomy represents the orbital motion of the Earth relative to the planets</note>.—Thirty-five, fourteen, sixteen, seven, and thirty—each multiplied by two—are the degrees of the epicycles of the Apsis <note>The Manda-paridhi, or the epicycle used to account for the planet's elliptical eccentricity</note>;

2. Six, eleven, eight, four, and twelve—each figure multiplied by twenty, with ten being deducted in the case of Mars—are the degrees of the longitude of the <term>Mandochchas</term> <note>The Apogees, or the points in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note> of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.

We therefore have the following epicycles and longitudes of the apogees of the five planets:

| | Mars. | Mercury. | Jupiter. | Venus. | Saturn. |
|----------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Degrees of epicycle... | 70 | 28 | 32 | 14 | 60 |
| Longitude of Apogee | 110 | 220 | 160 | 80 | 240 |

3. The degrees of the epicycles of the conjunction (<term>śîghraparidhi</term> <note>The epicycle used to account for the planet's anomaly relative to the Sun</note>) of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are 234, 132, 72, 260, and 40 respectively.

4. If, after the mean planet's position is subtracted from the <term>Śîghra</term>, the remainder is within three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, the sines of those parts which have been passed through and those yet to be passed through are the base sine (<term>bhuja</term> <note>The sine of the arc</note>) and the perpendicular sine (<term>koṭi</term> <note>The cosine of the arc</note>). If the remainder exceeds three signs, it is to be subtracted from six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, and after that the same method is to be followed.

5. The <term>sine of the base</term> <note>original: "bhujajyâ"</note> and <term>sine of the perpendicular</term> <note>original: "koṭijyâ"</note> found according to stanza 4 are to be multiplied by the degrees of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to represent planetary orbits</note> of the planet, and divided by 360; the results are those two sines reduced to the terms of the epicycle; namely, the so-called <term>result of the base-sine</term> <note>original: "bhujajyâ phala"</note> and <term>result of the perpendicular-sine</term> <note>original: "koṭijyâ phala"</note>. The result of the perpendicular is to be added to the Radius in the half circle beginning with Capricorn, and to be deducted in the half circle beginning with Cancer.

6. Take the square root of the sum of the squares of the Radius so increased or decreased and the result of the base, and divide thereby the result of the base multiplied by 120. Half of the corresponding arc is to be deducted from the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "mandochcha"; the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> (if the anomaly is in the half orbit beginning with Aries), and to be added to it (in the half orbit beginning with Libra).

->A rule for finding the equation of the conjunction which in all points agrees with that given in the modern *Sûrya Siddhânta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy</note>.—By half the equation found the place of the apogee is to be corrected, and the <term>equation of the center</term> <note>original: "manda equation"</note> to be calculated from the new place.<-

7. The apogee, having thus been made true, is deducted from the mean planet, and the <term>sine of the base</term> <note>original: "bâhu"</note> (of the resulting arc) is reduced to terms of the epicycle (by being multiplied by the degrees of the epicycle, and divided by 360); the corresponding arc is either added to the apogee (in the half orbit beginning with Aries), or deducted from it (in the half orbit beginning with Libra).

8. (The apogee so corrected) is again to be deducted from the mean planet, the corresponding sine is to be taken and to be reduced to terms of the epicycle, and the corresponding arc to be added to (in the half orbit beginning with Aries)—or deducted from (in the half orbit beginning with Libra)—the mean planet.

9. The planets, having thus been made what is called ‘true-mean’ (the mean planet having been made true as far as the apogee is concerned), are to be deducted from their <term>conjunctions</term> <note>original: "śîghrochchas"; the fast apogee or point of conjunction</note>. They are then to be treated according to the former method (*i. e.*, the equation of the conjunction is to be found as taught above); and, in the former way, the arc is to be added to (in the half orbit beginning with Aries)—or to be deducted from (in the half orbit beginning with Libra)—the true-mean planet.

<summary>This page details the iterative trigonometric calculations required to correct a planet's mean position to its "true-mean" position using the Sûrya Siddhânta method. It explains how to apply the results of the base and perpendicular sines to adjust the apogee and account for orbital anomalies.</summary>

10. In this manner the true position of all planets is ascertained. In the case of Mercury, however, the <term>mandochcha</term><note>The point of slowest motion or the apogee of the planet's slow cycle.</note> of the sun is to be deducted from Mercury's <term>śîghrochcha</term><note>The "fast apogee," representing the sun's mean position which governs the movement of inner planets.</note>; the base <term>sine</term><note>A trigonometric function used here to calculate the displacement of a planet from its mean position.</note> (of the remainder) is to be reduced to terms of the sun's <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain the complex orbits of planets.</note> (by being multiplied by the degrees of the sun's epicycle, and divided by 360), and the corresponding arc—as Mercury's equation—to be added to, or deducted from, Mercury (according as the anomaly found by deducting the sun's mandochcha from Mercury's śîghrochcha lies in the half orbit beginning with Aries or in that beginning with Libra).

11. In Venus' case sixty-seven minutes have to be deducted from the planet's longitude, after it has been made true (in the manner taught before).——The time when a planet becomes <term>retrograde</term><note>Appearing to move backward in the sky relative to the stars.</note> has to be ascertained from the difference of its motion.

12. The degrees of the distance from the sun at which the true planets become visible are 12 for the moon, 19 for Mars, 17 for Mercury, 13 for Jupiter, 11 for Venus, 15 for Saturn.

13. Take the <term>sine</term> of the interval between the planet made true with regard to the <term>apogee</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> (and the <term>node</term><note>The point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic or the sun's path.</note>), and add to it its eighth part, in the case of Mars, Jupiter and Saturn; the <term>latitude</term><note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the planet, which is either southern or northern, is found from that difference. Another latitude is found by applying the conjunction (in the case of Venus and Mercury).

14. In the case of Jupiter, Mars and Venus (the sine mentioned above) is to be lessened by its fourth part; while in the case of Mercury and Saturn it is merely to be increased by its eighth part. The sine is then to be multiplied by Radius, and divided by the hypothenuse; the result is the latitude whose direction (whether north or south) depends on that of the interval (between node and planet).

->The above two stanzas teach how to calculate the latitude of the planets.<-

The latitude is made to depend, in the case of the superior planets <note>Planets further from the sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, on the distance of the true planet (*i. e.*, the true place of the planet with regard to the apogee) from the node; in the case of the inferior planets <note>Planets closer to the sun than Earth: Mercury and Venus.</note> on the distance of the node from the <term>Sîghra</term><note>The "fast" point of the planet, often identified with the sun's position in these calculations.</note> of the planet, *i. e.*, the place of the sun. The latitude for any given moment is then calculated by means of a proportion basing on the assumed amount of the greatest latitude of each planet.

These amounts have to be inferred from the indirect statements of the text, which directs us to add, in the case of <term>Mercury</term> <note>The innermost planet, associated with rapid motion</note> and <term>Saturn</term> <note>The outermost known planet in this system</note>, one eighth to the <term>sine</term> <note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the side opposite an angle to the hypotenuse</note> of the interval between <term>node</term> <note>The point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> and <term>planet</term> (or <term>node</term> and <term>conjunction</term>), and, in the case of the three other planets, to lessen that sum by its fourth part. We thus have, for <term>Mercury</term> and <term>Saturn</term>, the following formula

->Latitude = 9 × sine of the interval / 8 ,<-

->and, for the three other planets,<-

->Latitude = 9 × sine of the interval / 8 — 9 × sine of the interval / 8 × 4 .<-

If we substitute 120 = <term>Radius</term> <note>The standard length used in these trigonometric calculations, often set to 120 units in ancient and medieval astronomy</note> for the 8 forming the <term>divisor</term>, we have to substitute 135 for the 9 of the <term>numerator</term>; whence we conclude that the greatest <term>latitude</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</note> of <term>Mercury</term> and <term>Saturn</term> is assumed to amount to 135'. And taking into account the subtraction of one-fourth part, which is prescribed for the three other planets, we find that their greatest <term>latitude</term> is supposed to amount to 121'.

1. Deduct from the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>The total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a given date.</note> 147, and divide by 584; the quotient indicates the risings of Venus. The portion passed through by Venus during that time is five degrees of Scorpio (that is, seven signs plus five degrees) together with the third part of a degree.

2. Having proceeded, by means of the degrees of time, for twenty-six days, Venus goes to its rising in the west. Add to the days the eleventh part of the risings, and from that result calculate the motions.

3. In three periods of sixty days each, Venus passes through seventy degrees, increased respectively by four, three, and two; thereupon in eighty-five days through seventy-seven degrees; then in three days through one and a quarter degree.

Then it sets; it passes thereupon in fifty-six days through fifteen degrees and becomes <term>niraṃśa</term> <note>literally "without degrees," referring to a planet being in conjunction with the sun and thus invisible</note>.

70. Lessen the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <note>the count of elapsed days since the beginning of a specific epoch</note> by 14,681, multiply by 29, and divide by 3,312; divide the remainder by the multiplier (29); you thus obtain the days of Mercury.

71. Mercury, having fallen behind the sun by twelve degrees—which takes place within ten days—rises in the east; thereupon he falls behind by ten degrees in fourteen days. Advancing thereupon nine degrees within eighteen days he sets, and again rises in the west, having advanced thirteen degrees within thirty days.

72. Then he advances nine degrees within eighteen days, and then, falling behind eight degrees within sixteen days, he sets in the west. After that, falling behind nine degrees in eight days, he again becomes <term>niraṃśa</term>.

73. Deduct from the <term>ahargaṇa</term> <unclear>illegible value</unclear>, multiply by seven, and divide by 2,752. Divide the remainder by seven; the result is the number of days for Jupiter, calculated from the <term>niraṃśa</term> position.

74. These days are to be counted from the position of the sun. Having fallen back twelve degrees within sixteen days, Jupiter rises in the east. He then passes through forty-four degrees within fifty-four days; through sixty-four degrees in seventy days.

75. Through one hundred and twenty degrees in one hundred and nine days; through seventy-six degrees in eighty-eight days; through thirty-two degrees in forty days. Thereupon he sets, and then passes in sixteen days through twelve degrees, at which point he becomes <term>niraṃśa</term>.

76. Lessen the <term>ahargaṇa</term> by 11,122, multiply by two, and divide by 1,151. Divide the remainder by two. The result is the number of days for Venus, counted from the <term>niraṃśa</term> position.

77. Falling behind nine degrees within five days, Venus rises in the east. It then falls behind twenty-one degrees within fifteen days; after that, fifteen degrees within two hundred and eight days; after that, it advances five degrees <note>original text is uncertain</note> within twelve days <note>original text is uncertain</note>, and sets.

78. Then it advances ten degrees within forty-eight (?) days, and becomes <term>degree-less<note>original: *niramśa*; refers to a planet having no longitudinal difference from the sun, i.e., in exact conjunction</note></term>. After that it moves in the opposite direction, and rises in the west within the time which it had taken to go to the <term>degree-less</term> position (?); and again moving in the opposite direction sets (in the west).

79. Lessen (the <term>count of days<note>original: *ahargaṇa*; the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch used in Indian astronomy</note></term>) by 16518 (?), multiply by three and multiply by 1118. Divide (the remainder) by three. (The result are the days since the last conjunction) of Saturn. In eighteen days he falls behind the sun sixteen and a half degrees, and then rises in the east.

80. Then he falls back ninety and a half degrees within ninety-eight days; then thirteen degrees within fourteen days. Then one hundred and twenty degrees within one hundred and thirteen days; then ninety-one degrees within ninety-eight days.

81. Then in thirteen days twelve degrees and a half. Then he sets, and, passing within twenty-one days through sixteen and a half degrees, he becomes <term>degree-less</term>, being always behind the sun.
